Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ [Ghafir: 17] ﴿And warn them of the Approaching Day, when hearts will be at the throats, choking with grief. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor who will be obeyed.﴾ [Ghafir: 18] ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the chests conceal.﴾ [Ghafir: 19] ﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they invoke besides Him do not judge anything. Indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ [Ghafir: 20] ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength and in traces left upon the earth, yet Allah seized them for their sins, and they had no protector against Allah.﴾ [Ghafir: 21] ﴿That is because their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so Allah seized them. Indeed He is Strong, Severe in punishment.﴾ [Ghafir: 22] ﴿And We sent Moses with Our signs and clear authority﴾ [Ghafir: 23] ﴿to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun. They said: "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ [Ghafir: 24] ﴿When he brought them the truth from Us, they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ [Ghafir: 25] ﴿Pharaoh said: "Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land."﴾ [Ghafir: 26] ﴿Moses said: "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ [Ghafir: 27] ﴿A believing man from Pharaoh's family, who was concealing his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? If he is a liar, his lie will fall upon him; but if he is truthful, some of what he threatens you with will befall you. Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar.﴾ [Ghafir: 28] ﴿O my people, yours is the kingdom today, dominant in the land. But who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?" Pharaoh said: "I only show you what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir: 29] ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ [Ghafir: 30] ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for His servants.﴾ [Ghafir: 31] ﴿O my people, I fear for you the Day of Calling Out﴾ [Ghafir: 32] ﴿the day you will turn your backs fleeing. You will have no protector from Allah, and whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ [Ghafir: 33] ﴿Yusuf had already brought you clear proofs before, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Then when he died, you said: "Allah will never send a messenger after him." Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.﴾ [Ghafir: 34] (p. 445) ﴿Those who dispute the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them, it is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and of those who believe. Thus Allah seals every heart of an arrogant, tyrannical person.﴾ [Ghafir: 35] ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾ [Ghafir: 36] ﴿the ways to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses. Indeed I think he is a liar." Thus the evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the way. And the plotting of Pharaoh was nothing but ruin.﴾ [Ghafir: 37] ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me, and I will guide you to the path of right conduct.﴾ [Ghafir: 38] ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.﴾ [Ghafir: 39] ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its equivalent, and whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account.﴾ [Ghafir: 40] ﴿O my people, what is wrong with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41] ﴿You invite me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him what I have no knowledge of, while I invite you to the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ [Ghafir: 42] ﴿Undoubtedly, what you invite me to has no call in this world or in the Hereafter, and our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾ [Ghafir: 43] ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed Allah is All-Seeing of the servants.﴾ [Ghafir: 44] ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ [Ghafir: 45] ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day the Hour is established: "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 46] ﴿And when they argue in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed we were following you, so will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?"﴾ [Ghafir: 47] ﴿Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed we are all in it. Indeed Allah has judged between the servants."﴾ [Ghafir: 48] ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 49] ﴿They will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Then call upon them." But the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ [Ghafir: 50] ﴿Indeed We will help Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51] ﴿the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers. For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾ [Ghafir: 52] ﴿And We gave Moses guidance, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book﴾ [Ghafir: 53] ﴿as guidance and a reminder for people of understanding.﴾ [Ghafir: 54] ﴿So be patient; indeed the promise of Allah is true. And ask forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.﴾ [Ghafir: 55] ﴿Indeed those who dispute the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them, there is nothing in their chests but pride, which they will never attain. So seek refuge in Allah; indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ [Ghafir: 56] ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know.﴾ [Ghafir: 57] ﴿The blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the evildoer. Little do you remember.﴾ [Ghafir: 58] ﴿Indeed the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, but most people do not believe.﴾ [Ghafir: 59] ﴿And your Lord says: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated."﴾ [Ghafir: 60] ﴿It is Allah who made the night for you that you may rest in it, and the day giving sight. Indeed Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most people do not give thanks.﴾ [Ghafir: 61] ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things. There is no god but Him. So how are you turned away?﴾ [Ghafir: 62] ﴿Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah.﴾ [Ghafir: 63] ﴿It is Allah who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a canopy, and shaped you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Ghafir: 64] ﴿He is the Living; there is no god but Him. So invoke Him, making your religion sincerely His. Praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Ghafir: 65] ﴿Say: "Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah, since clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [Ghafir: 66] ﴿It is He who created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then brings you out as a child, then that you may reach your maturity, then that you may become elders, though some of you are taken before that, and that you may reach a specified term, and that perhaps you will reason.﴾ [Ghafir: 67] ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Ghafir: 68] ﴿Have you not seen those who dispute the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ [Ghafir: 69] ﴿Those who denied the Book and what We sent with Our messengers; they will soon know﴾ [Ghafir: 70] ﴿when the shackles and chains are around their necks, and they are dragged﴾ [Ghafir: 71] ﴿in the scalding water, then in the Fire they are burned.﴾ [Ghafir: 72]

Azifa al-shay': it drew near. The poet said:
"The time of departure has drawn near, but our mounts have not yet moved from our saddles, and it is as if it had already come."

Al-tabab: ruin. Al-silsila: the chain, which is well known. Al-sahb: dragging. Sajjara al-tannur: I filled the oven with fire.

Ha, Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing; the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty; there is no god but Him; to Him is the final return. None dispute the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve, so do not let their movement throughout the land deceive you. The people of Noah denied before them, and so did the factions after them; and every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to refute the truth by it, so I seized them, and how was My punishment? Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who disbelieved: that they are the companions of the Fire.

The Hawamim (the seven surahs beginning with Ha-Mim) are all Meccan, according to unanimous agreement. It has been said that some verses of these surahs are Medinan, but Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is weak.

It is related in a hadith: "The Hawamim are the brocade of the Qur'an." And in it: "Whoever wishes to graze in the pleasant gardens of Paradise, let him recite the Hawamim." And in it: "The likeness of the Hawamim in the Qur'an is like the likeness of the striped patterns in garments."

These Hawamim are devoted to admonition, warning, and the paths of the Hereafter, and they are short, so weariness does not affect them.

The connection of the beginning of this surah to the end of al-Zumar is that when He, the Exalted, mentioned the final state of the disbelievers and the believers, He mentioned here "the Forgiver of sin and the Acceptor of repentance," so that this would be an invitation for the disbeliever to faith, and to giving up what he is engaged in, and to show that the door of repentance is open. He mentioned the severity of His punishment, and that the whole world will be subject to it, so that one would refrain from what he is engaged in, and that his return is to his Lord, who will recompense him for what he does of good or evil.

It is read with a fatha on the ha' (Ha, with the vowel fatha), chosen by Abu al-Qasim ibn Jubara al-Hudhali, author of the book al-Kamil fi al-Qur'an. Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra, on the basis of the meeting of two unvocalized consonants. Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa read it with a fatha. It has been explained that the fatha is the vowel of meeting of two unvocalized consonants, and that it was a fatha for the sake of lightness, as in "ayna." Or it is an inflectional vowel, governed by an implied verb whose estimated form is: "Recite Ha Mim."

It is related in a hadith that a Bedouin asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about "Ha Mim," what is it? He said: "They are names and openings of surahs." Shurayh ibn Abi Awfa al-Absi said:
"Ha Mim reminds me, while the spear is shaking, so why did he not recite Ha Mim before the advance?"

Al-Kumayt said:
"We found among you, in the family of Hamim, a sign, which a pious and eloquent one interpreted for us."

They inflected "Hamim" and it was not declined (not given tanwin) because of being a proper noun, or because of being a proper noun together with a resemblance to foreign origin, since fa'il is not among the patterns of Arabic word forms, and this is found only in foreign words, like Qabil and Habil.

It has been mentioned in the hadith that "Ha Mim" is pluralized as "Hawamim," just as "Ta Sin" [al-Naml: 1] is pluralized as "Tawasin."

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 40, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 3):

Ṣāḥib Zād al-Masīr related on the authority of his teacher Ibn Manṣūr, the linguist, that he said: "It is an error to say, 'I recited the Ḥawāmīm' (al-Ḥawāmīm), for it is not from the speech of the Arabs; the correct form is to say, 'I recited Āl Ḥā Mīm.'" And in a ḥadīth of Ibn Mas'ūd: "If you come upon Āl Ḥamīm, you have come upon meadows, soft and fragrant." End of quotation.

If it is established that the Messenger (ﷺ) actually said, "al-Ḥawāmīm," it would be a proof against those who forbid it. But if it was transmitted by meaning, it is possible that it is a distortion by non-Arabs.

Do you not see Ibn Mas'ūd's wording, "If you come upon Āl Ḥamīm," and the verse of al-Kumayt: "We found for you in Āl Ḥāmīm"? The discussion of these disjoined letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭa'ah) has already passed at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Some have added other opinions concerning Ḥā Mīm here, which are transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf). We have dispensed with mentioning them, because they are confused and there is no evidence for the soundness of any of them.

If Ḥā Mīm is the name of the surah, it occupies a position of nominative (raf') as a subject (mubtadaʾ), and "Tanzīl" is then its predicate with "min Allāh" as the predicate. Otherwise, "Tanzīl" is a subject and "min Allāh" is the predicate; or it is the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "this is the tanzīl," and "min Allāh" is related to "tanzīl."

﴿al-ʿAzīz al-ʿAlīm﴾: two attributes indicating intensity in power, dominance, and knowledge, and they are among the attributes of the Essence (ṣifāt al-dhāt).

Al-Zajjāj said: "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" are attributes, and "Shadīd" is an apposition (badal). End of quotation.

He made "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" attributes even though they are active participles (ismā fāʿil), because it is understood from them that they are not intended to denote renewal or restriction to a time, but rather continuity and permanence. Their annexation (iḍāfah) is genuine (maḥḍah), so they are definite, and it is correct for a definite noun to be described by them. "Shadīd al-ʿiqāb" is parsed as an apposition because it belongs to the category of the attributive adjective (al-ṣifah al-mushabbahah), which does not become definite through annexation to a definite noun. Sībawayh has explicitly stated that any noun whose annexation is not genuine, when annexed to a definite noun, may be intended as genuine annexation, and thus becomes definite and can describe a definite noun, except for what belongs to the category of the attributive adjective, which does not become definite.

The author of al-Muqniʿ relates from the Kufans that they permitted, in "ḥusn al-wajh" and similar expressions, that it be an attribute of a definite noun. He said: "That is an error according to the Basrans, because ḥusn al-wajh is indefinite, and when you want to define it, you add al-." 

Abu al-Ḥajjāj al-Aʿlam said: "It is not far-fetched that ḥusn al-wajh be intended as definite, since annexation does not prevent it." End of quotation. This is a leaning toward the Kufan position.

Some have made "Ghāfir al-dhanb" and what follows it appositions, considering that they do not become definite through annexation, as if he had regarded the future time in "Ghāfir" and "Qābil."

It has also been said: "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" are not intended to refer to the past; they become definite through annexation and are attributes, meaning that His decree of forgiveness and acceptance of repentance is in this world.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Al-Zajjāj's making "Shadīd al-ʿiqāb" alone an apposition among the attributes contains a clear flaw. The proper view is to say: since a single indefinite noun is placed among these definite nouns, it indicates that all of them are appositions and not attributes. An example of this is a poem whose feet all come in the form of mustafʿilun; it is judged to be of the rajaz meter. If one foot in it comes as mutafāʿilun, it becomes of the kāmil meter, and there is no flaw in that, because following the established and sound rules is the original principle.

His statement, "it indicates that all of them are appositions," is itself a fault of composition not in Arabic, because he made "fa-qad ādhanat" the answer to "lammā," and it is not from their speech to say: "lammā qāma Zaydun fa-qad qāma ʿAmrun." His statement, "that all of them are appositions," involves repetition of appositions. As for an apposition of an apposition according to those who affirm it, appositions do repeat in it. As for apposition of whole from whole, partial apposition, and apposition of inclusion, I know of no statement from any grammarian permitting or forbidding repetition in them, except that in the words of one of our companions there is something indicating that an apposition is not repeated. That occurs in the verse of the poet:

Then to the son of Umm Unās I ride my she-camel,
ʿAmr, so that my she-camel reaches him or crawls to him.

A king, when the delegations alight at his gate,
they know the sources of his cloud, which do not run dry.

He said: "So 'malik' is an apposition of ʿAmr, an indefinite apposition of a definite noun." He said: "If you say, why is it not an apposition of Ibn Umm Unās? I say: because ʿAmr has already been made an apposition of it, so it is not permissible to make it an apposition again, since it has been dropped." End of quotation.

This indicates that an apposition is not repeated, and the appositive noun is one; and it indicates that an apposition of an apposition is permissible. His statement, "their feet come," is the plural of tif'āl, tif'ūl, tif'ūl, or tif'īl, and none of these patterns is a modified form at the end of the ʿarūḍ; rather its feet are limited, and none of them is among these patterns. So the correct statement would be: "its feet all come as mustafʿilun."

Sībawayh also said: "One may say they are attributes, and the alif and lam were omitted from 'Shadīd al-ʿiqāb' in order to match what precedes and follows it in sound. They have changed much of their speech from its rules for the sake of rhyme (izdiwāj), to the extent that they said: 'mā yaʿrifu suḥādilayhi min ʿanādilayhi,' so they made the dual of what is odd (witr) for the sake of what is even (shaf')." End of quotation.

Moreover, al-Khalīl said, regarding their saying: "It is not fitting for a man like you to do that, and it is fitting for a better man than you to do," that it is intended with the alif and lam, just as "al-jammāʾ al-ghafīr" is intended without the alif and lam. What facilitates this is the absence of confusion and the vagueness of the described noun. End of quotation.

There is no need to believe that the alif and lam were dropped from "Shadīd al-ʿiqāb," abandoning what is fundamental in grammar and likening it to a rare form deviating from the rules, namely the dual of the odd for the even. The Book of God is to be exalted above all of this.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be said that he deliberately made it indefinite and vague, to indicate the extreme severity and that there is nothing more grievous than it, and to increase the warning. It may also be said that this nuance is what motivates choosing apposition over attribute when one follows the path of apposition. End of quotation.

Makkī permitted in "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" apposition, considering them indefinite because of their reference to the future, and attribute, considering them definite because of their reference to the past. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: There is no dispute that "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" are attributes; they are so because they express the sense of permanence and continuity, and likewise "Shadīd al-ʿiqāb" conveys that, because His attributes are exempt from occurrence and renewal. Its meaning is: that His punishment is such that it is severe, and this meaning is always present; it is not described as having come about after it was not. End of quotation.

This is the statement of one who has not studied grammar or examined it, and it entails that "ḥakīm ʿalīm" in His saying "from the presence of One Wise, All-Knowing" (al-Naml: 6) and "malīk muqtadir" in His saying "in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful" (al-Qamar: 55) are definite for the sake of exalting His attributes above occurrence and renewal, and because they are attributes that did not come about after they were not; and that the definition of attributes by al-, and their indefiniteness, would be equal. No beginner in grammar would go this way, let alone one who has written on it and presumed to interpret the Book of God.

From this lengthy discussion it emerges that "Ghāfir al-dhanb" and what is conjoined to it, and "Shadīd al-ʿiqāb," are attributes, because what is conjoined to an attribute is an attribute, and all of them are definite according to what has been established; or they are appositions, because what is conjoined to an apposition is an apposition, given that all of them are indefinite.

Or "Ghāfir" and "Qābil" are attributes, and "Shadīd" is an apposition to the definiteness of those two and the indefiniteness of "Shadīd."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): what is the role of the waw in His saying "wa-Qābil al-tawb"? (I answer): in it is a magnificent nuance, namely the gathering for the sinning repentant one of two mercies: that He accepts his repentance and records it for him as one of the acts of obedience, and that He makes it an erasure of sins, as if he had not sinned; as if He said: "Gatherer of forgiveness and acceptance." End of quotation.

How much this man reaches for and bursts into eloquence! What he has conveyed, that the waw is for gathering, is well known from the apparent principles of grammar.

The author of al-Ghunyān said: "It only conjoined them because they are associated and inseparable, one from the other. And 'Shadīd al-ʿiqāb' was cut off from them and not conjoined, because it stands alone." End of quotation. This is a Muʿtazilī inclination.

The doctrine of the People of the Sunnah is that God may forgive the disobedient, even if he does not repent, except for shirk. "Al-tawb" may be understood as a collective noun like "al-dhanb," or as the plural of tawbah, like bashr and bashrah, or sāʿin and sāʿah. The apparent meaning of His saying "wa-Qābil al-tawb" is that the repentance of the disobedient one, short of disbelief, is certainly accepted, just as the repentance of one who has disbelieved.

Regarding the certainty of accepting the repentance of the disobedient, the People of the Sunnah mention two views.

When God mentioned the severity of His punishment, He followed it with what gives hope in His mercy, namely His saying "Dhī al-Ṭawl," so this came as a threat flanked by two promises. Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-ṭawl is abundance and wealth; Qatādah said: blessings; Ibn Zayd said: power. His saying "ṭawlihi" means the multiplication of the good deeds of His friends and His pardon of their evil deeds.

When He mentioned a portion of His supreme attributes, essential and active, He mentioned that He alone is the Deity, and that to Him is the return on the Day of Assembly. Then He mentioned the state of those who dispute concerning the Book, and followed it with mention of the obedient among His angels and righteous servants, saying: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. Their disputing about them was saying at one time, "magic," at another, "poetry," at another, "tales of the ancients," and at another, "a human only teaches him." So it is disputation by falsehood, and He indicated this by His saying: ﴿and they disputed by falsehood to refute the truth thereby﴾.

Al-Suddī said: "yujādilu" means "yumārī" (contends). Ibn Salām said: "yajḥadu" (denies). Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: it was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith ibn Qays, one of the mockers.

As for what takes place among the people of knowledge regarding reflection upon them, clarifying their meanings, deriving rulings and beliefs from them, and contending with the people of innovation through them, there is abundant reward in that.

Then He forbade the listener to be deceived by the movement of these disbelievers in the lands and their dealings there, with what I have granted them of dwellings, farms, dominions, trade, and gains; and Quraysh used to trade in Syria and Yemen. For that is a burden upon them and a cause of their destruction, just as those before them who denied the messengers were destroyed.

The majority read ﴿fa-lā yaghrurka﴾ with unassimilated form (bi-l-fakk), and this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "fa-lā yaghurrak," with assimilation and a fatḥah on the rāʾ, and this is the dialect of Tamīm.

Since the disputation of the disbelievers arose from denying what the Messenger (peace be upon him) brought of the signs of God, He mentioned those among the earlier nations who denied before them, and what their condition came to of the descent of God's vengeance upon them, so that the disbelievers to whom the Messenger (peace be upon him) was sent might be deterred. So He began with the people of Noah, since he (peace be upon him) was the first messenger on earth, and He joined to his people "al-aḥzāb," who are those who banded together against the messengers and did not accept what they came with from God; among them were ʿĀd, Thamūd, Pharaoh and his followers.

He placed the intention to seize before disputation by falsehood, because when God protected the messengers from them so that they could not kill them, they returned to disputation by falsehood. The majority read ﴿bi-rasūlihim﴾ ("their messenger"); ʿAbd Allāh read "bi-rasūlihā" ("its messenger"), the pronoun referring to the wording "ummah" (community).

﴿li-yaʾkhudhūhu﴾: that they might gain control over him, by imprisonment, torture, or killing. Ibn ʿAbbās said: li-yaʾkhudhūhu means li-yamlikūhu (that they might possess him), and Quṭrub recited:

If you seize me and kill me, how many a seizer has desired my immortality!

It is said of the slain and the captive: "akhīdh." Qatādah said: li-yaʾkhudhūhu means li-yaqtulūhu (that they might kill him), expressing the effect by its cause.

﴿wa-jādalū bi-l-bāṭil﴾: i.e., by that which is vanishing and perishing, having no stability. It was also said: "al-bāṭil" is disbelief; it was said: it is Satan; it was said: by their saying: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ (Yā-Sīn: 15).

﴿li-yudḥiḍū bihi al-ḥaqq﴾: that they might cause the truth to slip away; i.e., the firm, true thing.

﴿fa-akhadhtuhum﴾: so I seized them, i.e., I destroyed them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verse 1–6 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Then how was My punishment﴾ — this is a rhetorical question (istifham ta'ajjub) expressing wonder at their annihilation and magnifying what befell them, not a question about the manner (kayfiyyah) of their punishment. They used to pass by their dwellings and see the traces of God's blessing upon them. He dispensed with the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah), using the kasrah instead, because it falls at the end of a verse (fasilah); the original form is ʿiqābī.

﴿And thus was it decreed﴾ — i.e., just as that necessity of punishment was incumbent upon those [earlier peoples], so it was incumbent upon the disbelievers, by virtue of their being among the companions of the Fire, both those who came before them and those who came after.

(Annahum): it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the word of your Lord﴾, so it is in the nominative position (fi mawdi' raf'). It is also permissible that the implied phrase is li-annahum, with the lam of causation (lam al-'illah) omitted. The meaning: just as the destruction of those nations was necessary, so the destruction of these people is necessary, because the cause that necessitates their destruction is a common attribute that unites them, namely their being among the companions of the Fire.

In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it reads: "wa-kadhalika sabaqat" (and thus has preceded), which is an interpretation of meaning (tafsir ma'na), not a recitation (qira'ah). Ibn Hurmuz, Shaybah, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿kalimat﴾ in the plural; Abu Raja', Qatadah and the rest of the Seven recited it in the singular.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 7–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And protect them from evil deeds; and whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have truly shown him mercy. That is the supreme success."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾ ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great."﴾ ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky, but none remembers except one who turns back in repentance.﴾.

When he mentioned the disputing of the disbelievers concerning the signs of Allah and their disobedience, he mentioned the obedience of these chosen ones of His creation, namely the bearers of the Throne, ﴿and those around it﴾, who are the angels encircling it.

They mentioned some of the description of those bearers, the greatness of their creation, the description of the Throne, what it was created from, and the seventy veils whose kinds differ. They said: Allah is veiled from the Throne and from its bearers. And Allah knows best about it, on the basis that His power, exalted be He, is capable of all that they mentioned, which does not necessitate anthropomorphism (tajsim), but it requires a sound transmission (naql).

Al-Jumhur read (al-ʿarsh) with a fatha on the ʿayn; Ibn ʿAbbas and a group read it with a damma, as if it were the plural of ʿarsh, like saqf and suquf, or it is a dialectal form of ʿarsh.

﴿Glorify their Lord with His praise﴾: that is, they declare Him free of all deficiencies; ﴿with the praise of their Lord﴾: by extolling Him as the One who bestows blessings absolutely.

Tasbih (glorification) indicates exaltation (ijlal), and tahmid (praising) indicates honouring (ikram). Thus it is close to His saying: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Rahman: 78]. Its parallel is: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with the praise of their Lord, and judgment will be passed between them with truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]; and their saying: "And we glorify You with Your praise."

﴿And believe﴾: that is, they affirm His existence, exalted be He, and what He described Himself with of His lofty attributes; and their glorification of Him includes faith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and believe in Him﴾, when it is not hidden from anyone that the bearers of the Throne and those around it, the angels who glorify His praise, are believers?" I say: its benefit is to show the nobility and virtue of faith and to encourage it, just as He described the prophets in more than one place of His Book with righteousness for it, and just as He followed their good deeds with His saying: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], thereby manifesting the virtue of faith.

Another benefit: it is to alert that if the matter were as the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah) say, the bearers of the Throne and those around it would be witnessing and seeing directly, and they would not be described as believers, because faith is only ascribed to the unseen. And since they were described with it as praise for them, it is known that their faith, the faith of those on earth, and of everyone absent from that station, is alike in that the faith of all is through reflection and inference only, and that there is no way to know Him except this, and that He is exalted above the attributes of bodies.

The congruence (tanasub) has been observed in His saying: ﴿and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾, as if it was said: they believe and they ask forgiveness for those who are in a similar state and description to theirs. In this there is an alert that sharing in faith must be the most compelling cause for sincere advice and the strongest motive for purity of compassion, even if kinds differ and places are distant; for there is no homogeneity between an angel and a human, nor between heaven and earth at all. Then when the unifier of faith came, total homogeneity and true proportion came with it, to the point that those around the Throne ask forgiveness for those upon the earth. He, exalted be He, said: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. End of quotation, and it is a good statement.

However, his saying that the faith of all is through reflection and inference only is open to scrutiny, and his saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ specifies the generality of His saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "We found the most sincere of the servants to the servants to be the angels, and the most deceitful of the servants to the servants to be the devils," and he recited this verse. End of quotation.

It should be said: the most sincere of the servants to the servants are the prophets and the angels.

﴿Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge﴾: that is, they say: "Our Lord." This deleted element may serve as an explanation of (yastaghfirun), in which case it is in the nominative position, or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal), in which case it is in the accusative position. The call with the words "Our Lord" and "My Lord" has come frequently, and in it is an appeal of the servant to his master who raised him and attended to his welfare from his beginnings until the time of his calling; so he is worthy of calling Him only by the title "the Lord."

(Rahmatan wa ʿilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz); the original is: "Your mercy encompassed all things, and Your knowledge encompassed all things." The encompassing is ascribed to its possessor for emphasis, as if His very essence were mercy and knowledge, and He has encompassed all things.

He placed mercy first, because by it they seek His bounty and make it a means of attaining their desired goal of asking forgiveness.

When He, exalted be He, related their manner of praising Him and informed of their asking forgiveness, which is their saying: ﴿so forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾. Seeking forgiveness is the result of mercy, and "those who repent" implies that You know their repentance; so these two refer back to His saying ﴿mercy and knowledge﴾, and ﴿and follow Your way﴾, which is the way of truth that You laid down for Your servants. ﴿Indeed, You are the Mighty﴾: the One who is not overcome; ﴿the Wise﴾: the One who places things in their proper places which befit them.

Since seeking forgiveness includes the removal of punishment, they followed it with a plea for protection from punishment, for emphasis and affirmation, saying: ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾. Seeking forgiveness and protection from punishment are for the repentant righteous, and He has promised that by a true promise which stands in the place of intercession in increasing reward and honour.

Since they asked for the removal of punishment, they asked for the continuation of reward, and they repeated the supplication with "Our Lord," saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden﴾. Al-Jumhur read (Jannat) in the plural; Zayd ibn ʿAli and al-Aʿmash read (Jannata ʿadn) in the singular, and so it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. The discussion of the grammatical parsing of (alladhi) was previously treated in His saying: ﴿the Gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen﴾ [Maryam: 61] in Surat Maryam.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read (salaha) with a damma on the lam; it is said: salaha, so he is salih (righteous), and saluha, so he is salih (righteous) in another form.

ʿIsa read (wa dhurriyyatihim) in the singular; al-Jumhur read it in the plural.

On Ibn Jubayr's explanation of that: a man enters Paradise before his relatives, and he says: "Where is my father? Where is my mother? Where is my son? Where is my wife?" And they join him because of his righteousness, and because of his alerting them to it and his seeking them. And this is the supplication of the angels. End of quotation.

When a person is in goodness, with his kin and family with him, that is more pleasing to him and more delightful to his heart.

The apparent reading is that (wa man) is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿wa adkhilhum﴾, since they are the ones being spoken of and the ones for whom the request is made.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is from two positions: if you wish, on the pronoun in ﴿wa adkhilhum﴾, and if you wish, on the pronoun in ﴿wa ʿadtahum﴾.

﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾: that is, keep them from falling into them so that their consequence does not follow; or protect them from the requital of the evil deeds they committed, in which case the genitive is omitted, and there is no repetition in this. His saying ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ does not conflict, since the first supplication is for those who repented and the second is for them and for those among the aforementioned who are righteous; or because the two supplications differ, if by "evil deeds" is meant their own selves, then that is protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, and this is protection from falling into evil deeds.

The tanwin in (yawma'idhin) is the tanwin of replacement (ʿiwad), and the omitted element is a clause for which the tanwin is a replacement; there has not preceded a clause for which the tanwin would be a replacement, as in His saying: ﴿Why, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 83], ﴿and you at that time﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 84], meaning: at the time when it reaches the throat. So there must be an estimated clause for which the tanwin is a replacement, as in His saying, indicated by the meaning of the speech, and it is ﴿and whoever You protect from evil deeds﴾, meaning: their requital on the day when they will be held accountable for them; ﴿then You have truly shown him mercy﴾. None of the commentators whose statements we have reviewed on this verse addressed the clause for which the tanwin in (yawma'idhin) is a replacement; and that refers to forgiveness, entry into Paradise, and protection from punishment. ﴿That is the supreme success﴾: the attainment of the great victory, whose stake is immense and whose accomplishment is magnificent.

When He mentioned some of the states of the believers and some of the states of the disbelievers, and what will happen to them in the Hereafter, of their acknowledgment of their sins, their deserving of punishment, their request to return to the world, and their calling out. As-Suddi said: "In the Fire." Qatadah said: "On the Day of Resurrection," and those who call out to them are the Zabaniyah, in a manner of rebuke and reproach.

The lam in ﴿la-maqtu﴾ is the lam of inception and the lam of oath. Maqt is a verbal noun added to its agent; the estimation is: "The aversion of Allah towards you," or "The aversion of Allah towards yourselves"; and the object is omitted because of what follows it in His saying: ﴿greater than your aversion towards yourselves﴾. The apparent meaning is that Allah's aversion towards them is in this world, and it is weak that it is in the Hereafter, as some said, because of the remaining (idh tud'awna), which is detached from the speech, since it has no preceding governing element and no explainer of a governing element. If the earlier aversion is in this world, it is possible to posit a governing element for it, estimated as: "your aversion when you are called."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(idh tud'awna)" is in the accusative governed by the first maqt. The meaning: it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed Allah was averse to your commanding selves of evil and disbelief when the prophets were calling you to faith, and you refused to accept it and chose disbelief over it, a greater aversion than what you feel towards them today while you are in the Fire, since I placed you in it by following their desires." End of quotation, and in it is the subtle hint of Mu'tazilism.

He erred in his saying "(idh tud'awna)" is governed by the first maqt, because maqt is a verbal noun, and its complement is part of its complement; it is not permissible to inform about it except after completing its complement, and he has informed about it with His saying ﴿greater than your aversion towards yourselves﴾. This is among the obvious points of grammar which are hardly hidden from beginners, let alone what the non-Arabs claim is "the shaykh of the Arabs and non-Arabs" in Arabic.

Since separating the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate is not permissible, we estimate the governing element as implied, meaning: "your aversion when you are called." A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed He is capable of returning him on the day when secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 8–9]: they estimated the governing element as "returning him" for "the day when secrets are tested," because of the separation by "capable" between the verbal noun and "the day."

The difference of the times of the two aversions, the first in this world and the second in the Hereafter, is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and most scholars.

It has previously been mentioned that some said it is in the Hereafter, which is the view of al-Hasan.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And from al-Hasan: when they saw their wicked deeds they abhorred themselves, so they were called: ﴿the aversion of Allah﴾." It was also said: its meaning is: the aversion of Allah towards you now is greater than the aversion of some of you towards others, as in His saying: ﴿some of you disbelieve in others and curse some of you others﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]; and (idh tud'awna) is a reason clause. End of quotation.

His saying "(idh tud'awna) is a reason clause" was from al-Zamakhshari's words. Some said: (idh tud'awna) is governed by an omitted "remember," and this is sound on the basis that Allah's aversion towards them is in the Hereafter, according to al-Hasan's view; it was said to them as rebuke, reproach, and alerting them to what they missed of faith and reward.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 7–13 (part 2 of 2):

It is also possible that His words, ﴿from your hatred of yourselves﴾, mean that each one hates himself, or that some of you hate others. It has been said that the followers hate their leaders because the leaders led them into disbelief, and the leaders hate the followers.

It has also been said that they hate themselves when Satan said to them, ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. Maqt (hatred) is intense enmity, and it is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted, so its meaning here is denunciation and rebuke.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice."﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that they used to deny resurrection. Their self-hatred, and their seeing of their long grief, magnified this denial. When they hated themselves and saw their long sorrow, they returned to affirming resurrection. They acknowledged that He, the Exalted, caused them to die twice and gave them life twice, glorifying His power and seeking to win His pleasure. Then, by confessing their sins, they hoped that they would be returned to the world. That is, if we are returned to the world and called to faith, we will hasten to it.

Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Abu Malik said: their first death is their being water in the loins, then their being brought to life in the world, then their dying in it, then their being brought to life on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Suddi said: their being brought to life in the world, then their being made to die in it, then their being brought to life in the grave for the questioning of the two angels, then their being made to die in it, then their being brought to life at the gathering.

Ibn Zayd said: their being brought to life as souls (nasam) when the covenant was taken from them from the loins of Adam, then their being made to die after that, then their being brought to life in the world, then their being made to die, then their being brought to life. According to this and the previous view there would be three instances of life, and this contradicts the Qur'an.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the disbeliever in the world is alive in body and dead in heart, so the two states are both taken into account. Then there is their death in reality, then their being brought to life at resurrection. The discussion of the two deaths and the two lives was already covered at the beginning of al-Baqarah, in His words, ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28] and so on. We repeat it here because of the distance between the two places.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask) how is it correct to call His creating them dead "making them die"? (I answer) it is correct in the same way as: "Glory be to the One who made the body of the gnat small and the body of the elephant large," and as your saying to the digger, "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom." There is no transfer from largeness to smallness, nor from smallness to largeness, nor from narrowness to width, nor from width to narrowness. Rather, you intended the creating of it upon those attributes.

The reason it is correct is that smallness and largeness are both permissible for the same made thing without preference for either one. Likewise narrowness and width. When the maker chooses one of the two permissible options, while being equally able to do either, he has directed the made thing to the other permissible option, so his turning it away from one is like transferring it from that one. End of quote.

He means that ﴿He created them dead﴾ is as if it were a transfer from life, which is the other permissible option. The apparent sense of ﴿So they will confess their sins﴾ is that it follows as a result of their acceptance.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ There is an omitted element here: that is, "So we came to know Your power over causing death and giving life, and our denial of resurrection ceased. So we confess our sins﴾ that preceded, including the denial of resurrection and other things.

﴿Is there any way out?﴾ That is, quickly or slowly, from the Fire. ﴿Any way?﴾ This is the question of one who has despaired of leaving, but it is a pretext and bewilderment.

(That is for you): the apparent meaning is that the address is to the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the reference is to the punishment they are in, or to their hatred of themselves, or to the prevention from leaving and to the rebuke and humiliation. These are possibilities that have been stated. It has been said that the address is to those present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the pronoun in (fa-innahu) is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n).

﴿When God alone is called upon﴾, that is, when He is singled out for divinity and it is denied for anything else, ﴿you disbelieve; but when partners are associated with Him﴾, that is, when al-Lat, al-Uzza and similar idols are mentioned, ﴿you believe.﴾ You affirm their divinity and your souls are at rest with them.

﴿The judgment﴾ concerning your punishment belongs to ﴿God﴾, not to those idols that you associated with God, ﴿the Most High﴾ above association, ﴿the Great﴾, meaning the One of great majesty.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the people of the Fire have five supplications. God speaks to them in four of them. When the fifth comes, they fall silent.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice…"﴾ and so on. In Ibrahim: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾ [Ibrahim: 44] and so on. In al-Sajdah: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12] and so on. In Fatir: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾ [Fatir: 37] and so on. In al-Mu'minun: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106] and so on. He answers them, ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. He said: so that was their last speech.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned what calls for severe warning against the polytheists, He followed it with mention of what shows the perfection of His power and wisdom, so that this would be proof that it is not permissible to make carved stones and worshipped wood into partners with God. So He said: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs﴾, O people, which include the signs of His power, such as the wind, the clouds, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts and similar celestial phenomena, the signs of His Book which contains the first and the last, and the signs of miracles through the hands of His messengers.

These signs return to the light of reason that calls to the Oneness of God. Then He said: ﴿and sends down for you provision from the sky﴾, which is the rain that is the cause of the sustaining of the body's structure. Thus those signs are for religions as this provision is for bodies.

﴿But none is mindful﴾, that is, none takes heed or reflects. He described it as remembrance because the proofs of Oneness are fixed in the minds. Then the occupation with worshipping other than God may arise and prevent the light of reason from shining, so when one repents to God, he remembers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 7–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And protect them from evil deeds; and whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have truly shown him mercy. That is the supreme success."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾ ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great."﴾ ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky, but none remembers except one who turns back in repentance.﴾.

They mentioned some of the description of those bearers, the greatness of their creation, the description of the Throne, what it was created from, and the seventy veils whose kinds differ. They said: Allah is veiled from the Throne and from its bearers. Al-Jumhur read (al-ʿarsh) with a fatha on the ʿayn; Ibn ʿAbbas and a group read it with a damma, as if it were the plural of ʿarsh, like saqf and suquf, or it is a dialectal form of ʿarsh.

As-Suddi said: "In the Fire." Qatadah said: "On the Day of Resurrection," and those who call out to them are the Zabaniyah, in a manner of rebuke and reproach.

The lam in ﴿la-maqtu﴾ is the lam of inception and the lam of oath. Maqt is a verbal noun added to its agent; the estimation is: "The aversion of Allah towards you," or "The aversion of Allah towards yourselves"; and the object is omitted because of what follows it in His saying: ﴿greater than your aversion towards yourselves﴾. The apparent meaning is that Allah's aversion towards them is in this world, and it is weak that it is in the Hereafter, as some said, because of the remaining (idh tud'awna), which is detached from the speech, since it has no preceding governing element and no explainer of a governing element. If the earlier aversion is in this world, it is possible to posit a governing element for it, estimated as: "your aversion when you are called."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(idh tud'awna)" is in the accusative governed by the first maqt. The meaning: it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed Allah was averse to your commanding selves of evil and disbelief when the prophets were calling you to faith, and you refused to accept it and chose disbelief over it, a greater aversion than what you feel towards them today while you are in the Fire, since I placed you in it by following their desires." End of quotation, and in it is the subtle hint of Mu'tazilism.

He erred in his saying "(idh tud'awna)" is governed by the first maqt, because maqt is a verbal noun, and its complement is part of its complement; it is not permissible to inform about it except after completing its complement, and he has informed about it with His saying ﴿greater than your aversion towards yourselves﴾. This is among the obvious points of grammar which are hardly hidden from beginners, let alone what the non-Arabs claim is "the shaykh of the Arabs and non-Arabs" in Arabic.

Since separating the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate is not permissible, we estimate the governing element as implied, meaning: "your aversion when you are called." A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed He is capable of returning him on the day when secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 8–9]: they estimated the governing element as "returning him" for "the day when secrets are tested," because of the separation by "capable" between the verbal noun and "the day."

The difference of the times of the two aversions, the first in this world and the second in the Hereafter, is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and most scholars.

It has previously been mentioned that some said it is in the Hereafter, which is the view of al-Hasan.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And from al-Hasan: when they saw their wicked deeds they abhorred themselves, so they were called: ﴿the aversion of Allah﴾." It was also said: its meaning is: the aversion of Allah towards you now is greater than the aversion of some of you towards others, as in His saying: ﴿some of you disbelieve in others and curse some of you others﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]; and (idh tud'awna) is a reason clause. End of quotation.

His saying "(idh tud'awna) is a reason clause" was from al-Zamakhshari's words. Some said: (idh tud'awna) is governed by an omitted "remember," and this is sound on the basis that Allah's aversion towards them is in the Hereafter, according to al-Hasan's view; it was said to them as rebuke, reproach, and alerting them to what they missed of faith and reward.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 7–13 (part 2 of 2):

It is also possible that His words, ﴿from your hatred of yourselves﴾, mean that each one hates himself, or that some of you hate others. It has been said that the followers hate their leaders because the leaders led them into disbelief, and the leaders hate the followers.

It has also been said that they hate themselves when Satan said to them, ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. Maqt (hatred) is intense enmity, and it is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted, so its meaning here is denunciation and rebuke.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice."﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that they used to deny resurrection. Their self-hatred, and their seeing of their long grief, magnified this denial. When they hated themselves and saw their long sorrow, they returned to affirming resurrection. They acknowledged that He, the Exalted, caused them to die twice and gave them life twice, glorifying His power and seeking to win His pleasure. Then, by confessing their sins, they hoped that they would be returned to the world. That is, if we are returned to the world and called to faith, we will hasten to it.

Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Abu Malik said: their first death is their being water in the loins, then their being brought to life in the world, then their dying in it, then their being brought to life on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Suddi said: their being brought to life in the world, then their being made to die in it, then their being brought to life in the grave for the questioning of the two angels, then their being made to die in it, then their being brought to life at the gathering.

Ibn Zayd said: their being brought to life as souls (nasam) when the covenant was taken from them from the loins of Adam, then their being made to die after that, then their being brought to life in the world, then their being made to die, then their being brought to life. According to this and the previous view there would be three instances of life, and this contradicts the Qur'an.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the disbeliever in the world is alive in body and dead in heart, so the two states are both taken into account. Then there is their death in reality, then their being brought to life at resurrection. The discussion of the two deaths and the two lives was already covered at the beginning of al-Baqarah, in His words, ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28] and so on. We repeat it here because of the distance between the two places.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask) how is it correct to call His creating them dead "making them die"? (I answer) it is correct in the same way as: "Glory be to the One who made the body of the gnat small and the body of the elephant large," and as your saying to the digger, "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom." There is no transfer from largeness to smallness, nor from smallness to largeness, nor from narrowness to width, nor from width to narrowness. Rather, you intended the creating of it upon those attributes.

The reason it is correct is that smallness and largeness are both permissible for the same made thing without preference for either one. Likewise narrowness and width. When the maker chooses one of the two permissible options, while being equally able to do either, he has directed the made thing to the other permissible option, so his turning it away from one is like transferring it from that one. End of quote.

He means that ﴿He created them dead﴾ is as if it were a transfer from life, which is the other permissible option. The apparent sense of ﴿So they will confess their sins﴾ is that it follows as a result of their acceptance.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ There is an omitted element here: that is, "So we came to know Your power over causing death and giving life, and our denial of resurrection ceased. So we confess our sins﴾ that preceded, including the denial of resurrection and other things.

﴿Is there any way out?﴾ That is, quickly or slowly, from the Fire. ﴿Any way?﴾ This is the question of one who has despaired of leaving, but it is a pretext and bewilderment.

(That is for you): the apparent meaning is that the address is to the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the reference is to the punishment they are in, or to their hatred of themselves, or to the prevention from leaving and to the rebuke and humiliation. These are possibilities that have been stated. It has been said that the address is to those present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the pronoun in (fa-innahu) is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n).

﴿When God alone is called upon﴾, that is, when He is singled out for divinity and it is denied for anything else, ﴿you disbelieve; but when partners are associated with Him﴾, that is, when al-Lat, al-Uzza and similar idols are mentioned, ﴿you believe.﴾ You affirm their divinity and your souls are at rest with them.

﴿The judgment﴾ concerning your punishment belongs to ﴿God﴾, not to those idols that you associated with God, ﴿the Most High﴾ above association, ﴿the Great﴾, meaning the One of great majesty.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the people of the Fire have five supplications. God speaks to them in four of them. When the fifth comes, they fall silent.

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice…"﴾ and so on. In Ibrahim: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾ [Ibrahim: 44] and so on. In al-Sajdah: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12] and so on. In Fatir: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾ [Fatir: 37] and so on. In al-Mu'minun: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106] and so on. He answers them, ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. He said: so that was their last speech.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned what calls for severe warning against the polytheists, He followed it with mention of what shows the perfection of His power and wisdom, so that this would be proof that it is not permissible to make carved stones and worshipped wood into partners with God. So He said: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs﴾, O people, which include the signs of His power, such as the wind, the clouds, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts and similar celestial phenomena, the signs of His Book which contains the first and the last, and the signs of miracles through the hands of His messengers.

These signs return to the light of reason that calls to the Oneness of God. Then He said: ﴿and sends down for you provision from the sky﴾, which is the rain that is the cause of the sustaining of the body's structure. Thus those signs are for religions as this provision is for bodies.

﴿But none is mindful﴾, that is, none takes heed or reflects. He described it as remembrance because the proofs of Oneness are fixed in the minds. Then the occupation with worshipping other than God may arise and prevent the light of reason from shining, so when one repents to God, he remembers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 7–13 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And protect them from evil deeds; and whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have truly shown him mercy. That is the supreme success."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾ ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great."﴾ ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky, but none remembers except one who turns back in repentance.﴾.

When he mentioned the disputing of the disbelievers concerning the signs of Allah and their disobedience, he mentioned the obedience of these chosen ones of His creation, namely the bearers of the Throne, ﴿and those around it﴾, who are the angels encircling it.

They mentioned some of the description of those bearers, the greatness of their creation, the description of the Throne, what it was created from, and the seventy veils whose kinds differ. They said: Allah is veiled from the Throne and from its bearers. And Allah knows best about it, on the basis that His power, exalted be He, is capable of all that they mentioned, which does not necessitate anthropomorphism (tajsim), but it requires a sound transmission (naql).

Al-Jumhur read (al-ʿarsh) with a fatha on the ʿayn; Ibn ʿAbbas and a group read it with a damma, as if it were the plural of ʿarsh, like saqf and suquf, or it is a dialectal form of ʿarsh.

﴿Glorify their Lord with His praise﴾: that is, they declare Him free of all deficiencies; ﴿with the praise of their Lord﴾: by extolling Him as the One who bestows blessings absolutely.

Tasbih (glorification) indicates exaltation (ijlal), and tahmid (praising) indicates honouring (ikram). Thus it is close to His saying: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Rahman: 78]. Its parallel is: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with the praise of their Lord, and judgment will be passed between them with truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]; and their saying: "And we glorify You with Your praise."

﴿And believe﴾: that is, they affirm His existence, exalted be He, and what He described Himself with of His lofty attributes; and their glorification of Him includes faith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and believe in Him﴾, when it is not hidden from anyone that the bearers of the Throne and those around it, the angels who glorify His praise, are believers?" I say: its benefit is to show the nobility and virtue of faith and to encourage it, just as He described the prophets in more than one place of His Book with righteousness for it, and just as He followed their good deeds with His saying: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], thereby manifesting the virtue of faith.

Another benefit: it is to alert that if the matter were as the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah) say, the bearers of the Throne and those around it would be witnessing and seeing directly, and they would not be described as believers, because faith is only ascribed to the unseen. And since they were described with it as praise for them, it is known that their faith, the faith of those on earth, and of everyone absent from that station, is alike in that the faith of all is through reflection and inference only, and that there is no way to know Him except this, and that He is exalted above the attributes of bodies.

The congruence (tanasub) has been observed in His saying: ﴿and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾, as if it was said: they believe and they ask forgiveness for those who are in a similar state and description to theirs. In this there is an alert that sharing in faith must be the most compelling cause for sincere advice and the strongest motive for purity of compassion, even if kinds differ and places are distant; for there is no homogeneity between an angel and a human, nor between heaven and earth at all. Then when the unifier of faith came, total homogeneity and true proportion came with it, to the point that those around the Throne ask forgiveness for those upon the earth. He, exalted be He, said: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. End of quotation, and it is a good statement.

However, his saying that the faith of all is through reflection and inference only is open to scrutiny, and his saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ specifies the generality of His saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "We found the most sincere of the servants to the servants to be the angels, and the most deceitful of the servants to the servants to be the devils," and he recited this verse. End of quotation.

It should be said: the most sincere of the servants to the servants are the prophets and the angels.

﴿Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge﴾: that is, they say: "Our Lord." This deleted element may serve as an explanation of (yastaghfirun), in which case it is in the nominative position, or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal), in which case it is in the accusative position. The call with the words "Our Lord" and "My Lord" has come frequently, and in it is an appeal of the servant to his master who raised him and attended to his welfare from his beginnings until the time of his calling; so he is worthy of calling Him only by the title "the Lord."

(Rahmatan wa ʿilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz); the original is: "Your mercy encompassed all things, and Your knowledge encompassed all things." The encompassing is ascribed to its possessor for emphasis, as if His very essence were mercy and knowledge, and He has encompassed all things.

He placed mercy first, because by it they seek His bounty and make it a means of attaining their desired goal of asking forgiveness.

When He, exalted be He, related their manner of praising Him and informed of their asking forgiveness, which is their saying: ﴿so forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾. Seeking forgiveness is the result of mercy, and "those who repent" implies that You know their repentance; so these two refer back to His saying ﴿mercy and knowledge﴾, and ﴿and follow Your way﴾, which is the way of truth that You laid down for Your servants. ﴿Indeed, You are the Mighty﴾: the One who is not overcome; ﴿the Wise﴾: the One who places things in their proper places which befit them.

Since seeking forgiveness includes the removal of punishment, they followed it with a plea for protection from punishment, for emphasis and affirmation, saying: ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾. Seeking forgiveness and protection from punishment are for the repentant righteous, and He has promised that by a true promise which stands in the place of intercession in increasing reward and honour.

Since they asked for the removal of punishment, they asked for the continuation of reward, and they repeated the supplication with "Our Lord," saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden﴾. Al-Jumhur read (Jannat) in the plural; Zayd ibn ʿAli and al-Aʿmash read (Jannata ʿadn) in the singular, and so it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. The discussion of the grammatical parsing of (alladhi) was previously treated in His saying: ﴿the Gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen﴾ [Maryam: 61] in Surat Maryam.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read (salaha) with a damma on the lam; it is said: salaha, so he is salih (righteous), and saluha, so he is salih (righteous) in another form.

ʿIsa read (wa dhurriyyatihim) in the singular; al-Jumhur read it in the plural.

On Ibn Jubayr's explanation of that: a man enters Paradise before his relatives, and he says: "Where is my father? Where is my mother? Where is my son? Where is my wife?" And they join him because of his righteousness, and because of his alerting them to it and his seeking them. And this is the supplication of the angels. End of quotation.

When a person is in goodness, with his kin and family with him, that is more pleasing to him and more delightful to his heart.

The apparent reading is that (wa man) is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿wa adkhilhum﴾, since they are the ones being spoken of and the ones for whom the request is made.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: its accusative is from two positions: if you wish, on the pronoun in ﴿wa adkhilhum﴾, and if you wish, on the pronoun in ﴿wa ʿadtahum﴾.

﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾: that is, keep them from falling into them so that their consequence does not follow; or protect them from the requital of the evil deeds they committed, in which case the genitive is omitted, and there is no repetition in this. His saying ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ does not conflict, since the first supplication is for those who repented and the second is for them and for those among the aforementioned who are righteous; or because the two supplications differ, if by "evil deeds" is meant their own selves, then that is protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, and this is protection from falling into evil deeds.
