Since each warning carried a kind of severity and fear and the like, the repetition of "the Approaching" (the imminent) was fitting, as previously mentioned. It is the nearness of their arrival at the Fire, for at that time the hearts will swerve from their places out of extreme fear.

Abu Muslim said: ﴿يَوْمَ الآزِفَةِ﴾ is the day of death and the arrival of the appointed term. Evidence for this is that the description of the Day of Resurrection as the Day of Meeting and the Day of their Emerging would be out of place here, so this day must be other than that. This attribute (of nearness) is specific in the other verses, and the Day of Death being near is more fitting than the Day of Resurrection being near. Also, the attributes mentioned after His words ﴿the Approaching Day﴾ are suited to the day of the arrival of death, because a man, when he sees the angels of punishment, from the greatness of his fear, his heart almost reaches his throat from the severity of fear, and he will have no intimate friend or intercessor to remove from him the kinds of fear he suffers.

﴿إذِ القُلُوبُ لَدى الحَناجِرِ﴾ (idh al-qulubu ladaa al-hanajir, "when hearts are at the throats"). It was said: it is possible that this is literally the Day of Resurrection, and they will remain alive despite it, unlike the state of this world, because whoever has his heart moved to his throat dies. It is also possible that it is an expression of the extreme anguish they reach.

Just as you say: "My soul almost left me."

﴿كاظِمِينَ﴾ (kazimin, "suppressing") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a hal from the owners of the hearts in meaning, since the meaning is: when their hearts are at their throats, suppressing them (their grief). It is also permitted for it to be a hal from the hearts, meaning the hearts are suppressing upon distress and anguish within them, even while reaching the throats. The word kazimin is in the sound masculine plural form because He described them with suppressing, which is one of the acts of rational beings, as He said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said: ﴿so their necks remained humbly bowed﴾. This is supported by the reading of those who read kazimun (in the nominative). End of quote.

It is also permitted that it is a hal from the pronoun in His words (the speech), meaning: "Warn them while being those who determine." Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿كاظِمِينَ﴾ is a hal from what was substituted for: His words ﴿their eyes will stare﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], ﴿hurrying forward﴾ [Ibrahim: 43]. He meant: their eyes will stare fixedly in it. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿القُلُوبُ﴾ (al-qulub) is raised as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿لَدى الحَناجِرِ﴾ (ladaa al-hanajir) is the predicate, linked to the meaning of being fixed in place. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿كاظِمِينَ﴾ is a hal from the hearts, because what is meant is their owners. End of quote.

﴿ما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِن حَمِيمٍ﴾ (ma lil-zalimina min hamim, "The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend") means: a loving, compassionate friend. ﴿ولا شَفِيعٍ يُطاعُ﴾ (wa la shafi'in yut'a, "nor any intercessor who is obeyed"): ﴿يُطاعُ﴾ (yut'a, "is obeyed") is in the position of a qualifier for ﴿شَفِيعٍ﴾ (shafi'in). It is possible that it is in the genitive position according to the wording, and in the nominative position according to the place (the grammatical position). It is also possible that the negation applies only to the qualifier, so that the sense is "an intercessor, but he is not obeyed," meaning his intercession is not accepted. It is also possible that the negation applies to the qualified noun and its qualifier together, meaning "no intercessor who is obeyed," and this is the intended meaning of the verse: the intercessor with Allah is only from among His friends, and intercession is only for those whom Allah has approved. Also, it contributes to the increase of grace and reward, and none of this is possible for the disbeliever.

From al-Hasan: "By Allah, there will be no intercessor for them at all."

﴿يَعْلَمُ خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ﴾ (ya'lamu kha'innata al-a'yun, "He knows the treachery of the eyes") is like His words: "If you give drink to the noble people, then give us drink" (poetic usage). Meaning: the noble people.

(Translator's note: the passage ends here as the text given; the remaining commentary continues in part 2.)

The treachery of the eyes" may be a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "al-'āfiyah" and "al-'āqibah," meaning: He knows the treachery of the eyes. Since the acts intended for concealment are physical, He specified them as ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾: a winking of the eyelid, a gesture, or a glance that conveys one meaning while indicating another. The concealed matter is what the hearts contain, and He divided what is concealed into these two categories, mentioning that His knowledge is connected to both with complete connection.

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said: "It is not good to take 'the treachery' as referring to the eyes, because His words ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ do not support it." He means that it is not appropriate for the counterpart of the meaning to be anything other than meaning. It has already been noted that the apparent reading is that the implied phrase is "the treacherous eyes."

The apparent view is that His words ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ are connected to what precedes them. When He commanded warning them of the Day of the Imminent (al-Āzifah), and of what occurs on it of intense distress and grief, and that the wrongdoer will find no one to protect him from that or to intercede for him, He mentioned His awareness of everything that proceeds from the servant, and that he will be recompensed for what he did, so that he would be wary of that Day, knowing that God is aware of his deeds.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ is connected to His words ﴿swift in reckoning﴾, because the swiftness of His reckoning of creatures is only by His knowledge, which requires no deliberation or thought, nor anything that accountants need."

A group said: "(He knows)" is connected to His words ﴿nothing of them is hidden from God﴾. This is a good view, strengthened by the correspondence of the two meanings, but weakened by the distance between the verses and the large number of intervening words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: To what is His words 'He knows the treachery of the eyes' connected? I say: It is a predicate of the predicates of 'He' in His words ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:12), like ﴿He casts down the Spirit﴾, but He who casts down the Spirit was given a reason in His words ﴿to warn of the Day of Meeting﴾; then He omitted and mentioned the conditions of the Day of Meeting up to His words ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾, so it became distant from its counterparts." 

In some of the revealed books it is said: "I am the watcher of the aspirations; I am the knower of the state of thought and the glances of the eyes."

Mujahid said: ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾ is the furtive glance at what is not permitted. The exegetes illustrated ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾ by the second look at the forbidden for one who is not the looker, and ﴿what the breasts conceal﴾ by the first look, which cannot be avoided.

﴿And God judges with truth﴾: this necessitates great fear, because when the Judge has knowledge of all conditions, he judges only with truth in what is subtle and great, and creatures fear him exceedingly.

﴿And those they call upon besides Him do not judge anything﴾: this is a disparagement of their idols and a mockery of them, because what is not described with power cannot be said of it that it judges or does not judge. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur, "the majority") read "they call upon" (yad'ūna) with the third-person prefix, to match the third-person pronouns mentioned before. 

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi' (with a variant from him), and Hisham read "you call upon" (tad'ūna) with the second-person prefix, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad.

﴿Indeed, God is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾: this confirms His words ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾, and is a warning to them that He hears what they say and sees what they do, and an allusion that their idols neither hear nor see.

﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾: He referred the Quraysh to taking lessons from travel. It is permissible for "and see" (fa-yanẓurū) to be jussive (majzūm) as a conjunction with "travel" (yasīrū), and for it to be accusative (manṣūb) as an answer to the negation, as the poet said:

Did you not ask, so the traces would inform you?

The discussion of this type of sentence has already preceded. Al-Zamakhshari took "they" (hum) as a separating pronoun (faṣl, "separator") and said it is not definite, since it is permissible for "they" to be an emphatic (tawkīd) of the pronoun in "were" (kānū).

The majority read "from them" (minhum) with the third-person pronoun; Ibn 'Amir read "from you" (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, as a shift in person (iltifāt, "turning").

﴿And monuments in the land﴾: coordinated with "strength" (quwwah), meaning: their buildings, their fortresses, and their numbers were at the utmost degree of might.

﴿And you hew out houses from the mountains﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:149). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or they intended more monuments, based on his words:

Girded with a sword and a spear."

(p. 458) He means: and bearing a spear. There is no need to claim an ellipsis when the meaning is sound without it.

﴿From any protector﴾: meaning, they had no one among the punishment of God who would shield them from His punishment.

﴿That﴾: meaning, the seizing. The explanation of a similar expression has already preceded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 14–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion, even though the disbelievers dislike it.﴾ ﴿Raised in degrees, Possessor of the Throne, He casts the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that He may warn of the Day of Meeting.﴾ ﴿The Day they will come forth, nothing of them concealed from Allah. "To whom belongs dominion today?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾ ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿And warn them of the Approaching Day, when hearts will be at the throats, suppressing [their grief]. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor who is obeyed.﴾ ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal.﴾ ﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they call upon besides Him judge nothing. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in power and in traces upon the earth, but Allah seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from Allah.﴾ ﴿That was because their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong, Severe in punishment.﴾

The command in His words ﴿So call upon Allah﴾ is addressed to the penitent believers, the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That is, worship Him ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 65], free from polytheism in every state, even in the state of anger at your enemies who conspire against you and seek your annihilation. The word ﴿رَفِيعُ﴾ (Rafi'u, "Raised") is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Al-Zamakhshari said: They are three predicates following His words ﴿He is the One who shows you﴾ [Ghafir: 13], or they are predicates of an omitted subject, and they differ in definiteness and indefiniteness. End of quote.

As for their following His words ﴿He is the One who shows you﴾ [Ghafir: 13], that is far-fetched because of the long separation. As for their being predicates of an omitted subject, that is based on the permissibility of multiple predicates when they do not have the meaning of a single predicate, and prohibiting it is the choice of our companions (the Basran grammarians, from Basra).

﴿رَفِيعُ﴾ has also been read in the accusative (Rafi'a) as praise. It is possible that ﴿رَفِيعُ﴾ is an intensive form (fa'il pattern) from "raising" (rafi'), so that ﴿الدَّرَجاتِ﴾ (al-darajat, "the degrees") is the object: "Raiser of the degrees of the believers and their dwellings in Paradise." Ibn Salam interpreted it this way. Or "degrees" is an expression for the heavens, the highest of which is a heaven above a heaven, and the Throne is above them. Ibn Jubayr interpreted it this way. It is also possible that ﴿رَفِيعُ﴾ is a form (fa'il) from "to raise", meaning "he rose high," so it is of the type of the adjectival form (sifa mushabbaha), and "the degrees" are the ascending stairways of the angels up to the Throne. It is attributed to Him to show His might and authority, meaning: the degrees of His angels, as He described Himself with His words ﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 3]. Or it is an expression for the exaltedness of His rank and the height of His dominion.

Likewise His words ﴿Possessor of the Throne﴾ are an expression of His dominion. Ibn Zayd interpreted it similarly, saying: "Great in attributes."

﴿الرُّوحَ﴾ (al-ruh, "the Spirit") means prophethood, as said by Qatada and al-Suddi, just as He said ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Also from Qatada: revelation.

Ibn Abbas said: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Jibril, whom He sends to whomever He wills. It has been said: mercy. It has been said: the spirits of the servants. These two sayings are weak. The preferred view is revelation, and the spirit is used figuratively for it because of the life it gives to the accepted religions, as He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life?﴾ [al-An'am: 122].

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that the casting of the Spirit is the means of every blessing Allah bestows upon His guided servants in conveying faith and noble understandings. End of quote.

Al-Zajjaj said: The spirit is everything through which people have life. Every guided person is alive, and every astray person is dead. End of quote.

Ibn Abbas said: ﴿مِن أمْرِهِ﴾ (min amrihi, "by His command") means "from His decree." Muqatil said: "by His command." Al-Sha'bi related it from his words. It appears that ﴿مِن﴾ (min) denotes the starting point.

The majority read ﴿لِيُنْذِرَ﴾ (liyundhira, "that He may warn") in the active voice, with ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (yawma) in the accusative. The apparent subject is Allah, because He is the one spoken of. ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ may be an object by extension (ittisa'), or an adverb of time (zarf), and the object of the warning is omitted. Ubayy and a group read it the same way, except that they put ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ in the nominative as the subject, metaphorically. It has been said: in the first reading, the subject is a pronoun referring to the Spirit. It has also been said: a pronoun referring to "whom."

Al-Yamani, as mentioned by the author of al-Lawami, read ﴿لِيُنْذَرَ﴾ in the passive voice, with ﴿يَوْمُ التَّلاقِ﴾ (yawmu al-talaq) in the nominative. Al-Hasan and al-Yamani, as mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh, read ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ with the letter ta' (litundhira, "that it may warn"). They said: the subject is a pronoun referring to the Spirit, because it is feminine, or the pronoun of the addressee within the relative clause.

It has been read: ﴿التَّلاقِ﴾ (al-talaq) and ﴿التَّنادِ﴾ (al-tanad), with a ya' and without a ya'. It was called the Day of Meeting because creation meets in it, as said by Ibn Abbas. Qatada and Muqatil said: the Creator meets the created in it.

Maymun ibn Mihran said: the oppressor meets the oppressed in it. Al-Tha'labi related: a person meets his deeds. Al-Suddi said: the people of heaven meet the people of earth. It has been said: the worshippers meet their object of worship.

﴿يَوْمَ هم بارِزُونَ﴾ (yawma hum barizun, "the day they will come forth") means: manifest, emerging from their graves, with nothing concealing them, whether mountain, hill or building, because the earth on that day will be a level plain, nor any garments, because they will be gathered barefoot and naked. ﴿يَوْمًا﴾ (yawman) is a substitute for ﴿يَوْمَ التَّلاقِ﴾ (yawma al-talaq), and both are future adverbs of time (zarf mustaqbal).

According to Sibawayh, it is not permitted to add a future time adverb to a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya). It is not permitted to say: "I will come to you the day Zayd is going," treating it like ﴿إذا﴾ (idha, "when"). Just as you cannot say "I will come to you when Zayd is going," so this is also not permitted.

Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) held that this is permitted, so His words ﴿يَوْمَ هم بارِزُونَ﴾ are construed according to this view.

Some of our companions permitted this too, though rarely, and the evidences are mentioned in the science of grammar.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time, governed by His words ﴿لا يَخْفى﴾ (la yakhfa, "is not hidden"). This is an inflectional vowel (harakat i'rab), not a built vowel (harakat bina'), because a time adverb is not built except when it is added to a non-declinable (ghayr mutamakkin) word, as in ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ (yawma'idhin, "that day"). A poet said:

"In the time when I rebuked white hair for youth..."

And like His words: ﴿This is a day when truthfulness benefits﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119].

As for this verse, the sentence (al-jumla) is a declinable noun-phrase, as you say: "I came on the day Zayd is a governor," so building is not permitted. End of quote.

He means that the accusative as an adverb of time is ﴿يَوْمَ هم بارِزُونَ﴾. As for his saying that it is not built except when added to a non-declinable word, building is not obligatory; rather, both building and inflection are permitted with it. As for his illustration with ﴿يَوْمُ يَنْفَعُ﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119], the school of Basra holds that only inflection is permitted there, while the school of Kufa (the Kufans) holds that both building and inflection are permitted.

As for its being added to a nominal sentence, as in his example "I came on the day Zayd is a governor," the report from the Basrans is that inflection is obligatory, as mentioned, (p. 456) while the report from the Kufans is that both inflection and building are permitted. Some of our companions held this, and it is the correct view, because of the abundance of evidence for building in such cases. It occurs in some of our companions' works that building is obligatory in it, but no one has held this view, so it is an error.

﴿لا يَخْفى عَلى اللَّهِ مِنهم شَيْءٌ﴾ (la yakhfa 'ala Allahi minhum shay', "nothing of them is hidden from Allah") means: nothing of their inner secrets and hidden matters. Ibn Abbas said: when those in the heavens and those on earth have perished, and none remain but Allah, He says: ﴿To whom belongs dominion today?﴾ and no one answers Him, so He replies to Himself: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾

Ibn Mas'ud said: Allah will gather all creation on the Day of Resurrection on a white ground, as if it were a lump of silver, in which Allah has never been disobeyed. The first thing He says is that a caller calls out: "To whom belongs dominion today?" They all answer: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer." It is related that He asserts this and the entire world remains silent out of awe and dread, so He answers Himself with: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, and then the people answer.

He specified the assertion for that day, although dominion belongs to Him in that day and in every other, because that dominion becomes manifest to the disbelievers and ignorant on that day and becomes clear.

When a person with some measure of intellect reflects on the subjugation of the people of the heavens and the earth and the enforcement of decree over them, he becomes certain that there is no dominion except for Allah. Among the results of His dominion on that day are: the recompense of every soul for what it earned, the absence of injustice, and the swiftness of reckoning, which means that their reckoning occurs at one time, and no reckoning distracts Him from another reckoning.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse is a clear text that reward and punishment are tied to the acquisition (iktisab) of the servant. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Ash'ariyya (the school of al-Ash'ari).

It is related that the Day of Resurrection will not be halved until the believers take their midday rest in Paradise and the disbelievers take theirs in the Fire.

The apparent view is that His words ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ are connected to what precedes them. When He commanded warning them of the Day of the Imminent (al-Āzifah), and of what occurs on it of intense distress and grief, and that the wrongdoer will find no one to protect him from that or to intercede for him, He mentioned His awareness of everything that proceeds from the servant, and that he will be recompensed for what he did, so that he would be wary of that Day, knowing that God is aware of his deeds.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ is connected to His words ﴿swift in reckoning﴾, because the swiftness of His reckoning of creatures is only by His knowledge, which requires no deliberation or thought, nor anything that accountants need."

A group said: "(He knows)" is connected to His words ﴿nothing of them is hidden from God﴾. This is a good view, strengthened by the correspondence of the two meanings, but weakened by the distance between the verses and the large number of intervening words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: To what is His words 'He knows the treachery of the eyes' connected? I say: It is a predicate of the predicates of 'He' in His words ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:12), like ﴿He casts down the Spirit﴾, but He who casts down the Spirit was given a reason in His words ﴿to warn of the Day of Meeting﴾; then He omitted and mentioned the conditions of the Day of Meeting up to His words ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾, so it became distant from its counterparts." 

In some of the revealed books it is said: "I am the watcher of the aspirations; I am the knower of the state of thought and the glances of the eyes."

Mujahid said: ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾ is the furtive glance at what is not permitted. The exegetes illustrated ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾ by the second look at the forbidden for one who is not the looker, and ﴿what the breasts conceal﴾ by the first look, which cannot be avoided.

﴿And God judges with truth﴾: this necessitates great fear, because when the Judge has knowledge of all conditions, he judges only with truth in what is subtle and great, and creatures fear him exceedingly.

﴿And those they call upon besides Him do not judge anything﴾: this is a disparagement of their idols and a mockery of them, because what is not described with power cannot be said of it that it judges or does not judge. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur, "the majority") read "they call upon" (yad'ūna) with the third-person prefix, to match the third-person pronouns mentioned before. 

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi' (with a variant from him), and Hisham read "you call upon" (tad'ūna) with the second-person prefix, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad.

﴿Indeed, God is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾: this confirms His words ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾, and is a warning to them that He hears what they say and sees what they do, and an allusion that their idols neither hear nor see.

﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾: He referred the Quraysh to taking lessons from travel. It is permissible for "and see" (fa-yanẓurū) to be jussive (majzūm) as a conjunction with "travel" (yasīrū), and for it to be accusative (manṣūb) as an answer to the negation, as the poet said:

Did you not ask, so the traces would inform you?

The discussion of this type of sentence has already preceded. Al-Zamakhshari took "they" (hum) as a separating pronoun (faṣl, "separator") and said it is not definite, since it is permissible for "they" to be an emphatic (tawkīd) of the pronoun in "were" (kānū).

The majority read "from them" (minhum) with the third-person pronoun; Ibn 'Amir read "from you" (minkum) with the second-person pronoun, as a shift in person (iltifāt, "turning").

﴿And monuments in the land﴾: coordinated with "strength" (quwwah), meaning: their buildings, their fortresses, and their numbers were at the utmost degree of might.

﴿And you hew out houses from the mountains﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:149). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or they intended more monuments, based on his words:

Girded with a sword and a spear."

(p. 458) He means: and bearing a spear. There is no need to claim an ellipsis when the meaning is sound without it.

﴿From any protector﴾: meaning, they had no one among the punishment of God who would shield them from His punishment.

﴿That﴾: meaning, the seizing. The explanation of a similar expression has already preceded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 23–31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We indeed sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun. They said: "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the scheming of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ ﴿Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."﴾ ﴿Musa said: "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, his lie is upon him; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾ ﴿"O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land. But who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?" Fir'awn said: "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾

Allah, exalted is He, began the story of Musa, peace be upon him, with Fir'awn as a consolation to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and as a warning to the Quraysh that there may befall them what befell Fir'awn and his people of the vengeances of Allah, (p-459) and as a promise to the believers of victory, triumph and a good end. The signs of Musa, peace be upon him, were many, and the miracles with which he challenged were the staff and the hand.

ʿĪsā read (wa-sulṭānin) with a ḍamma on the lām. Al-sulṭān al-mubīn means the clear proof and the evident demonstration. The apparent view is that Qarun is the one whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was among the people of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and he was from the Children of Israel.

It has been said that he is someone other than that one. He specified Haman and Qarun because of their standing in disbelief, and because they were the most well-known followers of Fir'awn.

﴿They said: "A sorcerer, a liar"﴾, meaning: this is a sorcerer, because of what appeared at his hands of turning the staff into a serpent and the shining light that appeared on his hand; a liar, because he claimed that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, meaning: with the miracles, the prophethood, and the call to faith in Allah. (They said), that is, those three, (kill). Ibn ʿAbbās said: that is, repeat the killing against them as it was the first time. End of quotation.

He means that this is other than the first killing. They were ordered to kill the sons of the believers so that Musa, peace be upon him, would not be strengthened by them, and to spare the women for service and enslavement. But what they were ordered to do did not happen, nor was it accomplished for them, and Allah did not help them in it.

﴿And the scheming of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, meaning: in confusion and bewilderment. Nothing of it came to pass, and their effort did not succeed. They had already begun killing earlier, but the decree of Allah was carried out in making appear the one whose destruction they feared at his hands.

It has been said that Fir'awn had stopped killing the sons, and when Musa was sent and he sensed that what he had been fearing had come to pass, he renewed the killing against them out of rage and fury, thinking that by this he would turn them away from supporting Musa; but he did not know that his scheme was lost in both instances together.

﴿Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord"﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: part of this is from the words of al-Ḥasan. Whenever he intended to kill him, they would restrain him by saying: "He is not the one you fear; he is less than that and weaker. He is only one of the sorcerers, and no one like him can be opposed except by a sorcerer like him." And they would say: "If you kill him, you will introduce doubt among the people, and they will believe that you were unable to oppose him with proof."

The apparent view is that Fir'awn, may Allah curse him, was certain that he was a prophet and that what he brought were signs and not sorcery. But the man had wickedness and tyranny in him, and he was a killer who shed blood over the slightest matter. How then would he not kill one whom he sensed would be the one to uproot his throne and demolish his kingdom? But he feared that if he intended to kill him he would be overtaken by destruction.

His saying: ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾ is a witness to the excess of his fear of him and of his supplication to his Lord. His saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa﴾ was a deception to his people and an illusion that they were the ones restraining him, whereas what restrained him was only what was in his soul of the terror of fright.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The apparent matter of Fir'awn is that when the signs of Musa dazzled, his support collapsed, and the beliefs of his companions were shaken, and there was none left among them who would contest with him over his matter. This is clear without any need in the account of the two of them. In this, according to this view, there are two proofs. One of them is his saying ﴿Leave me﴾, for these are not the words of tyrants who are able to carry out their commands.

The second proof is in the statement of the believing man and what he declared openly, and that his disclosure to Fir'awn was better than his concealment, and that his judgment for the prophethood of Musa was clearer than his bringing it near in the matter. As for Fir'awn, he turned to deceit, agitation and evasion, and of that is his saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa and let him call upon his Lord﴾, meaning: I do not care about the Lord of Musa. Then he returned to his people, showing them counsel and treachery toward them, and said: ﴿I fear that he will change your religion﴾. The word religion here means authority, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"If you were to settle among the Banu Asad in the realm of ʿAmr, and Fadak came between us..."

End of quotation.

Changing their religion means altering it. They used to worship him and also worship idols, as He said: ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 127]. ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, which is by the licentiousness that takes away security, causes the fields and livelihoods to be ruined, and makes people perish by killing and loss. So he feared the corruption of both your religion and your worldly life together.

Fir'awn began with his fear of the change of their religion before the change of their worldly life, because their love for their religions is above their love for their wealth.

It has been said that ﴿Leave me﴾ indicates that they were preventing him from killing him, either because some of them believed in him and so sought to prevent his killing by stratagem, or because of what was narrated from al-Ḥasan, which al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, or to occupy the heart of Fir'awn with Musa so that he would not have time for them, and so they would be safe from his evil, just as they do with a king when a rebel rises against him: they occupy him with it until they are safe from his evil. (p-460)

Al-Kūfiyyūn read (aw an), with the fear split between the change of religion or the appearance of corruption. The rest of the Seven read (wa-an), with the fear governed by both together.

Anas ibn Mālik, Ibn al-Musayyab, Mujāhid, Qatāda, Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ read (yuẓhira) from aẓhara in the active voice, with (al-fasād) in the accusative. The rest of the Seven, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Wathāb and ʿĪsā read (yaẓhara) from ẓahara in the active voice, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative.

Mujāhid read (yaẓẓahhara) with the ẓāʾ and hāʾ doubled, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read (yuẓharu), with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the hāʾ, in the passive voice, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative.

When Musa heard the statement of Fir'awn, he sought refuge in Allah from the evil of every arrogant one who denies the return. He said (wa-Rabbikum), urging them to follow his example, so that they would seek refuge in Allah and hold fast to Him.

And ﴿every arrogant one﴾ includes Fir'awn and others among the tyrants. This was by way of allusion, and it was more eloquent.

Takabbur (arrogance) is a person's exaggerated opinion of himself together with his lowliness, because he acts (accordingly). And ﴿does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning: in the recompense. This was more emphatic in his boldness, since he had acquired an exaggerated opinion of himself and a lack of concern for what he had committed. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read (ʿudtu) with idghām (assimilation of the two identical consonants); the rest of the Seven read it with izhār (clear pronunciation, without assimilation).

﴿A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, said﴾. It has been said that he was a Copt, a cousin of Fir'awn, who functioned in the position of crown prince and in the position of chief of police. It has been said that he was a Copt who was not of his kin. It has been said that he was described as "from the family of Fir'awn" because outwardly he was upon the religion of Fir'awn and his followers.

It has been said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, and that (from the family of Fir'awn) is connected to his saying ﴿who was concealing his faith﴾, not in the position of a description of a man, as the apparent meaning indicates. This has a remoteness to it, since none of the Children of Israel would have dared to speak before Fir'awn with the like of what this man said.

The view of those who connected (from the family of Fir'awn) with (yaktumu, he conceals) has been rejected, because one does not say: "I concealed such-and-such from so-and-so." One says: "I concealed so-and-so such-and-such." The Exalted said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 42], and the poet said:

"I concealed you by night, keeping watch with the Jamūmayn, and two concerns, one hidden and one apparent.
The inner talk of a soul that complains of what troubles it, and a watering place of cares that will not find a way out."

That is: I concealed from you the inner talk of a soul and two concerns. It has been said: his name was Simʿān. It has been said: Ḥabīb. It has been said: Ḥizqīl. The majority read (rajulun) with a ḍamma on the jīm. ʿĪsā, ʿAbd al-Wārith, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUqayl and Ḥamza ibn al-Qāsim, from Abū ʿAmr, read it with a sukūn (the pause of the consonant), and this is the dialect of Tamīm and Najd.

﴿Will you kill a man because he says﴾, meaning: because he says ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾. This was a great denunciation from him and a rebuke of them, as if he said: Will you commit the heinous act, which is killing a sacred soul, and you have no justification for committing it except the word of truth that he uttered, which is his saying ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾, when ﴿he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord﴾, meaning: from the One to whom he attributed lordship, and He is your Lord and not only his Lord? This was a means of drawing them toward acknowledgment. Al-Zamakhsharī said: You may posit an omitted genitive construction, meaning: at the time when he says. The meaning would then be: will you kill him at the moment you heard this statement from him without deliberation or reflection on his matter? End of quotation.

What he permitted, of positing an omitted noun (a time-noun) in this way, is not allowed. You say: "I came at the crowing of the rooster," meaning: at the time of the crowing of the rooster; you do not say "I come that the rooster crows." The grammarians have stated this explicitly. The condition for this is that the verbal noun be explicitly stated, not implied, and that the verb (an yaqūla, "that he says") not be an explicit verbal noun.

(bil-bayyināt): with the proofs of the oneness of Allah, which are those he mentioned in (Ṭā-Hā and al-Shuʿarāʾ) during his dialogue with him when he asked about his Lord, exalted is He.

When he had explicitly denounced them, he then misled them by dividing his matter into falsehood and truth, and he conveyed this in the form of possibility and counsel. He began the division with his saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, his lie is upon him﴾, showing courtesy and following the path of fairness in speech, and out of fear that if he denied their killing him, they would suspect him of supporting and defending him. So by this division and by beginning with the case of lying, he gave them the impression that he was unsure, in order to remain safe from their evil, and so that this would make it easier for them to accept. The meaning of ﴿his lie is upon him﴾ is: its harm will not pass beyond him.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾. He himself believed that he was a truthful prophet with certainty, but he used the word (some) in order to make the proof binding in its entirety on the matter, and there is in it no negation that everything he promises them would befall them.

A group said: some of the punishment that he mentions will befall you, and that was in their destruction, and the meaning would be: the single oath from what he threatens will befall you, and that is a part of what he promises, because he, peace be upon him, promised them that if they believed there would be blessing, and if they disbelieved there would be vengeance.

Another group said: some of what he promises you is the punishment of this world, because it is a part of the punishment of the Hereafter, and after that they will go to the Fire.

Abū ʿUbayda and others said: (some) carries the meaning of (all), and they cited the verse of ʿAmr ibn Shasim al-Qaṭāmī:

"The one who takes his time may reach some of his need, and haste may bring a slip."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: That is because when he supposed him truthful, he had affirmed that he is truthful in everything he promises. But he appended ﴿some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ so as to reduce for them part of his right in the outward meaning of the speech, so that he would show them that he is not one whose speech is given in full, let alone one who would be zealous for him. End of quotation.

(If you say): It is reported from Abū ʿUbayda that he divided (some) by (all), and he cited the verse of Labīd, which is:

"Abandoner of places when I do not like them, and he shows you from the portion of souls their death."

(I say): If the report from him is authentic, then what al-Mazini said in the matter of "al-Afi" has come true: "He was more ignorant than to understand what I say to him." End of quote. He means that Abu Ubayda was criticized by people for his belief that "ba'd" (some) can mean "kull" (all). They also cited, as evidence that "ba'd" can mean "kull," the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, affairs, when the youths manage them without the elders, you see in some of them a flaw."

That is: when he sees the youths. For this reason he said "dabbarahā" (he managed them) and did not say "dabbarūhā" (they managed them), taking into account the omitted noun it is attached to.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ In this there is an indication of the high standing of Musa, peace be upon him, and that one whom Allah has chosen for prophethood cannot commit transgression or lying. There is also an allusion to Pharaoh, for he was the extreme of transgression against himself by killing the sons of the believers, and the extreme of lying, since he claimed divinity and lordship; and one of such a state, Allah does not guide.

In a hadith: "The sincere (siddiqun) are three: Habib the carpenter, the believer of the family of Yasin, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, and Ali ibn Abi Talib."

And in a hadith: that he (ﷺ) circled the House (the Ka'ba), and when he finished, he took hold of the edges of his garment. They said to him: "Are you the one who forbids us what our fathers used to worship?" He said: "I am that one." Then Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, embraced him from behind, and said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?" raising his voice with that, while his eyes shed tears, until they released him.

And from Ja'far al-Sadiq: the believer of Pharaoh's family said that secretly, while Abu Bakr said it openly. And al-Suddi said: "(transgressor)" means by killing. Qatada said: "(transgressor)" means by disbelief.

The author of al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir said: This is a type of the sciences of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan) which our scholars call "istidraj al-mukhatab" (drawing the addressee along). When he saw that Pharaoh had resolved to kill Musa, and the people were set on denying him, he wished to defend him by a means through which he would conceal from them that he was partisan to him and one of his followers. So he came to them by way of advice and gentleness and said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ He did not mention his name, but said "a man," giving the impression that he does not know him and is not partisan to him, ﴿because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, and did not say "a man who believes in Allah" or "he is a prophet of Allah," for had he said any of that they would have known he was partisan. They would not have accepted his words. Then he followed it with what came after, putting first his words: ﴿And if he is a liar﴾, in agreement with their opinion of him. Then he followed it with: ﴿and if he is truthful﴾. Had he said, "He is truthful, and all that he promises you," they would have known he was partisan and that he claims he is a prophet and that he confirms him, for prophets do not omit anything of what they say. Then he followed it with words from which it is understood that he is not a confirmer: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ End of quote.

Then he said: "(O my people)" — a gentle call in his admonition.

﴿O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land﴾, that is: knowing, "in the land": in the land of Egypt, you have prevailed over the Children of Israel in it, subdued them, and enslaved them. He called them to the kingdom, which is the greatest and most exalted rank of this world, and it is from the aspect of their desires. "Dominant" (zahirin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the governing element in it is the same as that governing the prepositional phrase, and its owner of the state is the pronoun in "lakum" (for you).

Then he warned them against ruining themselves: that if the might of Allah came upon them, they would find no helper for them nor any repeller. He included himself in his words ﴿to help us﴾ and "came to us," because he is one of them by kinship, and to make them know that what he advises them with is something he shares with them.

The words of this believer indicate that the awe of Pharaoh had left his heart, and for this reason Pharaoh was subdued and said: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, that is: I advise you only to kill him, and I think only that is right. This is the statement of one who has no authority. He used "ma" with "illa" for restriction and emphasis.

﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, not what you say of leaving him alone. He lied, for he was fearful and anxious, and he knew that what Musa, peace be upon him, brought was true, but he was forcing himself and showing outwardly the opposite of what he concealed.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, and Abu'l-Qasim al-Hudhali mention here that Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited "al-Rashshad" with a shadda on the shin.

Abu'l-Fath said: It is an active participle in the intensive pattern from the triliteral verb rashada, so it is like 'abbad from 'abada.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or from rashida, like 'allam from 'alima. Al-Nahhas said: It is a solecism (lahn), and he imagined it was from the quadriliteral verb. It was answered that it is not necessarily from the quadriliteral; rather, it is from the triliteral. However, some have held that it is from the quadriliteral, so they formed fa''al from af'al, like darrak from adraka, sa'ir from asar, jabbar from ajbara, and qassar from aqsara. But this is not regular, so it should not be applied where there is an alternative; and fa''al from the triliteral is regular, so it was applied to it.

Abu Hatim said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to interpret it as "the path of Allah."

Ibn Atiyya said: This is far from Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him.

Was Pharaoh anything but claiming that he is a god? And the form of the word is connected to this interpretation. End of quote.

Mentioning the disagreement about this letter, which is part of Pharaoh's speech, is an error, and attributing Mu'adh's statement to it is an error. The correct view is that the disagreement concerns the believer's words: ﴿Follow me, I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Abu'l-Fadl al-Razi in his book "al-Lawami'" on the anomalous readings says, with this text: Mu'adh ibn Jabal: ﴿sabil al-rashad﴾ [Ghafir: 38], the second letter with a shadda, and likewise al-Hasan. It is the path of Allah the Exalted, which made clear the laws; thus Mu'adh ibn Jabal interpreted it. It is derived from "mursid," like darrak from mudrik, jabbar from mujbir, and qassar from muqsir an al-amr; and it has counted parallels. As for qassar, it is from qasara (for) the cloth, qisara. Ibn Khalawayh, after mentioning the disagreement over "al-tanad" and over "sadd 'an al-sabil," said: "(sabil al-rashshad with a shadda on the shin)" — Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Ibn Khalawayh said: he means by al-rashshad Allah the Exalted. End of quote.

So he did not mention any disagreement except in the believer's words: ﴿I guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Therefore mentioning the disagreement in it in Pharaoh's words is an error, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal did not interpret "al-rashshad" as Allah the Exalted except in the believer's words, not in Pharaoh's words. Ibn Atiyya said: That interpretation is from Pharaoh's words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 23–31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We indeed sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun. They said: "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the scheming of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ ﴿Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."﴾ ﴿Musa said: "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, his lie is upon him; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾ ﴿"O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land. But who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?" Fir'awn said: "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾

Allah, exalted is He, began the story of Musa, peace be upon him, with Fir'awn as a consolation to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and as a warning to the Quraysh that there may befall them what befell Fir'awn and his people of the vengeances of Allah, (p-459) and as a promise to the believers of victory, triumph and a good end. The signs of Musa, peace be upon him, were many, and the miracles with which he challenged were the staff and the hand.

ʿĪsā read (wa-sulṭānin) with a ḍamma on the lām. Al-sulṭān al-mubīn means the clear proof and the evident demonstration. The apparent view is that Qarun is the one whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was among the people of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and he was from the Children of Israel.

It has been said that he is someone other than that one. He specified Haman and Qarun because of their standing in disbelief, and because they were the most well-known followers of Fir'awn.

﴿They said: "A sorcerer, a liar"﴾, meaning: this is a sorcerer, because of what appeared at his hands of turning the staff into a serpent and the shining light that appeared on his hand; a liar, because he claimed that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, meaning: with the miracles, the prophethood, and the call to faith in Allah. (They said), that is, those three, (kill). Ibn ʿAbbās said: that is, repeat the killing against them as it was the first time. End of quotation.

He means that this is other than the first killing. They were ordered to kill the sons of the believers so that Musa, peace be upon him, would not be strengthened by them, and to spare the women for service and enslavement. But what they were ordered to do did not happen, nor was it accomplished for them, and Allah did not help them in it.

﴿And the scheming of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, meaning: in confusion and bewilderment. Nothing of it came to pass, and their effort did not succeed. They had already begun killing earlier, but the decree of Allah was carried out in making appear the one whose destruction they feared at his hands.

It has been said that Fir'awn had stopped killing the sons, and when Musa was sent and he sensed that what he had been fearing had come to pass, he renewed the killing against them out of rage and fury, thinking that by this he would turn them away from supporting Musa; but he did not know that his scheme was lost in both instances together.

﴿Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord"﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: part of this is from the words of al-Ḥasan. Whenever he intended to kill him, they would restrain him by saying: "He is not the one you fear; he is less than that and weaker. He is only one of the sorcerers, and no one like him can be opposed except by a sorcerer like him." And they would say: "If you kill him, you will introduce doubt among the people, and they will believe that you were unable to oppose him with proof."

The apparent view is that Fir'awn, may Allah curse him, was certain that he was a prophet and that what he brought were signs and not sorcery. But the man had wickedness and tyranny in him, and he was a killer who shed blood over the slightest matter. How then would he not kill one whom he sensed would be the one to uproot his throne and demolish his kingdom? But he feared that if he intended to kill him he would be overtaken by destruction.

His saying: ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾ is a witness to the excess of his fear of him and of his supplication to his Lord. His saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa﴾ was a deception to his people and an illusion that they were the ones restraining him, whereas what restrained him was only what was in his soul of the terror of fright.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The apparent matter of Fir'awn is that when the signs of Musa dazzled, his support collapsed, and the beliefs of his companions were shaken, and there was none left among them who would contest with him over his matter. This is clear without any need in the account of the two of them. In this, according to this view, there are two proofs. One of them is his saying ﴿Leave me﴾, for these are not the words of tyrants who are able to carry out their commands.

The second proof is in the statement of the believing man and what he declared openly, and that his disclosure to Fir'awn was better than his concealment, and that his judgment for the prophethood of Musa was clearer than his bringing it near in the matter. As for Fir'awn, he turned to deceit, agitation and evasion, and of that is his saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa and let him call upon his Lord﴾, meaning: I do not care about the Lord of Musa. Then he returned to his people, showing them counsel and treachery toward them, and said: ﴿I fear that he will change your religion﴾. The word religion here means authority, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"If you were to settle among the Banu Asad in the realm of ʿAmr, and Fadak came between us..."

End of quotation.

Changing their religion means altering it. They used to worship him and also worship idols, as He said: ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 127]. ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, which is by the licentiousness that takes away security, causes the fields and livelihoods to be ruined, and makes people perish by killing and loss. So he feared the corruption of both your religion and your worldly life together.

Fir'awn began with his fear of the change of their religion before the change of their worldly life, because their love for their religions is above their love for their wealth.

It has been said that ﴿Leave me﴾ indicates that they were preventing him from killing him, either because some of them believed in him and so sought to prevent his killing by stratagem, or because of what was narrated from al-Ḥasan, which al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, or to occupy the heart of Fir'awn with Musa so that he would not have time for them, and so they would be safe from his evil, just as they do with a king when a rebel rises against him: they occupy him with it until they are safe from his evil. (p-460)

Al-Kūfiyyūn read (aw an), with the fear split between the change of religion or the appearance of corruption. The rest of the Seven read (wa-an), with the fear governed by both together.

Anas ibn Mālik, Ibn al-Musayyab, Mujāhid, Qatāda, Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ read (yuẓhira) from aẓhara in the active voice, with (al-fasād) in the accusative. The rest of the Seven, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Wathāb and ʿĪsā read (yaẓhara) from ẓahara in the active voice, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative.

Mujāhid read (yaẓẓahhara) with the ẓāʾ and hāʾ doubled, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read (yuẓharu), with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the hāʾ, in the passive voice, with (al-fasādu) in the nominative.

When Musa heard the statement of Fir'awn, he sought refuge in Allah from the evil of every arrogant one who denies the return. He said (wa-Rabbikum), urging them to follow his example, so that they would seek refuge in Allah and hold fast to Him.

And ﴿every arrogant one﴾ includes Fir'awn and others among the tyrants. This was by way of allusion, and it was more eloquent.

Takabbur (arrogance) is a person's exaggerated opinion of himself together with his lowliness, because he acts (accordingly). And ﴿does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning: in the recompense. This was more emphatic in his boldness, since he had acquired an exaggerated opinion of himself and a lack of concern for what he had committed. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read (ʿudtu) with idghām (assimilation of the two identical consonants); the rest of the Seven read it with izhār (clear pronunciation, without assimilation).

﴿A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, said﴾. It has been said that he was a Copt, a cousin of Fir'awn, who functioned in the position of crown prince and in the position of chief of police. It has been said that he was a Copt who was not of his kin. It has been said that he was described as "from the family of Fir'awn" because outwardly he was upon the religion of Fir'awn and his followers.

It has been said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, and that (from the family of Fir'awn) is connected to his saying ﴿who was concealing his faith﴾, not in the position of a description of a man, as the apparent meaning indicates. This has a remoteness to it, since none of the Children of Israel would have dared to speak before Fir'awn with the like of what this man said.

The view of those who connected (from the family of Fir'awn) with (yaktumu, he conceals) has been rejected, because one does not say: "I concealed such-and-such from so-and-so." One says: "I concealed so-and-so such-and-such." The Exalted said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 42], and the poet said:

"I concealed you by night, keeping watch with the Jamūmayn, and two concerns, one hidden and one apparent.
The inner talk of a soul that complains of what troubles it, and a watering place of cares that will not find a way out."

That is: I concealed from you the inner talk of a soul and two concerns. It has been said: his name was Simʿān. It has been said: Ḥabīb. It has been said: Ḥizqīl. The majority read (rajulun) with a ḍamma on the jīm. ʿĪsā, ʿAbd al-Wārith, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUqayl and Ḥamza ibn al-Qāsim, from Abū ʿAmr, read it with a sukūn (the pause of the consonant), and this is the dialect of Tamīm and Najd.

﴿Will you kill a man because he says﴾, meaning: because he says ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾. This was a great denunciation from him and a rebuke of them, as if he said: Will you commit the heinous act, which is killing a sacred soul, and you have no justification for committing it except the word of truth that he uttered, which is his saying ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾, when ﴿he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord﴾, meaning: from the One to whom he attributed lordship, and He is your Lord and not only his Lord? This was a means of drawing them toward acknowledgment. Al-Zamakhsharī said: You may posit an omitted genitive construction, meaning: at the time when he says. The meaning would then be: will you kill him at the moment you heard this statement from him without deliberation or reflection on his matter? End of quotation.

What he permitted, of positing an omitted noun (a time-noun) in this way, is not allowed. You say: "I came at the crowing of the rooster," meaning: at the time of the crowing of the rooster; you do not say "I come that the rooster crows." The grammarians have stated this explicitly. The condition for this is that the verbal noun be explicitly stated, not implied, and that the verb (an yaqūla, "that he says") not be an explicit verbal noun.

(bil-bayyināt): with the proofs of the oneness of Allah, which are those he mentioned in (Ṭā-Hā and al-Shuʿarāʾ) during his dialogue with him when he asked about his Lord, exalted is He.

When he had explicitly denounced them, he then misled them by dividing his matter into falsehood and truth, and he conveyed this in the form of possibility and counsel. He began the division with his saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, his lie is upon him﴾, showing courtesy and following the path of fairness in speech, and out of fear that if he denied their killing him, they would suspect him of supporting and defending him. So by this division and by beginning with the case of lying, he gave them the impression that he was unsure, in order to remain safe from their evil, and so that this would make it easier for them to accept. The meaning of ﴿his lie is upon him﴾ is: its harm will not pass beyond him.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾. He himself believed that he was a truthful prophet with certainty, but he used the word (some) in order to make the proof binding in its entirety on the matter, and there is in it no negation that everything he promises them would befall them.

A group said: some of the punishment that he mentions will befall you, and that was in their destruction, and the meaning would be: the single oath from what he threatens will befall you, and that is a part of what he promises, because he, peace be upon him, promised them that if they believed there would be blessing, and if they disbelieved there would be vengeance.

Another group said: some of what he promises you is the punishment of this world, because it is a part of the punishment of the Hereafter, and after that they will go to the Fire.

Abū ʿUbayda and others said: (some) carries the meaning of (all), and they cited the verse of ʿAmr ibn Shasim al-Qaṭāmī:

"The one who takes his time may reach some of his need, and haste may bring a slip."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: That is because when he supposed him truthful, he had affirmed that he is truthful in everything he promises. But he appended ﴿some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ so as to reduce for them part of his right in the outward meaning of the speech, so that he would show them that he is not one whose speech is given in full, let alone one who would be zealous for him. End of quotation.

(If you say): It is reported from Abū ʿUbayda that he divided (some) by (all), and he cited the verse of Labīd, which is:

"Abandoner of places when I do not like them, and he shows you from the portion of souls their death."

(I say): If the report from him is authentic, then what al-Mazini said in the matter of "al-Afi" has come true: "He was more ignorant than to understand what I say to him." End of quote. He means that Abu Ubayda was criticized by people for his belief that "ba'd" (some) can mean "kull" (all). They also cited, as evidence that "ba'd" can mean "kull," the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, affairs, when the youths manage them without the elders, you see in some of them a flaw."

That is: when he sees the youths. For this reason he said "dabbarahā" (he managed them) and did not say "dabbarūhā" (they managed them), taking into account the omitted noun it is attached to.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ In this there is an indication of the high standing of Musa, peace be upon him, and that one whom Allah has chosen for prophethood cannot commit transgression or lying. There is also an allusion to Pharaoh, for he was the extreme of transgression against himself by killing the sons of the believers, and the extreme of lying, since he claimed divinity and lordship; and one of such a state, Allah does not guide.

In a hadith: "The sincere (siddiqun) are three: Habib the carpenter, the believer of the family of Yasin, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, and Ali ibn Abi Talib."

And in a hadith: that he (ﷺ) circled the House (the Ka'ba), and when he finished, he took hold of the edges of his garment. They said to him: "Are you the one who forbids us what our fathers used to worship?" He said: "I am that one." Then Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, embraced him from behind, and said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?" raising his voice with that, while his eyes shed tears, until they released him.

And from Ja'far al-Sadiq: the believer of Pharaoh's family said that secretly, while Abu Bakr said it openly. And al-Suddi said: "(transgressor)" means by killing. Qatada said: "(transgressor)" means by disbelief.

The author of al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir said: This is a type of the sciences of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan) which our scholars call "istidraj al-mukhatab" (drawing the addressee along). When he saw that Pharaoh had resolved to kill Musa, and the people were set on denying him, he wished to defend him by a means through which he would conceal from them that he was partisan to him and one of his followers. So he came to them by way of advice and gentleness and said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ He did not mention his name, but said "a man," giving the impression that he does not know him and is not partisan to him, ﴿because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, and did not say "a man who believes in Allah" or "he is a prophet of Allah," for had he said any of that they would have known he was partisan. They would not have accepted his words. Then he followed it with what came after, putting first his words: ﴿And if he is a liar﴾, in agreement with their opinion of him. Then he followed it with: ﴿and if he is truthful﴾. Had he said, "He is truthful, and all that he promises you," they would have known he was partisan and that he claims he is a prophet and that he confirms him, for prophets do not omit anything of what they say. Then he followed it with words from which it is understood that he is not a confirmer: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ End of quote.

Then he said: "(O my people)" — a gentle call in his admonition.

﴿O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land﴾, that is: knowing, "in the land": in the land of Egypt, you have prevailed over the Children of Israel in it, subdued them, and enslaved them. He called them to the kingdom, which is the greatest and most exalted rank of this world, and it is from the aspect of their desires. "Dominant" (zahirin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the governing element in it is the same as that governing the prepositional phrase, and its owner of the state is the pronoun in "lakum" (for you).

Then he warned them against ruining themselves: that if the might of Allah came upon them, they would find no helper for them nor any repeller. He included himself in his words ﴿to help us﴾ and "came to us," because he is one of them by kinship, and to make them know that what he advises them with is something he shares with them.

The words of this believer indicate that the awe of Pharaoh had left his heart, and for this reason Pharaoh was subdued and said: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, that is: I advise you only to kill him, and I think only that is right. This is the statement of one who has no authority. He used "ma" with "illa" for restriction and emphasis.

﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, not what you say of leaving him alone. He lied, for he was fearful and anxious, and he knew that what Musa, peace be upon him, brought was true, but he was forcing himself and showing outwardly the opposite of what he concealed.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, and Abu'l-Qasim al-Hudhali mention here that Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited "al-Rashshad" with a shadda on the shin.

Abu'l-Fath said: It is an active participle in the intensive pattern from the triliteral verb rashada, so it is like 'abbad from 'abada.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or from rashida, like 'allam from 'alima. Al-Nahhas said: It is a solecism (lahn), and he imagined it was from the quadriliteral verb. It was answered that it is not necessarily from the quadriliteral; rather, it is from the triliteral. However, some have held that it is from the quadriliteral, so they formed fa''al from af'al, like darrak from adraka, sa'ir from asar, jabbar from ajbara, and qassar from aqsara. But this is not regular, so it should not be applied where there is an alternative; and fa''al from the triliteral is regular, so it was applied to it.

Abu Hatim said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to interpret it as "the path of Allah."

Ibn Atiyya said: This is far from Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him.

Was Pharaoh anything but claiming that he is a god? And the form of the word is connected to this interpretation. End of quote.

Mentioning the disagreement about this letter, which is part of Pharaoh's speech, is an error, and attributing Mu'adh's statement to it is an error. The correct view is that the disagreement concerns the believer's words: ﴿Follow me, I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Abu'l-Fadl al-Razi in his book "al-Lawami'" on the anomalous readings says, with this text: Mu'adh ibn Jabal: ﴿sabil al-rashad﴾ [Ghafir: 38], the second letter with a shadda, and likewise al-Hasan. It is the path of Allah the Exalted, which made clear the laws; thus Mu'adh ibn Jabal interpreted it. It is derived from "mursid," like darrak from mudrik, jabbar from mujbir, and qassar from muqsir an al-amr; and it has counted parallels. As for qassar, it is from qasara (for) the cloth, qisara. Ibn Khalawayh, after mentioning the disagreement over "al-tanad" and over "sadd 'an al-sabil," said: "(sabil al-rashshad with a shadda on the shin)" — Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Ibn Khalawayh said: he means by al-rashshad Allah the Exalted. End of quote.

So he did not mention any disagreement except in the believer's words: ﴿I guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Therefore mentioning the disagreement in it in Pharaoh's words is an error, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal did not interpret "al-rashshad" as Allah the Exalted except in the believer's words, not in Pharaoh's words. Ibn Atiyya said: That interpretation is from Pharaoh's words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 23–31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We indeed sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun. They said: "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the scheming of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ ﴿Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."﴾ ﴿Musa said: "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, his lie is upon him; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾ ﴿"O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land. But who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?" Fir'awn said: "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾

It has been said that he is someone other than that one. He specified Haman and Qarun because of their standing in disbelief, and because they were the most well-known followers of Fir'awn.

﴿They said: "A sorcerer, a liar"﴾, meaning: this is a sorcerer, because of what appeared at his hands of turning the staff into a serpent and the shining light that appeared on his hand; a liar, because he claimed that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.

He means that this is other than the first killing. They were ordered to kill the sons of the believers so that Musa, peace be upon him, would not be strengthened by them, and to spare the women for service and enslavement. But what they were ordered to do did not happen, nor was it accomplished for them, and Allah did not help them in it.

"If you were to settle among the Banu Asad in the realm of ʿAmr, and Fadak came between us..."

End of quotation.

They used to worship him and also worship idols, as He said: ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 127]. ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, which is by the licentiousness that takes away security, causes the fields and livelihoods to be ruined, and makes people perish by killing and loss.
