So by this division and by beginning with the case of lying, he gave them the impression that he was unsure, in order to remain safe from their evil, and so that this would make it easier for them to accept. The meaning of ﴿his lie is upon him﴾ is: its harm will not pass beyond him.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾. He himself believed that he was a truthful prophet with certainty, but he used the word (some) in order to make the proof binding in its entirety on the matter, and there is in it no negation that everything he promises them would befall them.

A group said: some of the punishment that he mentions will befall you, and that was in their destruction, and the meaning would be: the single oath from what he threatens will befall you, and that is a part of what he promises, because he, peace be upon him, promised them that if they believed there would be blessing, and if they disbelieved there would be vengeance.

Another group said: some of what he promises you is the punishment of this world, because it is a part of the punishment of the Hereafter, and after that they will go to the Fire.

Abū ʿUbayda and others said: (some) carries the meaning of (all), and they cited the verse of ʿAmr ibn Shasim al-Qaṭāmī:

"The one who takes his time may reach some of his need, and haste may bring a slip."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: That is because when he supposed him truthful, he had affirmed that he is truthful in everything he promises. But he appended ﴿some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ so as to reduce for them part of his right in the outward meaning of the speech, so that he would show them that he is not one whose speech is given in full, let alone one who would be zealous for him. End of quotation.

(If you say): It is reported from Abū ʿUbayda that he divided (some) by (all), and he cited the verse of Labīd, which is:

"Abandoner of places when I do not like them, and he shows you from the portion of souls their death."

(I say): If the report from him is authentic, then what al-Mazini said in the matter of "al-Afi" has come true: "He was more ignorant than to understand what I say to him." End of quote. He means that Abu Ubayda was criticized by people for his belief that "ba'd" (some) can mean "kull" (all). They also cited, as evidence that "ba'd" can mean "kull," the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, affairs, when the youths manage them without the elders, you see in some of them a flaw."

That is: when he sees the youths. For this reason he said "dabbarahā" (he managed them) and did not say "dabbarūhā" (they managed them), taking into account the omitted noun it is attached to.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ In this there is an indication of the high standing of Musa, peace be upon him, and that one whom Allah has chosen for prophethood cannot commit transgression or lying. There is also an allusion to Pharaoh, for he was the extreme of transgression against himself by killing the sons of the believers, and the extreme of lying, since he claimed divinity and lordship; and one of such a state, Allah does not guide.

In a hadith: "The sincere (siddiqun) are three: Habib the carpenter, the believer of the family of Yasin, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, and Ali ibn Abi Talib."

And in a hadith: that he (ﷺ) circled the House (the Ka'ba), and when he finished, he took hold of the edges of his garment. They said to him: "Are you the one who forbids us what our fathers used to worship?" He said: "I am that one." Then Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, embraced him from behind, and said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?" raising his voice with that, while his eyes shed tears, until they released him.

And from Ja'far al-Sadiq: the believer of Pharaoh's family said that secretly, while Abu Bakr said it openly. And al-Suddi said: "(transgressor)" means by killing. Qatada said: "(transgressor)" means by disbelief.

The author of al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir said: This is a type of the sciences of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan) which our scholars call "istidraj al-mukhatab" (drawing the addressee along). When he saw that Pharaoh had resolved to kill Musa, and the people were set on denying him, he wished to defend him by a means through which he would conceal from them that he was partisan to him and one of his followers. So he came to them by way of advice and gentleness and said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ He did not mention his name, but said "a man," giving the impression that he does not know him and is not partisan to him, ﴿because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, and did not say "a man who believes in Allah" or "he is a prophet of Allah," for had he said any of that they would have known he was partisan. They would not have accepted his words. Then he followed it with what came after, putting first his words: ﴿And if he is a liar﴾, in agreement with their opinion of him. Then he followed it with: ﴿and if he is truthful﴾. Had he said, "He is truthful, and all that he promises you," they would have known he was partisan and that he claims he is a prophet and that he confirms him, for prophets do not omit anything of what they say. Then he followed it with words from which it is understood that he is not a confirmer: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar.﴾ End of quote.

Then he said: "(O my people)" — a gentle call in his admonition.

﴿O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land﴾, that is: knowing, "in the land": in the land of Egypt, you have prevailed over the Children of Israel in it, subdued them, and enslaved them. He called them to the kingdom, which is the greatest and most exalted rank of this world, and it is from the aspect of their desires. "Dominant" (zahirin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), the governing element in it is the same as that governing the prepositional phrase, and its owner of the state is the pronoun in "lakum" (for you).

Then he warned them against ruining themselves: that if the might of Allah came upon them, they would find no helper for them nor any repeller. He included himself in his words ﴿to help us﴾ and "came to us," because he is one of them by kinship, and to make them know that what he advises them with is something he shares with them.

The words of this believer indicate that the awe of Pharaoh had left his heart, and for this reason Pharaoh was subdued and said: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, that is: I advise you only to kill him, and I think only that is right. This is the statement of one who has no authority. He used "ma" with "illa" for restriction and emphasis.

﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, not what you say of leaving him alone. He lied, for he was fearful and anxious, and he knew that what Musa, peace be upon him, brought was true, but he was forcing himself and showing outwardly the opposite of what he concealed.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, and Abu'l-Qasim al-Hudhali mention here that Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited "al-Rashshad" with a shadda on the shin.

Abu'l-Fath said: It is an active participle in the intensive pattern from the triliteral verb rashada, so it is like 'abbad from 'abada.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Or from rashida, like 'allam from 'alima. Al-Nahhas said: It is a solecism (lahn), and he imagined it was from the quadriliteral verb. It was answered that it is not necessarily from the quadriliteral; rather, it is from the triliteral. However, some have held that it is from the quadriliteral, so they formed fa''al from af'al, like darrak from adraka, sa'ir from asar, jabbar from ajbara, and qassar from aqsara. But this is not regular, so it should not be applied where there is an alternative; and fa''al from the triliteral is regular, so it was applied to it.

Abu Hatim said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to interpret it as "the path of Allah."

Ibn Atiyya said: This is far from Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him.

Was Pharaoh anything but claiming that he is a god? And the form of the word is connected to this interpretation. End of quote.

Mentioning the disagreement about this letter, which is part of Pharaoh's speech, is an error, and attributing Mu'adh's statement to it is an error. The correct view is that the disagreement concerns the believer's words: ﴿Follow me, I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Abu'l-Fadl al-Razi in his book "al-Lawami'" on the anomalous readings says, with this text: Mu'adh ibn Jabal: ﴿sabil al-rashad﴾ [Ghafir: 38], the second letter with a shadda, and likewise al-Hasan. It is the path of Allah the Exalted, which made clear the laws; thus Mu'adh ibn Jabal interpreted it. It is derived from "mursid," like darrak from mudrik, jabbar from mujbir, and qassar from muqsir an al-amr; and it has counted parallels. As for qassar, it is from qasara (for) the cloth, qisara. Ibn Khalawayh, after mentioning the disagreement over "al-tanad" and over "sadd 'an al-sabil," said: "(sabil al-rashshad with a shadda on the shin)" — Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Ibn Khalawayh said: he means by al-rashshad Allah the Exalted. End of quote.

So he did not mention any disagreement except in the believer's words: ﴿I guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 38]. Therefore mentioning the disagreement in it in Pharaoh's words is an error, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal did not interpret "al-rashshad" as Allah the Exalted except in the believer's words, not in Pharaoh's words. Ibn Atiyya said: That interpretation is from Pharaoh's words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 32–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾ [Ghafir: 30] ﴿"like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants"﴾ [Ghafir: 31] ﴿"And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out"﴾ ﴿"the day you turn back fleeing. You will have no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide"﴾ ﴿"And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Until, when he died, you said: 'Allah will never send after him a messenger.' Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter"﴾ ﴿"Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believed. Thus does Allah seal over every heart of an arrogant tyrant"﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the means"﴾ ﴿"the means to the heavens, and look at the God of Moses, though I think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deed made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the way. And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct"﴾ ﴿"O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence"﴾ ﴿"Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its equivalent, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account"﴾.

[p. 445] The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that this believer is the man who said: ﴿Will you kill a man…﴾ [Ghafir: 28], whose statements Allah related up to the end of the verses.

When he saw what had befallen Pharaoh of weakness and fear, he brought another kind of warning and frightened them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. His soul grew strong until he recited to him what he recited, and he did not fear Pharaoh.

A group said: Rather, the speech of that believer was complete, and Allah the Exalted meant by "the one who believed" the one who believed in Moses (peace be upon him). They argued from the strength of his speech, and that he inclined with them toward faith, and mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter and other things, and the earlier speech was only openly addressed to them. He used the singular "day," either because the meaning is "like the days of the factions," or he meant the plural by it, i.e., "like the days of the factions," because it is known that each faction had a day. The factions (al-Ahzab) are those who formed factions against the prophets of Allah.

As for ﴿like the custom of﴾ [Ghafir: 31], Ibn Atiyya said it is a badal (substitution). Al-Zamakhshari said it is an 'atf bayan (explicative apposition).

Al-Zajjaj said: "like the day of a faction," and "custom" (da'b) means their habit and wont in disbelief and sins.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 31], i.e., His destroying them was justice from Him, and in it is an emphasis on the negation of injustice, since He attached it to the will. If He negates it from the will, then negating it from occurrence is more fitting and more appropriate.

When he frightened them that what befell the factions might befall them in this world, he frightened them about the matter of the Hereafter, saying, showing tenderness to them by calling them: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out﴾, and it is the Day of Gathering. "Al-tanad" is the verbal noun of "tanadA al-qawm," i.e., some of them called out to one another. The poet said:

[p. 464]
They called out to one another, saying: "Did you want a horseman for the horses?" I said: "Do I worship Allah? That is your destruction."

It was named the Day of Calling Out either because of some of them calling to others with woe and perdition, or because of the calling between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, as mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, or because people are called to the place of gathering, or because of the calling of the believer: ﴿Here, read my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19], and the disbeliever: ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 25]. A group read "al-tanad" with a sukun on the dal in pausal form in connected speech, treating it as a pause. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, al-Za'faranI, and Ibn Miqsam read "al-tannadd" with a shadda on the dal, from "nadda al-ba'ir" when it fled, as He said: ﴿The day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34], etc. Ibn Abbas and others said: in ﴿al-tanad﴾ with a light dal it is al-tanadi, i.e., there will be calling among people at the blowing of the Trumpet, and the blast of terror in this world, and they will flee on their faces due to the terror that has seized them, and some will call out to others.

This interpretation was related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the reminder with every call on the Day of Resurrection is a hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners. End.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

And He spread the creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling out.

In a hadith: "Indeed the people will have a turmoil on the Day of Resurrection, they will flee," thinking they will find a refuge; then he recited: ﴿The day you turn back fleeing﴾.

Mujahid said: its meaning is "fleeing." Al-Suddi said: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾ in your fleeing, until you are punished in the Fire. Qatada said: you will have no protector in going toward it, i.e., no preventer who prevents you from it, or helper.

When the believer despaired of their accepting it, he said: ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾.

Then he began to rebuke them for denying the messengers, by saying that Joseph had come to them with clear proofs. The apparent meaning is that it was Joseph son of Jacob, and Pharaoh is the Pharaoh of Moses. Ashhab related from Malik that it reached him that Pharaoh lived four hundred and forty years.

It was also said: rather, the one who came to them was Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob, and that Pharaoh is a Pharaoh other than the Pharaoh of Moses.

﴿With clear proofs﴾: with miracles. They continued doubting his mission and disbelieving, until when he died, ﴿you said: Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. This is not an affirmation of his mission, and how could it be, when they remained in doubt about him? Rather the meaning is: there is no messenger from Allah so that He would send him to the creation; so in it is the negation of a messenger and the negation of his sending.

It was read: "a-lan yab'atha" (with the interrogative hamza before the negative particle), as if some of them were confirming to others the negation of sending.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like the misguidance of Allah of you, i.e., when you did not accept from Joseph, ﴿Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾: meaning them, since they are the transgressors and the doubters concerning the messages of the prophets.

They permitted in ﴿those who dispute﴾ that it be an attribute of "man" (man), and a badal from it: i.e., its meaning is plural and a subject, by omitting a modifier, i.e., "the disputation of those who dispute," so that the pronoun in ﴿greatly hateful﴾ returns to that disputation first, or by omitting a modifier, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from His saying ﴿dispute﴾, or a pronoun returning to "man" according to its wording, on the condition that "those who" is an attribute or a badal, returned first to the wording of "man" in His saying: ﴿he is a transgressor, a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Then He made "those who" plural according to the meaning of "man," then He made it singular in His saying ﴿greatly hateful﴾ according to the wording of "man."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that ﴿those who dispute﴾ be the subject and ﴿without authority having come to them﴾ the predicate, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is His saying: "thus," i.e., ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ like that disputation, and ﴿Allah seals﴾ is a resumed statement. And whoever says ﴿greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾ is their disputation, has omitted the agent, and the agent cannot be omitted. End. What he permitted cannot be like this in eloquent speech, let alone in the speech of Allah. Because in it there is a dislocation of the speech, part from part, and committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one.

As for dislocating the speech: the apparent meaning is that ﴿without authority﴾ is connected to ﴿dispute﴾, and it cannot be understood to make it a predicate of "those who," because it is a prepositional phrase, so the estimate becomes: ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ are: existing, or residing, ﴿without authority﴾, i.e., in the absence of authority; because the bi' in that case is adverbial, a predicate reporting about the body. Likewise in His saying "seals," that it is resumed is a dislocation of the speech, because what came in the Qur'an of ﴿thus He seals﴾, or "we seal," came linked part to part, so here likewise. As for committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one: he made the kaf a noun acting as an agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and that is not permitted according to the doctrine of the Basrans except al-Akhfash, and it has not been established in the speech of the Arabs, I mean its prose: "he came to me like Zayd," meaning "like Zayd," so its nominality has not been established, so that it would be an agent.

As for His saying "and whoever says, etc.," the one who says that is al-Hawfi, and it is assumed of him that he explained the meaning and did not intend the i'rab (grammatical analysis). As for the explanation of the i'rab: that the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from ﴿dispute﴾, as they said: "whoever lies, it is worse for him," i.e., it is he, i.e., the lie understood from "lied." The preferable analysis of this sentence is that ﴿those who﴾ is the subject, its predicate ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and the agent is a pronoun of the verbal noun understood from ﴿dispute﴾. This attribute exists in Pharaoh and his people, and the admonisher to them has turned from addressing them to the third person, for the goodness of his discourse with them and winning their hearts, and presenting that in the form of reminding them, and not surprising them with direct address. In His saying ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ there is a kind of wonder and magnification at their disputation and a testimony to its going beyond the limit of its being a grave sin.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that sealing upon the hearts of the disputants. ﴿Allah seals﴾, i.e., He seals with misguidance and veils from guidance. Abu 'Amr ibn Dhakwan, al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "qalbin" with tanwin, describing the heart as arrogant and tyrannical, since it is their center and source, as they say: "the eye saw," and as He said: ﴿for indeed he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], and "al-ithm" is the whole. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be by omitting the modifier, i.e., "upon every heart-possessor who is arrogant," by making the attribute for the possessor of the heart. End. There is no necessity to hold the omission.

The rest of the seven read ﴿qalbi mutakabbirin﴾ with idafa, and the general word in it is general, so the generality of "arrogant tyrant" is entailed. Muqatil said: "al-mutakabbir" is one who is obstinate in magnifying the command of Allah, and "al-jabbar" is one who is empowered over the creation of Allah.

﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower"﴾. The statements of Pharaoh: "Leave me to kill Moses," "I show you only what I see," "O Haman, build for me a tower," are an evasion from disputing with Moses, and a return to things that are not sound. All of that is due to the dread and fear that had permeated him, and the lack of resistance, and his recognition that his destruction and the destruction of his people would be at the hand of Moses, and that his power had failed to affect Moses. This is despite his great shedding of blood.

The discussion of the tower (sarh) has preceded in Surat al-Qasas, so it suffices without repeating it.

Al-Suddi said: "al-asbab" are the paths. Qatada said: the doors. It was also said: he meant that perhaps, despite his nearness to the sky, he would find a means to hold onto. Whatever leads you to something is a means. He first mentioned "the means" in general, then substituted from it what clarified it. Clarification after generality conveys the magnification of the thing, since in the generality there is longing for the intended thing and wonder at the object sought; then through clarification the goal is attained and specified.

The majority read ﴿fa-attali'u﴾ in the nominative, coordinated with ﴿ablugh﴾, so both are hoped for. Al-A'raj, Abu Haywa, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Za'faranI, Ibn Miqsam, and Hafs read ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ with the 'ain in the accusative. Abu al-Qasim ibn Jibara and Ibn Atiyya said: it is in answer to a wish (tamanni). Al-Zamakhshari said: in answer to a hope (tarajji), likening hope to wish. End.

The grammarians differentiate between wish (tamanni) and hope (tarajji): they mention that wish occurs with both the possible and the impossible, while hope occurs only with the possible.

Reaching the means of the heavens is not possible, but Pharaoh presented the impossible in the form of the possible to deceive his listeners.

As for the accusative after the fa' in answer to hope, it is something the Kufans permitted and the Basrans prohibited. The Kufans argued (p. 466) with this reading and with the reading of Asim, ﴿then the reminder will benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 4] in Surat Abasa, since it is the answer to hope in His saying ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3], ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 3–4]. We have interpreted that as being a coordination upon an assumption, because the predicate of "la'alla" frequently comes in the Qur'anic text connected with "an," and in prose rarely.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verse 32–40 (part 2 of 2):

As for the one who put it in the accusative, he imagined that the verb in the nominative standing as a predicate was in the accusative governed by "an" (that). Coordinating on the basis of such imagined case (al-'atf 'ala al-tawahhum) is common, though it is not systematic (la yankas). Yet if something occurs and can be construed upon it, it is accepted. As for here, ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ (so that I may look), some have made it the answer (jawab) to the imperative, which is His saying: ﴿Build for me a tower﴾, as the poet said:
Oh she-camel, march with a wide stride
To Sulayman, so that we may rest.
When he said ﴿so that I may look upon the God of Musa﴾, that was an affirmation of the God of Musa, so he corrected this affirmation by saying ﴿and indeed I think him to be a liar﴾, meaning in his claim of divinity, just as he said in al-Qasas: ﴿Perhaps I may look upon the God of Musa, but indeed I think him to be among the liars﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿And thus﴾, meaning: like that adornment, in deluding Pharaoh into thinking that he would look upon the God of Musa.

﴿The evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾. The majority read ﴿zuyyina li-Fir'awna﴾ in the passive voice; it was also read as (zayyana), in the active voice. The majority read ﴿wa-suddu﴾ in the active voice, meaning: and Pharaoh barred (the way); the Kufans read it with a damma on the sad, in harmony with ﴿zuyyina﴾ in the passive voice; Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad, its origin being (sadada), the vowel was moved to the sad after imagining the deletion of the vowel; Ibn Ishaq and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read it with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal, nunated, in coordination with ﴿su'u 'amalihi﴾.

Al-tibab (ruin): loss. He lost his kingdom in this world through drowning, and in the Hereafter through the eternal abiding of the Fire. The believer's admonition was repeated after Pharaoh's speech by his calling to his people twice, following each call with what contains reproach and admonition, were there anyone who would accept it. Here he commanded them to follow him, so that he might guide them to the path of rectitude.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with a shadda on the shin (ya-shuddu), and the discussion of that has already preceded. The refutation of those who made this reading part of Pharaoh's speech: he summarized at first in His saying ﴿the path of rectitude﴾, which is the path of faith in God and following His law.

Then he explained, beginning with the condemnation of this world and the smallness of its affair, and that it is a passing enjoyment, it and whoever takes pleasure in it, and that the Hereafter is the abode of permanence from which there is no escape, either to Paradise or to the Fire.

And thus He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'mash, the two Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), the two Sahibs (Ibn Kathir? [see note]), and Hafs read ﴿yadkhulun﴾ in the active voice; the rest of the seven, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Isa read it in the passive voice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 32–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾ [Ghafir: 30] ﴿"like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants"﴾ [Ghafir: 31] ﴿"And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out"﴾ ﴿"the day you turn back fleeing. You will have no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide"﴾ ﴿"And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Until, when he died, you said: 'Allah will never send after him a messenger.' Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter"﴾ ﴿"Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believed. Thus does Allah seal over every heart of an arrogant tyrant"﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the means"﴾ ﴿"the means to the heavens, and look at the God of Moses, though I think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deed made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the way. And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct"﴾ ﴿"O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence"﴾ ﴿"Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its equivalent, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account"﴾.

[p. 445] The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that this believer is the man who said: ﴿Will you kill a man…﴾ [Ghafir: 28], whose statements Allah related up to the end of the verses.

When he saw what had befallen Pharaoh of weakness and fear, he brought another kind of warning and frightened them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. His soul grew strong until he recited to him what he recited, and he did not fear Pharaoh.

A group said: Rather, the speech of that believer was complete, and Allah the Exalted meant by "the one who believed" the one who believed in Moses (peace be upon him). They argued from the strength of his speech, and that he inclined with them toward faith, and mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter and other things, and the earlier speech was only openly addressed to them. He used the singular "day," either because the meaning is "like the days of the factions," or he meant the plural by it, i.e., "like the days of the factions," because it is known that each faction had a day. The factions (al-Ahzab) are those who formed factions against the prophets of Allah.

As for ﴿like the custom of﴾ [Ghafir: 31], Ibn Atiyya said it is a badal (substitution). Al-Zamakhshari said it is an 'atf bayan (explicative apposition).

Al-Zajjaj said: "like the day of a faction," and "custom" (da'b) means their habit and wont in disbelief and sins.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 31], i.e., His destroying them was justice from Him, and in it is an emphasis on the negation of injustice, since He attached it to the will. If He negates it from the will, then negating it from occurrence is more fitting and more appropriate.

When he frightened them that what befell the factions might befall them in this world, he frightened them about the matter of the Hereafter, saying, showing tenderness to them by calling them: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out﴾, and it is the Day of Gathering. "Al-tanad" is the verbal noun of "tanadA al-qawm," i.e., some of them called out to one another. The poet said:

[p. 464]
They called out to one another, saying: "Did you want a horseman for the horses?" I said: "Do I worship Allah? That is your destruction."

It was named the Day of Calling Out either because of some of them calling to others with woe and perdition, or because of the calling between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, as mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, or because people are called to the place of gathering, or because of the calling of the believer: ﴿Here, read my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19], and the disbeliever: ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 25]. A group read "al-tanad" with a sukun on the dal in pausal form in connected speech, treating it as a pause. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, al-Za'faranI, and Ibn Miqsam read "al-tannadd" with a shadda on the dal, from "nadda al-ba'ir" when it fled, as He said: ﴿The day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34], etc. Ibn Abbas and others said: in ﴿al-tanad﴾ with a light dal it is al-tanadi, i.e., there will be calling among people at the blowing of the Trumpet, and the blast of terror in this world, and they will flee on their faces due to the terror that has seized them, and some will call out to others.

This interpretation was related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the reminder with every call on the Day of Resurrection is a hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners. End.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

And He spread the creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling out.

In a hadith: "Indeed the people will have a turmoil on the Day of Resurrection, they will flee," thinking they will find a refuge; then he recited: ﴿The day you turn back fleeing﴾.

Mujahid said: its meaning is "fleeing." Al-Suddi said: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾ in your fleeing, until you are punished in the Fire. Qatada said: you will have no protector in going toward it, i.e., no preventer who prevents you from it, or helper.

When the believer despaired of their accepting it, he said: ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾.

Then he began to rebuke them for denying the messengers, by saying that Joseph had come to them with clear proofs. The apparent meaning is that it was Joseph son of Jacob, and Pharaoh is the Pharaoh of Moses. Ashhab related from Malik that it reached him that Pharaoh lived four hundred and forty years.

It was also said: rather, the one who came to them was Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob, and that Pharaoh is a Pharaoh other than the Pharaoh of Moses.

﴿With clear proofs﴾: with miracles. They continued doubting his mission and disbelieving, until when he died, ﴿you said: Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. This is not an affirmation of his mission, and how could it be, when they remained in doubt about him? Rather the meaning is: there is no messenger from Allah so that He would send him to the creation; so in it is the negation of a messenger and the negation of his sending.

It was read: "a-lan yab'atha" (with the interrogative hamza before the negative particle), as if some of them were confirming to others the negation of sending.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like the misguidance of Allah of you, i.e., when you did not accept from Joseph, ﴿Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾: meaning them, since they are the transgressors and the doubters concerning the messages of the prophets.

They permitted in ﴿those who dispute﴾ that it be an attribute of "man" (man), and a badal from it: i.e., its meaning is plural and a subject, by omitting a modifier, i.e., "the disputation of those who dispute," so that the pronoun in ﴿greatly hateful﴾ returns to that disputation first, or by omitting a modifier, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from His saying ﴿dispute﴾, or a pronoun returning to "man" according to its wording, on the condition that "those who" is an attribute or a badal, returned first to the wording of "man" in His saying: ﴿he is a transgressor, a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Then He made "those who" plural according to the meaning of "man," then He made it singular in His saying ﴿greatly hateful﴾ according to the wording of "man."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that ﴿those who dispute﴾ be the subject and ﴿without authority having come to them﴾ the predicate, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is His saying: "thus," i.e., ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ like that disputation, and ﴿Allah seals﴾ is a resumed statement. And whoever says ﴿greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾ is their disputation, has omitted the agent, and the agent cannot be omitted. End. What he permitted cannot be like this in eloquent speech, let alone in the speech of Allah. Because in it there is a dislocation of the speech, part from part, and committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one.

As for dislocating the speech: the apparent meaning is that ﴿without authority﴾ is connected to ﴿dispute﴾, and it cannot be understood to make it a predicate of "those who," because it is a prepositional phrase, so the estimate becomes: ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ are: existing, or residing, ﴿without authority﴾, i.e., in the absence of authority; because the bi' in that case is adverbial, a predicate reporting about the body. Likewise in His saying "seals," that it is resumed is a dislocation of the speech, because what came in the Qur'an of ﴿thus He seals﴾, or "we seal," came linked part to part, so here likewise. As for committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one: he made the kaf a noun acting as an agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and that is not permitted according to the doctrine of the Basrans except al-Akhfash, and it has not been established in the speech of the Arabs, I mean its prose: "he came to me like Zayd," meaning "like Zayd," so its nominality has not been established, so that it would be an agent.

As for His saying "and whoever says, etc.," the one who says that is al-Hawfi, and it is assumed of him that he explained the meaning and did not intend the i'rab (grammatical analysis). As for the explanation of the i'rab: that the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from ﴿dispute﴾, as they said: "whoever lies, it is worse for him," i.e., it is he, i.e., the lie understood from "lied." The preferable analysis of this sentence is that ﴿those who﴾ is the subject, its predicate ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and the agent is a pronoun of the verbal noun understood from ﴿dispute﴾. This attribute exists in Pharaoh and his people, and the admonisher to them has turned from addressing them to the third person, for the goodness of his discourse with them and winning their hearts, and presenting that in the form of reminding them, and not surprising them with direct address. In His saying ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ there is a kind of wonder and magnification at their disputation and a testimony to its going beyond the limit of its being a grave sin.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that sealing upon the hearts of the disputants. ﴿Allah seals﴾, i.e., He seals with misguidance and veils from guidance. Abu 'Amr ibn Dhakwan, al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "qalbin" with tanwin, describing the heart as arrogant and tyrannical, since it is their center and source, as they say: "the eye saw," and as He said: ﴿for indeed he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], and "al-ithm" is the whole. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be by omitting the modifier, i.e., "upon every heart-possessor who is arrogant," by making the attribute for the possessor of the heart. End. There is no necessity to hold the omission.

The rest of the seven read ﴿qalbi mutakabbirin﴾ with idafa, and the general word in it is general, so the generality of "arrogant tyrant" is entailed. Muqatil said: "al-mutakabbir" is one who is obstinate in magnifying the command of Allah, and "al-jabbar" is one who is empowered over the creation of Allah.

﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower"﴾. The statements of Pharaoh: "Leave me to kill Moses," "I show you only what I see," "O Haman, build for me a tower," are an evasion from disputing with Moses, and a return to things that are not sound. All of that is due to the dread and fear that had permeated him, and the lack of resistance, and his recognition that his destruction and the destruction of his people would be at the hand of Moses, and that his power had failed to affect Moses. This is despite his great shedding of blood.

The discussion of the tower (sarh) has preceded in Surat al-Qasas, so it suffices without repeating it.

Al-Suddi said: "al-asbab" are the paths. Qatada said: the doors. It was also said: he meant that perhaps, despite his nearness to the sky, he would find a means to hold onto. Whatever leads you to something is a means. He first mentioned "the means" in general, then substituted from it what clarified it. Clarification after generality conveys the magnification of the thing, since in the generality there is longing for the intended thing and wonder at the object sought; then through clarification the goal is attained and specified.

The majority read ﴿fa-attali'u﴾ in the nominative, coordinated with ﴿ablugh﴾, so both are hoped for. Al-A'raj, Abu Haywa, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Za'faranI, Ibn Miqsam, and Hafs read ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ with the 'ain in the accusative. Abu al-Qasim ibn Jibara and Ibn Atiyya said: it is in answer to a wish (tamanni). Al-Zamakhshari said: in answer to a hope (tarajji), likening hope to wish. End.

The grammarians differentiate between wish (tamanni) and hope (tarajji): they mention that wish occurs with both the possible and the impossible, while hope occurs only with the possible.

Reaching the means of the heavens is not possible, but Pharaoh presented the impossible in the form of the possible to deceive his listeners.

As for the accusative after the fa' in answer to hope, it is something the Kufans permitted and the Basrans prohibited. The Kufans argued (p. 466) with this reading and with the reading of Asim, ﴿then the reminder will benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 4] in Surat Abasa, since it is the answer to hope in His saying ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3], ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 3–4]. We have interpreted that as being a coordination upon an assumption, because the predicate of "la'alla" frequently comes in the Qur'anic text connected with "an," and in prose rarely.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verse 32–40 (part 2 of 2):

As for the one who put it in the accusative, he imagined that the verb in the nominative standing as a predicate was in the accusative governed by "an" (that). Coordinating on the basis of such imagined case (al-'atf 'ala al-tawahhum) is common, though it is not systematic (la yankas). Yet if something occurs and can be construed upon it, it is accepted. As for here, ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ (so that I may look), some have made it the answer (jawab) to the imperative, which is His saying: ﴿Build for me a tower﴾, as the poet said:
Oh she-camel, march with a wide stride
To Sulayman, so that we may rest.
When he said ﴿so that I may look upon the God of Musa﴾, that was an affirmation of the God of Musa, so he corrected this affirmation by saying ﴿and indeed I think him to be a liar﴾, meaning in his claim of divinity, just as he said in al-Qasas: ﴿Perhaps I may look upon the God of Musa, but indeed I think him to be among the liars﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿And thus﴾, meaning: like that adornment, in deluding Pharaoh into thinking that he would look upon the God of Musa.

﴿The evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾. The majority read ﴿zuyyina li-Fir'awna﴾ in the passive voice; it was also read as (zayyana), in the active voice. The majority read ﴿wa-suddu﴾ in the active voice, meaning: and Pharaoh barred (the way); the Kufans read it with a damma on the sad, in harmony with ﴿zuyyina﴾ in the passive voice; Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad, its origin being (sadada), the vowel was moved to the sad after imagining the deletion of the vowel; Ibn Ishaq and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read it with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal, nunated, in coordination with ﴿su'u 'amalihi﴾.

Al-tibab (ruin): loss. He lost his kingdom in this world through drowning, and in the Hereafter through the eternal abiding of the Fire. The believer's admonition was repeated after Pharaoh's speech by his calling to his people twice, following each call with what contains reproach and admonition, were there anyone who would accept it. Here he commanded them to follow him, so that he might guide them to the path of rectitude.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with a shadda on the shin (ya-shuddu), and the discussion of that has already preceded. The refutation of those who made this reading part of Pharaoh's speech: he summarized at first in His saying ﴿the path of rectitude﴾, which is the path of faith in God and following His law.

Then he explained, beginning with the condemnation of this world and the smallness of its affair, and that it is a passing enjoyment, it and whoever takes pleasure in it, and that the Hereafter is the abode of permanence from which there is no escape, either to Paradise or to the Fire.

And thus He said: ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'mash, the two Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), the two Sahibs (Ibn Kathir? [see note]), and Hafs read ﴿yadkhulun﴾ in the active voice; the rest of the seven, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Isa read it in the passive voice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 40, verses 32–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The one who believed said: "O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾ [Ghafir: 30] ﴿"like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants"﴾ [Ghafir: 31] ﴿"And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out"﴾ ﴿"the day you turn back fleeing. You will have no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide"﴾ ﴿"And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Until, when he died, you said: 'Allah will never send after him a messenger.' Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter"﴾ ﴿"Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believed. Thus does Allah seal over every heart of an arrogant tyrant"﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the means"﴾ ﴿"the means to the heavens, and look at the God of Moses, though I think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deed made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the way. And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct"﴾ ﴿"O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence"﴾ ﴿"Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its equivalent, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account"﴾.

[p. 445] The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that this believer is the man who said: ﴿Will you kill a man…﴾ [Ghafir: 28], whose statements Allah related up to the end of the verses.

When he saw what had befallen Pharaoh of weakness and fear, he brought another kind of warning and frightened them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. His soul grew strong until he recited to him what he recited, and he did not fear Pharaoh.

A group said: Rather, the speech of that believer was complete, and Allah the Exalted meant by "the one who believed" the one who believed in Moses (peace be upon him). They argued from the strength of his speech, and that he inclined with them toward faith, and mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter and other things, and the earlier speech was only openly addressed to them. He used the singular "day," either because the meaning is "like the days of the factions," or he meant the plural by it, i.e., "like the days of the factions," because it is known that each faction had a day. The factions (al-Ahzab) are those who formed factions against the prophets of Allah.

As for ﴿like the custom of﴾ [Ghafir: 31], Ibn Atiyya said it is a badal (substitution). Al-Zamakhshari said it is an 'atf bayan (explicative apposition).

Al-Zajjaj said: "like the day of a faction," and "custom" (da'b) means their habit and wont in disbelief and sins.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 31], i.e., His destroying them was justice from Him, and in it is an emphasis on the negation of injustice, since He attached it to the will. If He negates it from the will, then negating it from occurrence is more fitting and more appropriate.

When he frightened them that what befell the factions might befall them in this world, he frightened them about the matter of the Hereafter, saying, showing tenderness to them by calling them: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out﴾, and it is the Day of Gathering. "Al-tanad" is the verbal noun of "tanadA al-qawm," i.e., some of them called out to one another. The poet said:

[p. 464]
They called out to one another, saying: "Did you want a horseman for the horses?" I said: "Do I worship Allah? That is your destruction."

It was named the Day of Calling Out either because of some of them calling to others with woe and perdition, or because of the calling between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, as mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, or because people are called to the place of gathering, or because of the calling of the believer: ﴿Here, read my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19], and the disbeliever: ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 25]. This interpretation was related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the reminder with every call on the Day of Resurrection is a hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners. End.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

And He spread the creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling out.

In a hadith: "Indeed the people will have a turmoil on the Day of Resurrection, they will flee," thinking they will find a refuge; then he recited: ﴿The day you turn back fleeing﴾.

Mujahid said: its meaning is "fleeing." Al-Suddi said: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾ in your fleeing, until you are punished in the Fire. Qatada said: you will have no protector in going toward it, i.e., no preventer who prevents you from it, or helper.

When the believer despaired of their accepting it, he said: ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾.

Then he began to rebuke them for denying the messengers, by saying that Joseph had come to them with clear proofs. The apparent meaning is that it was Joseph son of Jacob, and Pharaoh is the Pharaoh of Moses. Ashhab related from Malik that it reached him that Pharaoh lived four hundred and forty years.

It was also said: rather, the one who came to them was Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob, and that Pharaoh is a Pharaoh other than the Pharaoh of Moses.

﴿With clear proofs﴾: with miracles. They continued doubting his mission and disbelieving, until when he died, ﴿you said: Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. This is not an affirmation of his mission, and how could it be, when they remained in doubt about him? Rather the meaning is: there is no messenger from Allah so that He would send him to the creation; so in it is the negation of a messenger and the negation of his sending.

It was read: "a-lan yab'atha" (with the interrogative hamza before the negative particle), as if some of them were confirming to others the negation of sending.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like the misguidance of Allah of you, i.e., when you did not accept from Joseph, ﴿Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾: meaning them, since they are the transgressors and the doubters concerning the messages of the prophets.

They permitted in ﴿those who dispute﴾ that it be an attribute of "man" (man), and a badal from it: i.e., its meaning is plural and a subject, by omitting a modifier, i.e., "the disputation of those who dispute," so that the pronoun in ﴿greatly hateful﴾ returns to that disputation first, or by omitting a modifier, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from His saying ﴿dispute﴾, or a pronoun returning to "man" according to its wording, on the condition that "those who" is an attribute or a badal, returned first to the wording of "man" in His saying: ﴿he is a transgressor, a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Then He made "those who" plural according to the meaning of "man," then He made it singular in His saying ﴿greatly hateful﴾ according to the wording of "man."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that ﴿those who dispute﴾ be the subject and ﴿without authority having come to them﴾ the predicate, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is His saying: "thus," i.e., ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ like that disputation, and ﴿Allah seals﴾ is a resumed statement. And whoever says ﴿greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾ is their disputation, has omitted the agent, and the agent cannot be omitted. End. What he permitted cannot be like this in eloquent speech, let alone in the speech of Allah. Because in it there is a dislocation of the speech, part from part, and committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one.

As for dislocating the speech: the apparent meaning is that ﴿without authority﴾ is connected to ﴿dispute﴾, and it cannot be understood to make it a predicate of "those who," because it is a prepositional phrase, so the estimate becomes: ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ are: existing, or residing, ﴿without authority﴾, i.e., in the absence of authority; because the bi' in that case is adverbial, a predicate reporting about the body. Likewise in His saying "seals," that it is resumed is a dislocation of the speech, because what came in the Qur'an of ﴿thus He seals﴾, or "we seal," came linked part to part, so here likewise. As for committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one: he made the kaf a noun acting as an agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and that is not permitted according to the doctrine of the Basrans except al-Akhfash, and it has not been established in the speech of the Arabs, I mean its prose: "he came to me like Zayd," meaning "like Zayd," so its nominality has not been established, so that it would be an agent.

As for His saying "and whoever says, etc.," the one who says that is al-Hawfi, and it is assumed of him that he explained the meaning and did not intend the i'rab (grammatical analysis). As for the explanation of the i'rab: that the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from ﴿dispute﴾, as they said: "whoever lies, it is worse for him," i.e., it is he, i.e., the lie understood from "lied." The preferable analysis of this sentence is that ﴿those who﴾ is the subject, its predicate ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and the agent is a pronoun of the verbal noun understood from ﴿dispute﴾. This attribute exists in Pharaoh and his people, and the admonisher to them has turned from addressing them to the third person, for the goodness of his discourse with them and winning their hearts, and presenting that in the form of reminding them, and not surprising them with direct address. In His saying ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ there is a kind of wonder and magnification at their disputation and a testimony to its going beyond the limit of its being a grave sin.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that sealing upon the hearts of the disputants. ﴿Allah seals﴾, i.e., He seals with misguidance and veils from guidance. Abu 'Amr ibn Dhakwan, al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "qalbin" with tanwin, describing the heart as arrogant and tyrannical, since it is their center and source, as they say: "the eye saw," and as He said: ﴿for indeed he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], and "al-ithm" is the whole. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be by omitting the modifier, i.e., "upon every heart-possessor who is arrogant," by making the attribute for the possessor of the heart. End. There is no necessity to hold the omission.

The rest of the seven read ﴿qalbi mutakabbirin﴾ with idafa, and the general word in it is general, so the generality of "arrogant tyrant" is entailed. Muqatil said: "al-mutakabbir" is one who is obstinate in magnifying the command of Allah, and "al-jabbar" is one who is empowered over the creation of Allah.

﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a tower"﴾. The statements of Pharaoh: "Leave me to kill Moses," "I show you only what I see," "O Haman, build for me a tower," are an evasion from disputing with Moses, and a return to things that are not sound. All of that is due to the dread and fear that had permeated him, and the lack of resistance, and his recognition that his destruction and the destruction of his people would be at the hand of Moses, and that his power had failed to affect Moses. This is despite his great shedding of blood.

The discussion of the tower (sarh) has preceded in Surat al-Qasas, so it suffices without repeating it.

Al-Suddi said: "al-asbab" are the paths. Qatada said: the doors. It was also said: he meant that perhaps, despite his nearness to the sky, he would find a means to hold onto. Whatever leads you to something is a means. He first mentioned "the means" in general, then substituted from it what clarified it. Clarification after generality conveys the magnification of the thing, since in the generality there is longing for the intended thing and wonder at the object sought; then through clarification the goal is attained and specified.

The majority read ﴿fa-attali'u﴾ in the nominative, coordinated with ﴿ablugh﴾, so both are hoped for. Al-A'raj, Abu Haywa, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Za'faranI, Ibn Miqsam, and Hafs read ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ with the 'ain in the accusative. Abu al-Qasim ibn Jibara and Ibn Atiyya said: it is in answer to a wish (tamanni). Al-Zamakhshari said: in answer to a hope (tarajji), likening hope to wish. End.

The grammarians differentiate between wish (tamanni) and hope (tarajji): they mention that wish occurs with both the possible and the impossible, while hope occurs only with the possible.

Reaching the means of the heavens is not possible, but Pharaoh presented the impossible in the form of the possible to deceive his listeners.

As for the accusative after the fa' in answer to hope, it is something the Kufans permitted and the Basrans prohibited. The Kufans argued (p. 466) with this reading and with the reading of Asim, ﴿then the reminder will benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 4] in Surat Abasa, since it is the answer to hope in His saying ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3], ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [Abasa: 3–4]. We have interpreted that as being a coordination upon an assumption, because the predicate of "la'alla" frequently comes in the Qur'anic text connected with "an," and in prose rarely.

As for the one who put it in the accusative, he imagined that the verb in the nominative standing as a predicate was in the accusative governed by "an" (that). As for here, ﴿fa-attali'a﴾ (so that I may look), some have made it the answer (jawab) to the imperative, which is His saying: ﴿Build for me a tower﴾, as the poet said:
Oh she-camel, march with a wide stride
To Sulayman, so that we may rest.
When he said ﴿so that I may look upon the God of Musa﴾, that was an affirmation of the God of Musa, so he corrected this affirmation by saying ﴿and indeed I think him to be a liar﴾, meaning in his claim of divinity, just as he said in al-Qasas: ﴿Perhaps I may look upon the God of Musa, but indeed I think him to be among the liars﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿And thus﴾, meaning: like that adornment, in deluding Pharaoh into thinking that he would look upon the God of Musa.

The factions (al-Ahzab) are those who formed factions against the prophets of Allah.

As for ﴿like the custom of﴾ [Ghafir: 31], Ibn Atiyya said it is a badal (substitution). Al-Zamakhshari said it is an 'atf bayan (explicative apposition).

Al-Zajjaj said: "like the day of a faction," and "custom" (da'b) means their habit and wont in disbelief and sins.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 31], i.e., His destroying them was justice from Him, and in it is an emphasis on the negation of injustice, since He attached it to the will. If He negates it from the will, then negating it from occurrence is more fitting and more appropriate.

When he frightened them that what befell the factions might befall them in this world, he frightened them about the matter of the Hereafter, saying, showing tenderness to them by calling them: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out﴾, and it is the Day of Gathering. "Al-tanad" is the verbal noun of "tanadA al-qawm," i.e., some of them called out to one another. The poet said:

[p. 464]
They called out to one another, saying: "Did you want a horseman for the horses?" I said: "Do I worship Allah? That is your destruction."

It was named the Day of Calling Out either because of some of them calling to others with woe and perdition, or because of the calling between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, as mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, or because people are called to the place of gathering, or because of the calling of the believer: ﴿Here, read my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19], and the disbeliever: ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my book﴾ [al-Haqqa: 25]. A group read "al-tanad" with a sukun on the dal in pausal form in connected speech, treating it as a pause. This interpretation was related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the reminder with every call on the Day of Resurrection is a hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners. End.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

And He spread the creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling out.

In a hadith: "Indeed the people will have a turmoil on the Day of Resurrection, they will flee," thinking they will find a refuge; then he recited: ﴿The day you turn back fleeing﴾.

Mujahid said: its meaning is "fleeing." Al-Suddi said: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾ in your fleeing, until you are punished in the Fire. Qatada said: you will have no protector in going toward it, i.e., no preventer who prevents you from it, or helper.

When the believer despaired of their accepting it, he said: ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾.

Then he began to rebuke them for denying the messengers, by saying that Joseph had come to them with clear proofs. The apparent meaning is that it was Joseph son of Jacob, and Pharaoh is the Pharaoh of Moses. Ashhab related from Malik that it reached him that Pharaoh lived four hundred and forty years.

It was also said: rather, the one who came to them was Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob, and that Pharaoh is a Pharaoh other than the Pharaoh of Moses.

﴿With clear proofs﴾: with miracles. They continued doubting his mission and disbelieving, until when he died, ﴿you said: Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾. This is not an affirmation of his mission, and how could it be, when they remained in doubt about him? Rather the meaning is: there is no messenger from Allah so that He would send him to the creation; so in it is the negation of a messenger and the negation of his sending.

It was read: "a-lan yab'atha" (with the interrogative hamza before the negative particle), as if some of them were confirming to others the negation of sending.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like the misguidance of Allah of you, i.e., when you did not accept from Joseph, ﴿Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾: meaning them, since they are the transgressors and the doubters concerning the messages of the prophets.

They permitted in ﴿those who dispute﴾ that it be an attribute of "man" (man), and a badal from it: i.e., its meaning is plural and a subject, by omitting a modifier, i.e., "the disputation of those who dispute," so that the pronoun in ﴿greatly hateful﴾ returns to that disputation first, or by omitting a modifier, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is a pronoun returning to the disputation understood from His saying ﴿dispute﴾, or a pronoun returning to "man" according to its wording, on the condition that "those who" is an attribute or a badal, returned first to the wording of "man" in His saying: ﴿he is a transgressor, a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Then He made "those who" plural according to the meaning of "man," then He made it singular in His saying ﴿greatly hateful﴾ according to the wording of "man."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that ﴿those who dispute﴾ be the subject and ﴿without authority having come to them﴾ the predicate, and the agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾ is His saying: "thus," i.e., ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ like that disputation, and ﴿Allah seals﴾ is a resumed statement. And whoever says ﴿greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾ is their disputation, has omitted the agent, and the agent cannot be omitted. End. What he permitted cannot be like this in eloquent speech, let alone in the speech of Allah. Because in it there is a dislocation of the speech, part from part, and committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one.

As for dislocating the speech: the apparent meaning is that ﴿without authority﴾ is connected to ﴿dispute﴾, and it cannot be understood to make it a predicate of "those who," because it is a prepositional phrase, so the estimate becomes: ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ are: existing, or residing, ﴿without authority﴾, i.e., in the absence of authority; because the bi' in that case is adverbial, a predicate reporting about the body. Likewise in His saying "seals," that it is resumed is a dislocation of the speech, because what came in the Qur'an of ﴿thus He seals﴾, or "we seal," came linked part to part, so here likewise. As for committing to a doctrine contrary to the correct one: he made the kaf a noun acting as an agent of ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and that is not permitted according to the doctrine of the Basrans except al-Akhfash, and it has not been established in the speech of the Arabs, I mean its prose: "he came to me like Zayd," meaning "like Zayd," so its nominality has not been established, so that it would be an agent.

As for His saying "and whoever says, etc.," the one who says that is al-Hawfi, and it is assumed of him that he explained the meaning and did not intend the i'rab (grammatical analysis). The preferable analysis of this sentence is that ﴿those who﴾ is the subject, its predicate ﴿greatly hateful﴾, and the agent is a pronoun of the verbal noun understood from ﴿dispute﴾. This attribute exists in Pharaoh and his people, and the admonisher to them has turned from addressing them to the third person, for the goodness of his discourse with them and winning their hearts, and presenting that in the form of reminding them, and not surprising them with direct address. In His saying ﴿greatly hateful in hatred﴾ there is a kind of wonder and magnification at their disputation and a testimony to its going beyond the limit of its being a grave sin.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that sealing upon the hearts of the disputants. ﴿Allah seals﴾, i.e., He seals with misguidance and veils from guidance. Abu 'Amr ibn Dhakwan, al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "qalbin" with tanwin, describing the heart as arrogant and tyrannical, since it is their center and source, as they say: "the eye saw," and as He said: ﴿for indeed he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], and "al-ithm" is the whole.
