This was transmitted from al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from al-Suddi: that their spirits are in the bellies of black birds, which go out with them and come back to the Fire. A man said to al-Awza'i: "I saw white birds coming from the sea, then in the evening returning black like them." Al-Awza'i said: "Those are the ones in whose bellies are the spirits of the family of Pharaoh; their feathers are burned, and they turn black from being exposed to the Fire."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others said: He meant that they are exposed in the Hereafter according to the measure of the interval between morning and evening, since there is no morning or evening in the Hereafter; rather that is by the measure of the days of this world.

From Ibn Mas'ud: The spirits of the family of Pharaoh and those like them among the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire in the morning and in the evening, and it is said: "This is your abode."

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and in the evening; if he is one of the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then from the people of the Fire; it is said: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, 'Ikrimah and Muqatil used as evidence His saying: ﴿The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, meaning: at their death, (exposed) to the punishment of the grave in this world. The apparent meaning is that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿and evening﴾, and that the Day of Resurrection is an object (ma'mul) of a deleted verb by implication of a saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: Enter﴾. It was said: "and the day" is conjoined to ﴿and evening﴾, so the governing element for it is ﴿they are exposed﴾, and ﴿Enter﴾ with a deleted verb. It was said: the governing element of "the day" is ﴿Enter﴾.

Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Ibn Wuthab, Talhah, Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿Admit﴾ as an imperative to the keepers, from the causative form (adkhala).

'Ali, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Kathir, the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir?), and Abu Bakr read it as an imperative from the basic form (dakhala): ﴿the family of Pharaoh to the most terrible punishment.﴾ It was said: that is the Hawiyah (the deepest pit of Hell). Al-Awza'i said: We have been told that they are one million six hundred thousand.

﴿And when they argue in the Fire﴾: the apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿they argue﴾ refers to all the disbelievers of the nations, and this is the beginning of a narrative not specific to the family of Pharaoh, and the governing element of "idh" (when) is a hidden verb, its estimate being: "and remember."

Al-Tabari said: This "idh" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿when the hearts are at the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and this is far-fetched. End of quote.

Al-muhajjah means mutual argument with proof and dispute. "The weak" means in the matter of destiny and status in this world. "Those who were arrogant" means: those who were arrogant toward faith and following the messengers.

﴿Indeed we were your followers﴾: meaning: possessors of following (dhawi taba'), so taba' is either a verbal noun or a collective noun for tabi', like ayim and aymin, khadim and khadam, ghayib and ghayab.

﴿So will you bear from us﴾: meaning: will you carry on our behalf? They answered them: ﴿Indeed we are all in it﴾, and that the judgment of God has been executed upon us and upon you; indeed we are abiding in the Fire.

Ibn al-Sumayqa and 'Isa ibn 'Imran read "kullan" with the accusative on "kull." Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is for emphasis of the subject of inna, which is definite, and the tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "Indeed all of us are in it." End of quote.

The predicate of inna is "fiha" (in it). Whoever reads "kull" with the nominative makes it the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "fiha," and the sentence is the predicate of inna.

Ibn Malik in his work Tashil al-Fawa'id said: He spoke about "kull," and it does not dispense with the intention of its being annexed, unlike al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari. End of quote. This view is transmitted from the Kufans, and Ibn Malik refuted this view with what he established in his commentary on the Tashil.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: is it permissible that "kullan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal) governed by "fiha"? I say: No, because the adverbial of place does not govern, and the circumstantial element is anterior, just as it governs in the adverbial of place when anterior, as one says: "kulla yawmin laka thawb" (every day you have a garment), and you do not say: "qa'iman fi al-dar Zayd" (standing in the house, Zayd). End of quote.

What he prohibited, al-Akhfash permitted when the circumstantial element is in the middle, like: "Zayd qa'iman fi al-dar" (Zayd, standing in the house) and "Zayd qa'iman 'indaka" (Zayd, standing with you). The example he mentioned does not match the verse, because in the verse the subject of the judgment came first, which is the subject of inna, and the circumstantial element came in the middle, if we say it is a circumstantial element, and the governing element for it came later. As for his example with his saying "and you do not say: standing in the house Zayd," the predicate and the subject are both postponed. Some of them mentioned that the prohibition in that is a consensus of the grammarians.

Ibn Malik said: The view I find acceptable is that "kullan" in the mentioned reading is in the accusative because the hidden nominative pronoun in "fiha" is the governing element, and the circumstantial element was placed before it despite its non-flexibility, just as it was placed in the reading of the one who read: ﴿and the heavens are folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. And in the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

"The clan of Ibn Kawz, wearing their armor on them, among them, and the clan of Rabi'ah ibn Hadhar."

And a poet of the Tayy said:

"He called, and we answered, while he was in humiliation to us, so victory was not near."

...[the commentary continues in the same argument] This is according to the view of al-Akhfash (a grammarian), as we have mentioned. What I choose regarding the reading of this recitation is that *kullan* (كُلًّا) is a *badal* (substitute or apposition, a grammatical term meaning a noun that replaces or restates the preceding noun) of the noun of *inna* (إنَّ), because *kullan* operates in both of them with the inchoative and the abrogating particles and otherwise. So it is as if he said: "Indeed *kullan* is a *badal* of the noun of *inna*, because *kullan* is in it." Since they have interpreted *hawlan aktaʿan* and *yawman ajmaʿan* as *badal*, even though these two do not follow governing particles, it is more appropriate to claim the *badal* for *kullun* (كُلٌّ). Also, the indefinite form of *kullan* and its being in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) is extremely rare, while the well-known view is that *kullan* is definite when it is detached from the genitive construction. It is related: "I passed by each one standing," and "by some sitting," in the eloquent and common usage of their speech. The accusative of *kullin* as a circumstantial is anomalous in the saying: "I passed by them *kullan*," meaning "all of them."

(If you say): How does he make it a *badal*, when it is a *badal* of *kullin* from the pronoun of the speaker, and that is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans?

(I say): The view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permitted, and this is the correct view. Moreover, this is not one of the matters in which there is disagreement. Rather, when the *badal* conveys comprehensiveness, it is permissible for it to be a substitute for the pronoun of the speaker and the pronoun of the addressee. We know of no disagreement about that, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿It will be a feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], and as in your saying: "I passed by you, your young and your old," meaning: "I passed by all of you," and "It will be a feast for all of us." When that is permissible in what has the meaning of comprehensiveness, its permissibility in what indicates comprehensiveness, which is *kullun*, is more appropriate. The objection of al-Mubarrad to the *badal* in it is not to be considered, because it is a *badal* from the pronoun of the speaker, since the point of disagreement has not been established.

When the weak ones who were arrogant answered, they all said: ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾. The noun to which the keepers were attributed was made explicit and was not given as a pronoun. The construction would have been "to its keepers," because of the awe-inspiring effect of mentioning Hell, and in it are the most tyrannical and rebellious of the disbelievers. Perhaps the disbelievers imagined that the angels of Hell, who are charged with punishing those tyrants, are closer in rank with Allah than the other angels who are charged with the remaining levels of the Fire. So they hoped that they would answer them and pray for them for lightening (the punishment). The keepers then rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?﴾ They answered that they had come to them. ﴿They said﴾, that is, the keepers: ﴿Then you pray﴾, in the sense of mockery of them; or "Then you pray," since we do not dare to do that. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿And the prayer of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ is from the words of the keepers, meaning: your prayer does not benefit and does not avail. It was said that it is from the words of Allah, the Most High, as information from Him to Muhammad ﷺ.

These reports came expressed in the past tense, to affirm that their occurrence is certain.

Then the Most High mentioned that He supports His messengers and grants them victory over their enemies, as He did with Musa (peace be upon him), when He destroyed his enemy Pharaoh and his people. In this there is good news for the Messenger (peace be upon him) of his victory over his people, (in the life of this world), the good outcome being theirs. ﴿And the day when the witnesses stand﴾: this is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He grants them victory by dominance, and in the Hereafter by punishment. al-Suddi said: by taking vengeance upon their enemies. Abu al-ʿAliyah said: by the success of their proof. al-Suddi also said: No people ever killed a prophet or a people of the callers to the truth except that Allah sent someone who would avenge them, so they became victorious in it even though they were killed. End of quote.

Do you not see the killers of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, how Allah empowered al-Mukhtar ibn ʿUbayd against them, pursuing them one by one until he killed them? And Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) pursued the Jews when they killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both? It was said: The victory is specific to the one whom Allah, the Most High, makes victorious over his nation, such as Nuh, Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them, because we find among the prophets those whom their people killed, such as Yahya, and those who were not given victory over them. al-Suddi said: The report is general, because the support of the messengers and prophets certainly occurs, either during the lifetime of the messenger who is supported, such as Nuh and Musa, peace be upon them both, or after his death. Do you not see what Allah, the Most High, did to the Children of Israel after they killed Yahya, peace be upon him, by empowering Bukhtnassar, until he gave victory to Yahya, peace be upon him?

The majority read *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ) with the *ya* (ياء); Ibn Hurmuz, Isma'il, and al-Minqari from Abu ʿAmr read it with the feminine *ta* (تاء). [This is] the consensus. *Al-ashhad* (الأشهاد) is the plural of *shahid* (شَهِيدٍ), like *sharif* and *ashraf*, or the plural of *shahid* (شاهِدٍ), like *sahib* and *ashab*, as the Most High said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41], and He said: ﴿That you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The apparent meaning is that it is from testimony (*shahadah*). It was said: it is from witnessing (*mushahadah*), in the sense of presence.

﴿The day when no excuse will benefit﴾: a *badal* from *yawm* (يَوْمَ) in *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ). It was read as *tanfaʿu* (تَنْفَعُ) with the *ta* and with the *ya*, and the disagreement regarding that was mentioned at the end of al-Rum. It is possible that they will make excuses and their excuses will not be accepted, or that they will have no excuse that would be accepted.

﴿And for them is the curse﴾: removal and distancing from Allah.

﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾: the evil outcome of the abode.

[p. 467]

﴿O my people, what is the matter with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, that to which you call me has no call (de facto) in this world or in the Hereafter, and that our return is to God, and that the wasteful (al-musrifun) are the companions of the Fire.﴾ ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. I entrust my affair to God; indeed God is Seeing of His servants.﴾ ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed, and the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ ﴿The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour arises, (it will be said): "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment!"﴾ ﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed we were your followers, so will you bear from us a share of the Fire?"﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed we are all in it. Indeed God has judged between the servants."﴾ ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Then call upon (Him)! But the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error."﴾ ﴿Indeed We will surely support Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand.﴾ ﴿The day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers; for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

The author (al-mu'min) began with mention of the one who causes their call (i.e., the consequence of their call), and displayed the difference between the two. When he mentioned the two causers (the two calls), he mentioned their cause, which is their calling to disbelief and polytheism, and his calling them to faith and monotheism.

He used the form "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty), who has no equal, and the Dominant, in whose grip the whole world is, who disposes of them as He wills, "al-Ghaffar" (the Forgiving) for the sins of whoever returns to Him and believes in Him. He connected the cause of their call with its effect, which is disbelief and the Fire, and postponed the cause of its effect, so that his speech would begin and end with what calls to good.

He began first with a nominal sentence, which is the interrogative that implies wonder at their condition, and he also concluded with a nominal sentence so that it would be more eloquent in emphasizing the report. As for their case, "and you call me" came in a verbal sentence, which does not require emphasis, since their calling (to their gods) is false and has no established reality, so it does not need to be emphasized. And "that of which I have no knowledge" refers to the idols, meaning: my knowledge is not connected to it, since they have no part in divinity, nor does Pharaoh.

Az-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he use the waw (and) in the third call and not in the second?" I say: "Because the second is embedded in a statement which is an explanation and clarification of the general (al-mujmal), so it gives the thing embedded in it its ruling regarding the impermissibility of the waw. As for the third, it is embedded in a statement that is not in that position." End of quote.

The discussion of "la jaram" has already preceded.

Az-Zamakhshari said here, and it was transmitted from the Arabs: "la jurma annahu yaf'alu" with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ra', meaning "la budda" (there is no doubt). Fa'l and fu'l are siblings, like rashad and rushd, and 'adam and 'udm.

(Anna-ma) means: that which "you call me to" (i.e., to worship Him) "has no call" means: it has no measure and no right that it should be called to. Or: it has no call to itself, because the inanimate does not call, whereas the God worthy of worship calls His servants to obedience to Him, and then calls the servants to it, manifesting the call of their Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: it has no answering of a call that would make it deserving of divinity in this world or in the Hereafter. Or it means "a call that is answered": the call which has no answer and no benefit was made like "no call," or the answering was named by the name of the call, just as the act being repaid is named by the name of the recompense, in the saying: "As you do, so it is done to you."

Al-Kalbi said: It has no intercession in this world or in the Hereafter. Pharaoh first called people to worship idols, then he called them to worship the cow. It was worshipped as long as it was young; when it became lean, he ordered it slaughtered and called for another to be worshipped. When much time had passed over him, he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

When he mentioned the negation of the call of what is worshipped besides God, and mentioned that the return of all is to God, that is, to His recompense, ﴿and that the wasteful﴾ (they are the polytheists according to the saying of Qatadah, and those who shed blood unlawfully according to the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid). It was said: the one whose evil overcomes his good is the wasteful. 'Ikrimah said: they are the tyrants, the arrogant.

[p. 468] The believer concluded his speech with a subtle conclusion that entails fear and threat, which is his saying: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾, meaning: when God's punishment descends upon you.

﴿And I entrust my affair﴾ to the decree and destiny of God, not to you nor to your idols; they had threatened him.

Then he mentioned what necessitates entrusting, which is that He, exalted is He, is Seeing of the conditions of the servants and of the measures of their needs.

Muqatil said: When he said these words, they intended to kill him, so this believer fled to the mountain, and they could not reach him.

It was said: When he displayed his faith, Pharaoh sent a thousand men in pursuit of him. Some of them reached him, and the wild beasts defended him and devoured them. Some of them died of thirst in the mountains, and some returned to Pharaoh disappointed, so he accused him, killed him, and crucified him. It was said: he was saved with Moses in the sea and fled among those who fled with him.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾, meaning: the severe harms of their scheming which would have grieved him, and the various kinds of torment they intended for whoever opposed them.

﴿And the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: It is what befell the thousand whom Pharaoh sent in pursuit of the believer: from being eaten by wild beasts, dying of thirst, killing and crucifixion, as has preceded.

It was said: ﴿the terrible punishment﴾ is drowning in this world and burning in the Hereafter.

"The Fire" is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the terrible punishment﴾, or the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject, as if it were said: "What is the terrible punishment? It was said: the Fire." Or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿they are exposed﴾. This aspect is strengthened by the reading of the one who put it in the accusative, meaning: "You will enter the Fire, they are exposed to it."

Az-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be put in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisas).

The apparent meaning is that their exposure to the Fire is specific to these two times. It is permissible that mention of the two extremes be intended to indicate continuity in this world. The apparent meaning is that exposure is other than burning. Az-Zamakhshari said: Their exposure to it is their burning in it; it is said: the Imam exposed the captives to the sword when he killed them by it. End of quote.

It is related: "I passed by each one standing," and "by some sitting," in the eloquent and common usage of their speech. The accusative of *kullin* as a circumstantial is anomalous in the saying: "I passed by them *kullan*," meaning "all of them."

(If you say): How does he make it a *badal*, when it is a *badal* of *kullin* from the pronoun of the speaker, and that is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans?

(I say): The view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permitted, and this is the correct view. Moreover, this is not one of the matters in which there is disagreement. Rather, when the *badal* conveys comprehensiveness, it is permissible for it to be a substitute for the pronoun of the speaker and the pronoun of the addressee. We know of no disagreement about that, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿It will be a feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], and as in your saying: "I passed by you, your young and your old," meaning: "I passed by all of you," and "It will be a feast for all of us." When that is permissible in what has the meaning of comprehensiveness, its permissibility in what indicates comprehensiveness, which is *kullun*, is more appropriate. The objection of al-Mubarrad to the *badal* in it is not to be considered, because it is a *badal* from the pronoun of the speaker, since the point of disagreement has not been established.

When the weak ones who were arrogant answered, they all said: ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾. The noun to which the keepers were attributed was made explicit and was not given as a pronoun. The construction would have been "to its keepers," because of the awe-inspiring effect of mentioning Hell, and in it are the most tyrannical and rebellious of the disbelievers. Perhaps the disbelievers imagined that the angels of Hell, who are charged with punishing those tyrants, are closer in rank with Allah than the other angels who are charged with the remaining levels of the Fire. So they hoped that they would answer them and pray for them for lightening (the punishment). The keepers then rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?﴾ They answered that they had come to them. ﴿They said﴾, that is, the keepers: ﴿Then you pray﴾, in the sense of mockery of them; or "Then you pray," since we do not dare to do that. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿And the prayer of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ is from the words of the keepers, meaning: your prayer does not benefit and does not avail. It was said that it is from the words of Allah, the Most High, as information from Him to Muhammad ﷺ.

These reports came expressed in the past tense, to affirm that their occurrence is certain.

Then the Most High mentioned that He supports His messengers and grants them victory over their enemies, as He did with Musa (peace be upon him), when He destroyed his enemy Pharaoh and his people. In this there is good news for the Messenger (peace be upon him) of his victory over his people, (in the life of this world), the good outcome being theirs. ﴿And the day when the witnesses stand﴾: this is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He grants them victory by dominance, and in the Hereafter by punishment. al-Suddi said: by taking vengeance upon their enemies. Abu al-ʿAliyah said: by the success of their proof. al-Suddi also said: No people ever killed a prophet or a people of the callers to the truth except that Allah sent someone who would avenge them, so they became victorious in it even though they were killed. End of quote.

Do you not see the killers of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, how Allah empowered al-Mukhtar ibn ʿUbayd against them, pursuing them one by one until he killed them? And Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) pursued the Jews when they killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both? It was said: The victory is specific to the one whom Allah, the Most High, makes victorious over his nation, such as Nuh, Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them, because we find among the prophets those whom their people killed, such as Yahya, and those who were not given victory over them. al-Suddi said: The report is general, because the support of the messengers and prophets certainly occurs, either during the lifetime of the messenger who is supported, such as Nuh and Musa, peace be upon them both, or after his death. Do you not see what Allah, the Most High, did to the Children of Israel after they killed Yahya, peace be upon him, by empowering Bukhtnassar, until he gave victory to Yahya, peace be upon him?

The majority read *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ) with the *ya* (ياء); Ibn Hurmuz, Isma'il, and al-Minqari from Abu ʿAmr read it with the feminine *ta* (تاء). [This is] the consensus. *Al-ashhad* (الأشهاد) is the plural of *shahid* (شَهِيدٍ), like *sharif* and *ashraf*, or the plural of *shahid* (شاهِدٍ), like *sahib* and *ashab*, as the Most High said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41], and He said: ﴿That you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The apparent meaning is that it is from testimony (*shahadah*). It was said: it is from witnessing (*mushahadah*), in the sense of presence.

﴿The day when no excuse will benefit﴾: a *badal* from *yawm* (يَوْمَ) in *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ). It was read as *tanfaʿu* (تَنْفَعُ) with the *ta* and with the *ya*, and the disagreement regarding that was mentioned at the end of al-Rum. It is possible that they will make excuses and their excuses will not be accepted, or that they will have no excuse that would be accepted.

﴿And for them is the curse﴾: removal and distancing from Allah.

﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾: the evil outcome of the abode.

[p. 467]

﴿O my people, what is the matter with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, that to which you call me has no call (de facto) in this world or in the Hereafter, and that our return is to God, and that the wasteful (al-musrifun) are the companions of the Fire.﴾ ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. I entrust my affair to God; indeed God is Seeing of His servants.﴾ ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed, and the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ ﴿The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour arises, (it will be said): "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment!"﴾ ﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed we were your followers, so will you bear from us a share of the Fire?"﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed we are all in it. Indeed God has judged between the servants."﴾ ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Then call upon (Him)! But the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error."﴾ ﴿Indeed We will surely support Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand.﴾ ﴿The day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers; for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

The author (al-mu'min) began with mention of the one who causes their call (i.e., the consequence of their call), and displayed the difference between the two. When he mentioned the two causers (the two calls), he mentioned their cause, which is their calling to disbelief and polytheism, and his calling them to faith and monotheism.

He used the form "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty), who has no equal, and the Dominant, in whose grip the whole world is, who disposes of them as He wills, "al-Ghaffar" (the Forgiving) for the sins of whoever returns to Him and believes in Him. He connected the cause of their call with its effect, which is disbelief and the Fire, and postponed the cause of its effect, so that his speech would begin and end with what calls to good.

He began first with a nominal sentence, which is the interrogative that implies wonder at their condition, and he also concluded with a nominal sentence so that it would be more eloquent in emphasizing the report. As for their case, "and you call me" came in a verbal sentence, which does not require emphasis, since their calling (to their gods) is false and has no established reality, so it does not need to be emphasized. And "that of which I have no knowledge" refers to the idols, meaning: my knowledge is not connected to it, since they have no part in divinity, nor does Pharaoh.

Az-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he use the waw (and) in the third call and not in the second?" I say: "Because the second is embedded in a statement which is an explanation and clarification of the general (al-mujmal), so it gives the thing embedded in it its ruling regarding the impermissibility of the waw. As for the third, it is embedded in a statement that is not in that position." End of quote.

The discussion of "la jaram" has already preceded.

Az-Zamakhshari said here, and it was transmitted from the Arabs: "la jurma annahu yaf'alu" with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ra', meaning "la budda" (there is no doubt). Fa'l and fu'l are siblings, like rashad and rushd, and 'adam and 'udm.

(Anna-ma) means: that which "you call me to" (i.e., to worship Him) "has no call" means: it has no measure and no right that it should be called to. Or: it has no call to itself, because the inanimate does not call, whereas the God worthy of worship calls His servants to obedience to Him, and then calls the servants to it, manifesting the call of their Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: it has no answering of a call that would make it deserving of divinity in this world or in the Hereafter. Or it means "a call that is answered": the call which has no answer and no benefit was made like "no call," or the answering was named by the name of the call, just as the act being repaid is named by the name of the recompense, in the saying: "As you do, so it is done to you."

Al-Kalbi said: It has no intercession in this world or in the Hereafter. Pharaoh first called people to worship idols, then he called them to worship the cow. It was worshipped as long as it was young; when it became lean, he ordered it slaughtered and called for another to be worshipped. When much time had passed over him, he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

When he mentioned the negation of the call of what is worshipped besides God, and mentioned that the return of all is to God, that is, to His recompense, ﴿and that the wasteful﴾ (they are the polytheists according to the saying of Qatadah, and those who shed blood unlawfully according to the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid). It was said: the one whose evil overcomes his good is the wasteful. 'Ikrimah said: they are the tyrants, the arrogant.

[p. 468] The believer concluded his speech with a subtle conclusion that entails fear and threat, which is his saying: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾, meaning: when God's punishment descends upon you.

﴿And I entrust my affair﴾ to the decree and destiny of God, not to you nor to your idols; they had threatened him.

Then he mentioned what necessitates entrusting, which is that He, exalted is He, is Seeing of the conditions of the servants and of the measures of their needs.

Muqatil said: When he said these words, they intended to kill him, so this believer fled to the mountain, and they could not reach him.

It was said: When he displayed his faith, Pharaoh sent a thousand men in pursuit of him. Some of them reached him, and the wild beasts defended him and devoured them. Some of them died of thirst in the mountains, and some returned to Pharaoh disappointed, so he accused him, killed him, and crucified him. It was said: he was saved with Moses in the sea and fled among those who fled with him.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾, meaning: the severe harms of their scheming which would have grieved him, and the various kinds of torment they intended for whoever opposed them.

﴿And the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: It is what befell the thousand whom Pharaoh sent in pursuit of the believer: from being eaten by wild beasts, dying of thirst, killing and crucifixion, as has preceded.

It was said: ﴿the terrible punishment﴾ is drowning in this world and burning in the Hereafter.

"The Fire" is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the terrible punishment﴾, or the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject, as if it were said: "What is the terrible punishment? It was said: the Fire." Or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿they are exposed﴾. This aspect is strengthened by the reading of the one who put it in the accusative, meaning: "You will enter the Fire, they are exposed to it."

Az-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be put in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisas).

The apparent meaning is that their exposure to the Fire is specific to these two times. It is permissible that mention of the two extremes be intended to indicate continuity in this world. The apparent meaning is that exposure is other than burning. Az-Zamakhshari said: Their exposure to it is their burning in it; it is said: the Imam exposed the captives to the sword when he killed them by it. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the exposure is in this world. This was transmitted from al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from al-Suddi: that their spirits are in the bellies of black birds, which go out with them and come back to the Fire. A man said to al-Awza'i: "I saw white birds coming from the sea, then in the evening returning black like them." Al-Awza'i said: "Those are the ones in whose bellies are the spirits of the family of Pharaoh; their feathers are burned, and they turn black from being exposed to the Fire."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others said: He meant that they are exposed in the Hereafter according to the measure of the interval between morning and evening, since there is no morning or evening in the Hereafter; rather that is by the measure of the days of this world.

From Ibn Mas'ud: The spirits of the family of Pharaoh and those like them among the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire in the morning and in the evening, and it is said: "This is your abode."

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and in the evening; if he is one of the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then from the people of the Fire; it is said: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, 'Ikrimah and Muqatil used as evidence His saying: ﴿The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, meaning: at their death, (exposed) to the punishment of the grave in this world. The apparent meaning is that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿and evening﴾, and that the Day of Resurrection is an object (ma'mul) of a deleted verb by implication of a saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: Enter﴾. It was said: "and the day" is conjoined to ﴿and evening﴾, so the governing element for it is ﴿they are exposed﴾, and ﴿Enter﴾ with a deleted verb. It was said: the governing element of "the day" is ﴿Enter﴾.

Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Ibn Wuthab, Talhah, Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿Admit﴾ as an imperative to the keepers, from the causative form (adkhala).

'Ali, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Kathir, the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir?), and Abu Bakr read it as an imperative from the basic form (dakhala): ﴿the family of Pharaoh to the most terrible punishment.﴾ It was said: that is the Hawiyah (the deepest pit of Hell). Al-Awza'i said: We have been told that they are one million six hundred thousand.

﴿And when they argue in the Fire﴾: the apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿they argue﴾ refers to all the disbelievers of the nations, and this is the beginning of a narrative not specific to the family of Pharaoh, and the governing element of "idh" (when) is a hidden verb, its estimate being: "and remember."

Al-Tabari said: This "idh" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿when the hearts are at the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and this is far-fetched. End of quote.

Al-muhajjah means mutual argument with proof and dispute. "The weak" means in the matter of destiny and status in this world. "Those who were arrogant" means: those who were arrogant toward faith and following the messengers.

﴿Indeed we were your followers﴾: meaning: possessors of following (dhawi taba'), so taba' is either a verbal noun or a collective noun for tabi', like ayim and aymin, khadim and khadam, ghayib and ghayab.

﴿So will you bear from us﴾: meaning: will you carry on our behalf? They answered them: ﴿Indeed we are all in it﴾, and that the judgment of God has been executed upon us and upon you; indeed we are abiding in the Fire.

Ibn al-Sumayqa and 'Isa ibn 'Imran read "kullan" with the accusative on "kull." Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is for emphasis of the subject of inna, which is definite, and the tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "Indeed all of us are in it." End of quote.

The predicate of inna is "fiha" (in it). Whoever reads "kull" with the nominative makes it the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "fiha," and the sentence is the predicate of inna.

Ibn Malik in his work Tashil al-Fawa'id said: He spoke about "kull," and it does not dispense with the intention of its being annexed, unlike al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari. End of quote. This view is transmitted from the Kufans, and Ibn Malik refuted this view with what he established in his commentary on the Tashil.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: is it permissible that "kullan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal) governed by "fiha"? I say: No, because the adverbial of place does not govern, and the circumstantial element is anterior, just as it governs in the adverbial of place when anterior, as one says: "kulla yawmin laka thawb" (every day you have a garment), and you do not say: "qa'iman fi al-dar Zayd" (standing in the house, Zayd). End of quote.

What he prohibited, al-Akhfash permitted when the circumstantial element is in the middle, like: "Zayd qa'iman fi al-dar" (Zayd, standing in the house) and "Zayd qa'iman 'indaka" (Zayd, standing with you). The example he mentioned does not match the verse, because in the verse the subject of the judgment came first, which is the subject of inna, and the circumstantial element came in the middle, if we say it is a circumstantial element, and the governing element for it came later. As for his example with his saying "and you do not say: standing in the house Zayd," the predicate and the subject are both postponed. Some of them mentioned that the prohibition in that is a consensus of the grammarians.

Ibn Malik said: The view I find acceptable is that "kullan" in the mentioned reading is in the accusative because the hidden nominative pronoun in "fiha" is the governing element, and the circumstantial element was placed before it despite its non-flexibility, just as it was placed in the reading of the one who read: ﴿and the heavens are folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. And in the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

"The clan of Ibn Kawz, wearing their armor on them, among them, and the clan of Rabi'ah ibn Hadhar."

And a poet of the Tayy said:

"He called, and we answered, while he was in humiliation to us, so victory was not near."

...[the commentary continues in the same argument] This is according to the view of al-Akhfash (a grammarian), as we have mentioned. What I choose regarding the reading of this recitation is that *kullan* (كُلًّا) is a *badal* (substitute or apposition, a grammatical term meaning a noun that replaces or restates the preceding noun) of the noun of *inna* (إنَّ), because *kullan* operates in both of them with the inchoative and the abrogating particles and otherwise. So it is as if he said: "Indeed *kullan* is a *badal* of the noun of *inna*, because *kullan* is in it." Since they have interpreted *hawlan aktaʿan* and *yawman ajmaʿan* as *badal*, even though these two do not follow governing particles, it is more appropriate to claim the *badal* for *kullun* (كُلٌّ). Indeed God has judged between the servants."﴾ ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Then call upon (Him)! But the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error."﴾ ﴿Indeed We will surely support Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand.﴾ ﴿The day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers; for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

The author (al-mu'min) began with mention of the one who causes their call (i.e., the consequence of their call), and displayed the difference between the two. When he mentioned the two causers (the two calls), he mentioned their cause, which is their calling to disbelief and polytheism, and his calling them to faith and monotheism.

He used the form "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty), who has no equal, and the Dominant, in whose grip the whole world is, who disposes of them as He wills, "al-Ghaffar" (the Forgiving) for the sins of whoever returns to Him and believes in Him. He connected the cause of their call with its effect, which is disbelief and the Fire, and postponed the cause of its effect, so that his speech would begin and end with what calls to good.

He began first with a nominal sentence, which is the interrogative that implies wonder at their condition, and he also concluded with a nominal sentence so that it would be more eloquent in emphasizing the report. As for their case, "and you call me" came in a verbal sentence, which does not require emphasis, since their calling (to their gods) is false and has no established reality, so it does not need to be emphasized. And "that of which I have no knowledge" refers to the idols, meaning: my knowledge is not connected to it, since they have no part in divinity, nor does Pharaoh.

Az-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he use the waw (and) in the third call and not in the second?" I say: "Because the second is embedded in a statement which is an explanation and clarification of the general (al-mujmal), so it gives the thing embedded in it its ruling regarding the impermissibility of the waw. As for the third, it is embedded in a statement that is not in that position." End of quote.

The discussion of "la jaram" has already preceded.

Az-Zamakhshari said here, and it was transmitted from the Arabs: "la jurma annahu yaf'alu" with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ra', meaning "la budda" (there is no doubt). Fa'l and fu'l are siblings, like rashad and rushd, and 'adam and 'udm.

(Anna-ma) means: that which "you call me to" (i.e., to worship Him) "has no call" means: it has no measure and no right that it should be called to. Or: it has no call to itself, because the inanimate does not call, whereas the God worthy of worship calls His servants to obedience to Him, and then calls the servants to it, manifesting the call of their Lord.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: it has no answering of a call that would make it deserving of divinity in this world or in the Hereafter. Or it means "a call that is answered": the call which has no answer and no benefit was made like "no call," or the answering was named by the name of the call, just as the act being repaid is named by the name of the recompense, in the saying: "As you do, so it is done to you."

Al-Kalbi said: It has no intercession in this world or in the Hereafter. Pharaoh first called people to worship idols, then he called them to worship the cow. It was worshipped as long as it was young; when it became lean, he ordered it slaughtered and called for another to be worshipped. When much time had passed over him, he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

When he mentioned the negation of the call of what is worshipped besides God, and mentioned that the return of all is to God, that is, to His recompense, ﴿and that the wasteful﴾ (they are the polytheists according to the saying of Qatadah, and those who shed blood unlawfully according to the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid). It was said: the one whose evil overcomes his good is the wasteful. 'Ikrimah said: they are the tyrants, the arrogant.

[p. 468] The believer concluded his speech with a subtle conclusion that entails fear and threat, which is his saying: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾, meaning: when God's punishment descends upon you.

﴿And I entrust my affair﴾ to the decree and destiny of God, not to you nor to your idols; they had threatened him.

Then he mentioned what necessitates entrusting, which is that He, exalted is He, is Seeing of the conditions of the servants and of the measures of their needs.

Muqatil said: When he said these words, they intended to kill him, so this believer fled to the mountain, and they could not reach him.

It was said: When he displayed his faith, Pharaoh sent a thousand men in pursuit of him. Some of them reached him, and the wild beasts defended him and devoured them. Some of them died of thirst in the mountains, and some returned to Pharaoh disappointed, so he accused him, killed him, and crucified him. It was said: he was saved with Moses in the sea and fled among those who fled with him.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾, meaning: the severe harms of their scheming which would have grieved him, and the various kinds of torment they intended for whoever opposed them.

﴿And the terrible punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: It is what befell the thousand whom Pharaoh sent in pursuit of the believer: from being eaten by wild beasts, dying of thirst, killing and crucifixion, as has preceded.

It was said: ﴿the terrible punishment﴾ is drowning in this world and burning in the Hereafter.

"The Fire" is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the terrible punishment﴾, or the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject, as if it were said: "What is the terrible punishment? It was said: the Fire." Or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿they are exposed﴾. This aspect is strengthened by the reading of the one who put it in the accusative, meaning: "You will enter the Fire, they are exposed to it."

Az-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be put in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisas).

The apparent meaning is that their exposure to the Fire is specific to these two times. It is permissible that mention of the two extremes be intended to indicate continuity in this world. The apparent meaning is that exposure is other than burning. Az-Zamakhshari said: Their exposure to it is their burning in it; it is said: the Imam exposed the captives to the sword when he killed them by it. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the exposure is in this world. This was transmitted from al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from al-Suddi: that their spirits are in the bellies of black birds, which go out with them and come back to the Fire. A man said to al-Awza'i: "I saw white birds coming from the sea, then in the evening returning black like them." Al-Awza'i said: "Those are the ones in whose bellies are the spirits of the family of Pharaoh; their feathers are burned, and they turn black from being exposed to the Fire."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others said: He meant that they are exposed in the Hereafter according to the measure of the interval between morning and evening, since there is no morning or evening in the Hereafter; rather that is by the measure of the days of this world.

From Ibn Mas'ud: The spirits of the family of Pharaoh and those like them among the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire in the morning and in the evening, and it is said: "This is your abode."

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and in the evening; if he is one of the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then from the people of the Fire; it is said: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, 'Ikrimah and Muqatil used as evidence His saying: ﴿The Fire: they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, meaning: at their death, (exposed) to the punishment of the grave in this world. The apparent meaning is that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿and evening﴾, and that the Day of Resurrection is an object (ma'mul) of a deleted verb by implication of a saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them: Enter﴾. It was said: "and the day" is conjoined to ﴿and evening﴾, so the governing element for it is ﴿they are exposed﴾, and ﴿Enter﴾ with a deleted verb. It was said: the governing element of "the day" is ﴿Enter﴾.

Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Ibn Wuthab, Talhah, Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿Admit﴾ as an imperative to the keepers, from the causative form (adkhala).

'Ali, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Kathir, the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir?), and Abu Bakr read it as an imperative from the basic form (dakhala): ﴿the family of Pharaoh to the most terrible punishment.﴾ It was said: that is the Hawiyah (the deepest pit of Hell). Al-Awza'i said: We have been told that they are one million six hundred thousand.

﴿And when they argue in the Fire﴾: the apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿they argue﴾ refers to all the disbelievers of the nations, and this is the beginning of a narrative not specific to the family of Pharaoh, and the governing element of "idh" (when) is a hidden verb, its estimate being: "and remember."

Al-Tabari said: This "idh" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿when the hearts are at the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and this is far-fetched. End of quote.

Al-muhajjah means mutual argument with proof and dispute. "The weak" means in the matter of destiny and status in this world. "Those who were arrogant" means: those who were arrogant toward faith and following the messengers.

﴿Indeed we were your followers﴾: meaning: possessors of following (dhawi taba'), so taba' is either a verbal noun or a collective noun for tabi', like ayim and aymin, khadim and khadam, ghayib and ghayab.

﴿So will you bear from us﴾: meaning: will you carry on our behalf? They answered them: ﴿Indeed we are all in it﴾, and that the judgment of God has been executed upon us and upon you; indeed we are abiding in the Fire.

Ibn al-Sumayqa and 'Isa ibn 'Imran read "kullan" with the accusative on "kull." Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is for emphasis of the subject of inna, which is definite, and the tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "Indeed all of us are in it." End of quote.

The predicate of inna is "fiha" (in it). Whoever reads "kull" with the nominative makes it the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "fiha," and the sentence is the predicate of inna.

Ibn Malik in his work Tashil al-Fawa'id said: He spoke about "kull," and it does not dispense with the intention of its being annexed, unlike al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari. End of quote. This view is transmitted from the Kufans, and Ibn Malik refuted this view with what he established in his commentary on the Tashil.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: is it permissible that "kullan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal) governed by "fiha"? I say: No, because the adverbial of place does not govern, and the circumstantial element is anterior, just as it governs in the adverbial of place when anterior, as one says: "kulla yawmin laka thawb" (every day you have a garment), and you do not say: "qa'iman fi al-dar Zayd" (standing in the house, Zayd). End of quote.

What he prohibited, al-Akhfash permitted when the circumstantial element is in the middle, like: "Zayd qa'iman fi al-dar" (Zayd, standing in the house) and "Zayd qa'iman 'indaka" (Zayd, standing with you). The example he mentioned does not match the verse, because in the verse the subject of the judgment came first, which is the subject of inna, and the circumstantial element came in the middle, if we say it is a circumstantial element, and the governing element for it came later. As for his example with his saying "and you do not say: standing in the house Zayd," the predicate and the subject are both postponed. Some of them mentioned that the prohibition in that is a consensus of the grammarians.

Ibn Malik said: The view I find acceptable is that "kullan" in the mentioned reading is in the accusative because the hidden nominative pronoun in "fiha" is the governing element, and the circumstantial element was placed before it despite its non-flexibility, just as it was placed in the reading of the one who read: ﴿and the heavens are folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. And in the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

"The clan of Ibn Kawz, wearing their armor on them, among them, and the clan of Rabi'ah ibn Hadhar."

And a poet of the Tayy said:

"He called, and we answered, while he was in humiliation to us, so victory was not near."

...[the commentary continues in the same argument] This is according to the view of al-Akhfash (a grammarian), as we have mentioned. What I choose regarding the reading of this recitation is that *kullan* (كُلًّا) is a *badal* (substitute or apposition, a grammatical term meaning a noun that replaces or restates the preceding noun) of the noun of *inna* (إنَّ), because *kullan* operates in both of them with the inchoative and the abrogating particles and otherwise. So it is as if he said: "Indeed *kullan* is a *badal* of the noun of *inna*, because *kullan* is in it." Since they have interpreted *hawlan aktaʿan* and *yawman ajmaʿan* as *badal*, even though these two do not follow governing particles, it is more appropriate to claim the *badal* for *kullun* (كُلٌّ). Also, the indefinite form of *kullan* and its being in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) is extremely rare, while the well-known view is that *kullan* is definite when it is detached from the genitive construction. It is related: "I passed by each one standing," and "by some sitting," in the eloquent and common usage of their speech. The accusative of *kullin* as a circumstantial is anomalous in the saying: "I passed by them *kullan*," meaning "all of them."

(If you say): How does he make it a *badal*, when it is a *badal* of *kullin* from the pronoun of the speaker, and that is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans?

(I say): The view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is that it is permitted, and this is the correct view. Moreover, this is not one of the matters in which there is disagreement. Rather, when the *badal* conveys comprehensiveness, it is permissible for it to be a substitute for the pronoun of the speaker and the pronoun of the addressee. We know of no disagreement about that, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿It will be a feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], and as in your saying: "I passed by you, your young and your old," meaning: "I passed by all of you," and "It will be a feast for all of us." When that is permissible in what has the meaning of comprehensiveness, its permissibility in what indicates comprehensiveness, which is *kullun*, is more appropriate. The objection of al-Mubarrad to the *badal* in it is not to be considered, because it is a *badal* from the pronoun of the speaker, since the point of disagreement has not been established.

When the weak ones who were arrogant answered, they all said: ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾. The noun to which the keepers were attributed was made explicit and was not given as a pronoun. The construction would have been "to its keepers," because of the awe-inspiring effect of mentioning Hell, and in it are the most tyrannical and rebellious of the disbelievers. Perhaps the disbelievers imagined that the angels of Hell, who are charged with punishing those tyrants, are closer in rank with Allah than the other angels who are charged with the remaining levels of the Fire. So they hoped that they would answer them and pray for them for lightening (the punishment). The keepers then rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?﴾ They answered that they had come to them. ﴿They said﴾, that is, the keepers: ﴿Then you pray﴾, in the sense of mockery of them; or "Then you pray," since we do not dare to do that. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿And the prayer of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ is from the words of the keepers, meaning: your prayer does not benefit and does not avail. It was said that it is from the words of Allah, the Most High, as information from Him to Muhammad ﷺ.

These reports came expressed in the past tense, to affirm that their occurrence is certain.

Then the Most High mentioned that He supports His messengers and grants them victory over their enemies, as He did with Musa (peace be upon him), when He destroyed his enemy Pharaoh and his people. In this there is good news for the Messenger (peace be upon him) of his victory over his people, (in the life of this world), the good outcome being theirs. ﴿And the day when the witnesses stand﴾: this is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He grants them victory by dominance, and in the Hereafter by punishment. al-Suddi said: by taking vengeance upon their enemies. Abu al-ʿAliyah said: by the success of their proof. al-Suddi also said: No people ever killed a prophet or a people of the callers to the truth except that Allah sent someone who would avenge them, so they became victorious in it even though they were killed. End of quote.

Do you not see the killers of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, how Allah empowered al-Mukhtar ibn ʿUbayd against them, pursuing them one by one until he killed them? And Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) pursued the Jews when they killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both? It was said: The victory is specific to the one whom Allah, the Most High, makes victorious over his nation, such as Nuh, Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them, because we find among the prophets those whom their people killed, such as Yahya, and those who were not given victory over them. al-Suddi said: The report is general, because the support of the messengers and prophets certainly occurs, either during the lifetime of the messenger who is supported, such as Nuh and Musa, peace be upon them both, or after his death. Do you not see what Allah, the Most High, did to the Children of Israel after they killed Yahya, peace be upon him, by empowering Bukhtnassar, until he gave victory to Yahya, peace be upon him?

The majority read *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ) with the *ya* (ياء); Ibn Hurmuz, Isma'il, and al-Minqari from Abu ʿAmr read it with the feminine *ta* (تاء). [This is] the consensus. *Al-ashhad* (الأشهاد) is the plural of *shahid* (شَهِيدٍ), like *sharif* and *ashraf*, or the plural of *shahid* (شاهِدٍ), like *sahib* and *ashab*, as the Most High said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41], and He said: ﴿That you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The apparent meaning is that it is from testimony (*shahadah*). It was said: it is from witnessing (*mushahadah*), in the sense of presence.

﴿The day when no excuse will benefit﴾: a *badal* from *yawm* (يَوْمَ) in *yaqumu* (يَقُومُ). It was read as *tanfaʿu* (تَنْفَعُ) with the *ta* and with the *ya*, and the disagreement regarding that was mentioned at the end of al-Rum. It is possible that they will make excuses and their excuses will not be accepted, or that they will have no excuse that would be accepted.

﴿And for them is the curse﴾: removal and distancing from Allah.

﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾: the evil outcome of the abode.

[p. 467]

﴿O my people, what is the matter with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, that to which you call me has no call (de facto) in this world or in the Hereafter, and that our return is to God, and that the wasteful (al-musrifun) are the companions of the Fire.﴾ ﴿So you will remember what I say to you.
