As for "perhaps you will understand," it refers to the lesson and proofs contained in this, if you reflect upon it and ponder it.

When He mentioned the stages of existence, He mentioned that He is the One characterized by giving life and causing death, and that whenever His will becomes related to the bringing into existence of a thing, He brings it into existence without delay. The discussion of similar sentences has already been presented.

Then, after these signs became manifest, He said: Do you not marvel at those who dispute the mission of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the Book that he brought? This is shown by His saying: ﴿those who denied the Book and what We sent with Our messengers﴾. Then He threatened them with His saying: ﴿They will come to know﴾. This is the view of the majority.

Muhammad ibn Sirin and others said: it is an allusion to the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') from among the community. They related a hadith to this effect and said: it refers to the people of qadar (divine decree and human will) and those who follow their path. It follows for those who hold this view that His saying ﴿those who denied﴾ be taken as a new independent statement about the disbelievers, with ﴿those who denied﴾ as the subject and ﴿They will come to know﴾ as its predicate. As for the apparent reading, ﴿those who﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the preceding ﴿those who﴾, or the predicate of an elided subject, or in the accusative by way of censure. And "idh" (when) is an adverb of time referring to the past, so the future verb does not govern it, just as one does not say "sa-aqumu amsi" (I will stand yesterday). It has been said that "idh" here takes the place of "idha" (whenever), and that its position is metaphorical; so "idh" here means "idha," and the certainty of the event's occurrence justified this, and it was expressed in the past tense even though the meaning is future.

Al-Nakha'i said: If one shackle of the shackles of Hell were placed upon a mountain, it would drag it until it reached the black water.

He recited ﴿wa-l-salasilu﴾ (and the chains) as a coordination with ﴿al-aghlal﴾ (the shackles), with ﴿yus'habun﴾ (they are dragged) in the passive voice.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Musi' in his choice of reading recited (p-475) ﴿wa-l-salasila﴾ with the accusative as the object, and ﴿yus'habun﴾ in the active voice. This is the coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence.

A group, including Ibn 'Abbas, recited (wa-l-salasili) with the lam in the genitive. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is by way of an assumed construction, "when their necks are in the shackles and the chains," so it coordinates upon the intended meaning of the speech and not upon the arrangement of the wording, since its arrangement in that case is inverted. This is in the manner of the Arabs' saying: "I put the qalansuwa (cap) on my head," and in the codex of Ubayy: (and in the chains they are dragged).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The reasoning is that if one were to say, "when their necks are in the shackles," in place of His saying ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾, it would be correct and sound. Since the two expressions are interchangeable, His saying ﴿wa-l-salasilu﴾ is taken as referring to the other expression. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

Ill-omened ones, they do not reform a tribe, nor a crier except with the separation of its crow.

It is as if it were said: "with those who reform." And it was recited (wa-bi-l-salasili). The end of his words. This is called "coordination upon an assumed construction" ('atf 'ala al-tawahhum). But the assumption of inserting a prepositional particle before "muslihin" is closer than altering the entire structure of the sentence, while the recitation alters the entire structure of the preceding sentence. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

Are you truly going to see, by the Thu'aylibat (a place), nor a desert (baydaa') bearing a swift camel that carries?
Nor one who overtakes while the night is young, with a loaded camel, among the rugged parts of the valley.

The assumed construction is: "you are not innocent, nor one who overtakes."

What Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari said was preceded by al-Farra', who said: Whoever puts "salasil" in the genitive has taken it according to the meaning, because the meaning is: their necks are in the shackles and the chains.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "wa-l-salasili" with the genitive, the meaning according to him is: "and in the chains they are dragged."

Ibn al-Anbari said: The genitive on this meaning is not permissible. If you say, "Zayd is in the house," it is not good to omit the preposition and say "Zayd the house." Then he mentioned al-Farra's interpretation, and explained the recitation, and then said: as you say, "'Abd Allah contended with Zayd, the two wise ones (al-'aqilayn)," with the accusative and nominative of al-'aqilayn, because when one of them contends with his companion, the other has contended with him. The end.

This matter is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians, and its permissibility is reported from Muhammad ibn Sa'fan al-Kufi, who said: because each of the two is both agent and object. And it is recited: (wa-bi-l-salasili yus'habun). Perhaps this recitation led al-Zajjaj to interpret the genitive as implying an elided preposition, which is an anomalous interpretation.

Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding the reading of the one who put ﴿wa-l-salasila﴾ in the accusative and opened the ya' of (yas'habun): if they drag them, it is harder for them; they are burdened with this while unable to bear it.

Mujahid said: ﴿yusjarun﴾ (they are kindled) means: they are thrown into it, and so they become fuel for it. Al-Suddi said: ﴿yusjarun﴾ means they are burned.

Then God, Exalted is He, informed that they will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection for rebuke and reproach. It will be said to them: "Where are the idols that you used to worship in the world?" They will say: ﴿They have strayed from us﴾, i.e., they have been lost to us, vanished, and disappeared. Then their statements become confused, and they resort to lying, saying: ﴿Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before.﴾ This is among the greatest confusion of mind and reasoning.

When it became clear to them that they had been nothing, and that their worship of them had achieved nothing, just as you say: "I thought that so-and-so was something, but when you test him he is nothing, so you find no reward from him."

Their saying ﴿They have strayed from us﴾, together with His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell; you will be coming to it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98], may be understood to mean that this occurs during their rebuke, so the idols were not with them at that time; or, when they did not benefit them, they said ﴿They have strayed from us﴾, even if they were with them.

﴿Thus﴾ means: like this quality and in this order, ﴿God leads astray the disbelievers.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., like the straying of their gods from them; He leads them astray from their gods, so that even if they sought the gods, or the gods sought them, they would not meet.

That leading astray is because of what you used to have of exultation and insolence, ﴿without right﴾, which is polytheism and worship of idols.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: That punishment in which you are is because of what you used to exult in on earth through sins and disbelief. The end.

As for ﴿tamrahun﴾ (you are insolent), Ibn 'Abbas said: it is boasting and arrogance; Mujahid said: it is pride and frivolity. The end. He said this to them as rebuke, meaning: this is because of what you used to display in the world of joy in sins and abundance of wealth, followers, and health.

Al-Dahhak said: "al-farah" is joy and delight, and "al-maraḥ" is transgression. In a hadith: "God hates the exulting, arrogant ones, and loves every grieving heart."

﴿Tafrahun﴾ and ﴿tamrahun﴾ are from the type of paronomasia by alteration (tajnis al-tahrif), mentioned in the science of rhetorical embellishment (ilm al-badi'), which is when a letter distinguishes between two words.

﴿Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is said to them: "Enter," after the preceding dialogue, and they had already been in the Fire; but this is a command restricted by "abiding," which is a lasting dwelling, so it is not a command for mere entry. Or, after entering it, they are commanded to enter the seven gates, for each gate has a specified portion of the disbelievers; this command to enter thus implies division into each gate.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Enter﴾ means: it is said to them before this dialogue, at the beginning of the matter: "Enter," because this address is only after they have entered, and at the time when the shackles are on their necks.

The gates of Hell are the seven leading to its layers and its seven levels. The end.

﴿Abiding﴾ is a circumstantial clause of anticipated state (hal muqaddara), and it indicates lasting dwelling. Thus the construction comes: ﴿How evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾; the meaning is: how evil is the entrance of the arrogant, because entry itself does not last, so he did not exaggerate in condemning it, unlike lasting dwelling.

[p-477] Allah commanded His Prophet to be patient, to comfort him, though he, peace be upon him, was already at the utmost of patience. He informed him that what He had promised him of victory, triumph, the elevation of His word, and the manifestation of His religion is true.

It has been said that the response (jawab) to ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: "then He will comfort your eye." It is not valid for ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ to be the response to both the conditional clause and its coordinated clause, because the structure ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ "some of what We promise them during your lifetime" followed by ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is not apparent. It can, however, be the response to ﴿أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, meaning ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾, so that We take vengeance on them and punish them because they did not follow you.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41] ﴿أوْ نُرِيَنَّكَ الَّذِي وعَدْناهم فَإنّا عَلَيْهِمْ مُقْتَدِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42], except that here the response to both conditions is stated explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, and the response to ﴿نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Then if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, which is their being killed on the day of Badr, then that is so; or if We take you (wafat) before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take vengeance on them with the utmost vengeance."

A similar discussion by al-Zamakhshari has already appeared in Surat Yunus in his saying: ﴿وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ بَعْضَ الَّذِي نَعِدُهم أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ فَإلَيْنا مَرْجِعُهُمْ﴾ [Yunus: 46]; we responded to him there, so refer to it there.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ originally was ﴿فَإنْ نُرِكَ﴾, and ma is added (mazidah) to emphasise the meaning of the conditional, and for this reason the nun (of emphasis) is attached to the verb. Do you not see that you do not say: "If you honour me, I will honour you," but rather: "Amma tukrimni ukrimka?" (end of his words).

What he held regarding the obligatory combination of the extra ma and the nun of emphasis after the conditional particle in is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj.

Sibawayh held that if you wish you may use ma without the nun, and if you wish you may use the nun without ma. Sibawayh said in this matter: "And if you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as when you come with (in) you do not bring ma with it, and you do not bring ma with your use of the nun."

[The majority] read ﴿يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a yā' of absence and in the passive voice. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yā'. Talha ibn Musarrif, and Ya'qub in the narration of al-Walid ibn Hassan, read it with a fatha on the tā' of address.

Then Allah answered the Arabs in their denial of the sending of messengers. There is disagreement about the number of the messengers.

It is narrated that they were eight thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from others. It is also narrated: Allah sent four thousand prophets.

﴿مِنهم مَن قَصَصْنا عَلَيْكَ﴾, that is: those about whom We informed you. As for the Qur'an, (they are) eighteen.

﴿ومِنهم مَن لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that Allah sent a black prophet to the Abyssinians, and he is among those whom We did not relate to you.

﴿وما كانَ لِرَسُولٍ أنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ إلّا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: this is not up to them. When they proposed (signs) to the messengers, he said: "That is not up to me; no sign comes except by the permission of Allah."

﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾: a rejection and a warning following their demand for signs. "The command of Allah" is the Resurrection.

﴿المُبْطِلُونَ﴾ are the obstinate ones who propose signs, though the signs had come to them; they denied them and called them magic. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: when He wished to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decided that and executed it ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾, and every person of falsehood lost and incurred the corruption of his Hereafter. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the killing at Badr.

Then Allah mentioned signs for reflection and a enumeration of blessings, saying: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأنْعامَ﴾. These are the eight pairs. The view of those who include horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived is weak, as is the view of those who restrict it to camels, which is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنها﴾: these are the camels, since riding other than them is not customary.

﴿ومِنها تَأْكُلُونَ﴾: general for the eight pairs. The first (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the second (min) is for explaining the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because the camel is eaten from among them, (end of his words). It does not appear that it is for explaining the kind; it may be partitive and also for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Since riding from them is the greater benefit, as it contains the benefit of both eating and riding.

He also mentioned that in all of them there are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. He emphasised the benefit of riding by His saying: ﴿ولِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْها حاجَةً في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾, namely reaching by means of them long journeys, carrying loads to distant lands, performing the obligation of the Hajj, going on raids, and similar religious and worldly benefits.

Since riding and reaching the need that follows from it may be a means to moving for a obligatory or recommended matter, such as Hajj and seeking knowledge, the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) entered upon riding and upon what follows from it of attaining needs, making that the cause for Allah making the cattle ours.

Since eating and gaining benefits belong to the category of permissible things, He did not make that the cause in the making; rather, He mentioned that from them we eat, and for us in them are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. Just as He introduced the lam of causation in ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوها﴾ [al-Nahl: 8] and did not introduce it upon adornment in His saying: ﴿والخَيْلَ والبِغالَ والحَمِيرَ لِتَرْكَبُوها وزِينَةً﴾ [al-Nahl: 8].

When Allah mentioned what He had bestowed as favour of riding camels on land, He mentioned what He had bestowed as the blessing of riding at sea, saying: ﴿وعَلَيْها وعَلى الفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ﴾.

Since ﴿الفُلْكِ﴾ (ships) may correctly be said of it "he carried in the ship" (hamala fi al-fulk), as in His saying ﴿احْمِلْ فِيها﴾ [Hud: 40], and it may also correctly be said "he carried upon the ship" (hamala 'ala al-fulk), the particle ʿalā was taken into account to match His saying ﴿وعَلَيْها﴾, although fi is also correct.

﴿ويُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾, that is: His proofs and evidences of His oneness.

﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تُنْكِرُونَ﴾, that is: they are many, so which of them do you deny? That is: it is not possible to deny any of them by reason. ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿تُنْكِرُونَ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ﴾ came in the widespread dialect; your saying "fa-ayyatu ayat Allah" is rare, because differentiating between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as ḥimār (donkey, masc.) and ḥimāra (she-donkey), is strange, and it is stranger in (ayy) because of its vagueness (end of his words). Among the rarity of feminising ayy is his saying:

"By which Book, or by which Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

As for his saying "it is stranger in ayy," if he means ayy in general, it is not correct, because what is widespread in vocative address is to feminise the vocative of a feminine noun, based on His saying: ﴿يا أيَّتُها النَّفْسُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]; and no one is known to masculinise it in saying "yā ayyuha al-mar'a," except the author of the book al-Badi' fi al-Nahw. If he means other than the vocative, then his words are correct, since feminising it is rare in interrogation and as a relative pronoun. And ma in His saying ﴿فَما أغْنى﴾ is negative, conditional, and interrogative in the sense of negation; and ma in ﴿ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is verbal-masdarial, or means "that which," and is in the place of the nominative. The pronoun in ﴿جاءَتْهُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾. His saying "(min al-'ilm)" comes as a mockery of them: in reality they have no knowledge, but rather they have fancies and dismissals of what the messengers brought; they repelled what the messengers brought with such words as: ﴿ولَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إلى رَبِّي لَأجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِنها مُنْقَلَبًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], or they believed that they had a knowledge by which they could dispense with the knowledge of the prophets, as the philosophers claim. The materialists, when they heard of the revelation of Allah, rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge.

When Socrates, may Allah curse him, heard of Musa, may the blessings of Allah be upon our Prophet and upon him, it was said to him: "If only you had migrated to him." He said: "We are a people who are refined, so we have no need for one who refines us."

On these two views the pronouns are consistent, referring to one single referent.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the messengers rejoiced in what they had been given of knowledge, and thanked Allah for it, when they saw the ignorance of those to whom they were sent and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the nations, and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the unbelievers rejoiced in what the messengers had of knowledge, with the joy of laughter and mockery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the aspects in the verse, in His saying ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾, is an exaggeration in negating their joy at revelation, which requires the utmost joy and happiness, in mockery of their extreme ignorance and emptiness of knowledge (end of his words).

A sentence whose affirmative form is apparent is expressed as a negated sentence, except in a little speech, such as their saying: "An evil that snarls at the one with a fang," with disagreement about it. When its matter came to the restricted giving (al-iyta' al-mahsur), it was permitted.

But in the verse it should not be taken as the rare case, because that mixes up the meanings of different sentences, and so none of them can be trusted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾ means their knowledge of worldly affairs and their awareness of managing them, as He says: ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ ظاهِرًا مِنَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وهم عَنِ الآخِرَةِ هم غافِلُونَ﴾ [al-Rum: 7]; that is the extent of their knowledge. When the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion, which are the furthest thing from their knowledge, since they called to abandoning the world and restraining from pleasures and desires, they did not pay attention to them, belittled them, mocked them, and believed that there is no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of gains than their own, so they rejoiced in it (end of his words).

This is a good interpretation, but it contains excess and verbosity.

﴿بَأْسَنا﴾, that is: Our severe punishment. It recounts the state of one who believes after the punishment has encompassed him, and that this does not benefit him. In this there is an urging to hasten to faith and a warning against delay. As for the people of Yunus, they saw the punishment had not yet befallen them, and their story has already passed.

﴿إيمانُهُمْ﴾ is in the nominative, either as the subject of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (its noun), or as the agent of ﴿يَنْفَعُهُمْ﴾.

The pronoun in (yakun) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), following the disagreement concerning *kāna yaqūmu Zaydun*. The negative particle entered upon the existence (al-kawn), not upon the negation, because it leads to the negation of validity, meaning it was not valid and was not right, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

As for the succession of these fā' particles: in ﴿So it did not avail﴾, it is because it was the consequence of His saying: "They were more numerous than them, and when their messengers came to them," and it functions as explanation and elaboration of His saying: ﴿so it did not avail them﴾. And ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ follows His saying: ﴿when there came to them﴾, as if He said: they disbelieved in it, then when they saw Our punishment they believed, but their faith did not benefit them when they saw the punishment of God. The word ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, meaning: what was done to them is ﴿the way of God﴾ which has passed and has been established among His servants, concerning the sending of messengers and their honouring (al-i'zāz), the punishment of those who denied them, their humiliation of them, their uprooting by destruction, and the non-benefit of faith at the time when the punishment has overtaken them.

There is also a place adverb (ẓarf makān) used for time, meaning: and the disbelievers lost at that time.

It has also been said: ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative by way of warning, meaning: beware of the way of God, O people of Makkah, regarding the sending of messengers.

[p-477] Allah commanded His Prophet to be patient, to comfort him, though he, peace be upon him, was already at the utmost of patience. He informed him that what He had promised him of victory, triumph, the elevation of His word, and the manifestation of His religion is true.

It has been said that the response (jawab) to ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: "then He will comfort your eye." It is not valid for ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ to be the response to both the conditional clause and its coordinated clause, because the structure ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ "some of what We promise them during your lifetime" followed by ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is not apparent. It can, however, be the response to ﴿أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, meaning ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾, so that We take vengeance on them and punish them because they did not follow you.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41] ﴿أوْ نُرِيَنَّكَ الَّذِي وعَدْناهم فَإنّا عَلَيْهِمْ مُقْتَدِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42], except that here the response to both conditions is stated explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, and the response to ﴿نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Then if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, which is their being killed on the day of Badr, then that is so; or if We take you (wafat) before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take vengeance on them with the utmost vengeance."

A similar discussion by al-Zamakhshari has already appeared in Surat Yunus in his saying: ﴿وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ بَعْضَ الَّذِي نَعِدُهم أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ فَإلَيْنا مَرْجِعُهُمْ﴾ [Yunus: 46]; we responded to him there, so refer to it there.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ originally was ﴿فَإنْ نُرِكَ﴾, and ma is added (mazidah) to emphasise the meaning of the conditional, and for this reason the nun (of emphasis) is attached to the verb. Do you not see that you do not say: "If you honour me, I will honour you," but rather: "Amma tukrimni ukrimka?" (end of his words).

What he held regarding the obligatory combination of the extra ma and the nun of emphasis after the conditional particle in is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj.

Sibawayh held that if you wish you may use ma without the nun, and if you wish you may use the nun without ma. Sibawayh said in this matter: "And if you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as when you come with (in) you do not bring ma with it, and you do not bring ma with your use of the nun."

[The majority] read ﴿يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a yā' of absence and in the passive voice. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yā'. Talha ibn Musarrif, and Ya'qub in the narration of al-Walid ibn Hassan, read it with a fatha on the tā' of address.

Then Allah answered the Arabs in their denial of the sending of messengers. There is disagreement about the number of the messengers.

It is narrated that they were eight thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from others. It is also narrated: Allah sent four thousand prophets.

﴿مِنهم مَن قَصَصْنا عَلَيْكَ﴾, that is: those about whom We informed you. As for the Qur'an, (they are) eighteen.

﴿ومِنهم مَن لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that Allah sent a black prophet to the Abyssinians, and he is among those whom We did not relate to you.

﴿وما كانَ لِرَسُولٍ أنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ إلّا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: this is not up to them. When they proposed (signs) to the messengers, he said: "That is not up to me; no sign comes except by the permission of Allah."

﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾: a rejection and a warning following their demand for signs. "The command of Allah" is the Resurrection.

﴿المُبْطِلُونَ﴾ are the obstinate ones who propose signs, though the signs had come to them; they denied them and called them magic. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: when He wished to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decided that and executed it ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾, and every person of falsehood lost and incurred the corruption of his Hereafter. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the killing at Badr.

Then Allah mentioned signs for reflection and a enumeration of blessings, saying: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأنْعامَ﴾. These are the eight pairs. The view of those who include horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived is weak, as is the view of those who restrict it to camels, which is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنها﴾: these are the camels, since riding other than them is not customary.

﴿ومِنها تَأْكُلُونَ﴾: general for the eight pairs. The first (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the second (min) is for explaining the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because the camel is eaten from among them, (end of his words). It does not appear that it is for explaining the kind; it may be partitive and also for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Since riding from them is the greater benefit, as it contains the benefit of both eating and riding.

He also mentioned that in all of them there are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. He emphasised the benefit of riding by His saying: ﴿ولِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْها حاجَةً في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾, namely reaching by means of them long journeys, carrying loads to distant lands, performing the obligation of the Hajj, going on raids, and similar religious and worldly benefits.

Since riding and reaching the need that follows from it may be a means to moving for a obligatory or recommended matter, such as Hajj and seeking knowledge, the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) entered upon riding and upon what follows from it of attaining needs, making that the cause for Allah making the cattle ours.

Since eating and gaining benefits belong to the category of permissible things, He did not make that the cause in the making; rather, He mentioned that from them we eat, and for us in them are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. Just as He introduced the lam of causation in ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوها﴾ [al-Nahl: 8] and did not introduce it upon adornment in His saying: ﴿والخَيْلَ والبِغالَ والحَمِيرَ لِتَرْكَبُوها وزِينَةً﴾ [al-Nahl: 8].

When Allah mentioned what He had bestowed as favour of riding camels on land, He mentioned what He had bestowed as the blessing of riding at sea, saying: ﴿وعَلَيْها وعَلى الفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ﴾.

Since ﴿الفُلْكِ﴾ (ships) may correctly be said of it "he carried in the ship" (hamala fi al-fulk), as in His saying ﴿احْمِلْ فِيها﴾ [Hud: 40], and it may also correctly be said "he carried upon the ship" (hamala 'ala al-fulk), the particle ʿalā was taken into account to match His saying ﴿وعَلَيْها﴾, although fi is also correct.

﴿ويُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾, that is: His proofs and evidences of His oneness.

﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تُنْكِرُونَ﴾, that is: they are many, so which of them do you deny? That is: it is not possible to deny any of them by reason. ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿تُنْكِرُونَ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ﴾ came in the widespread dialect; your saying "fa-ayyatu ayat Allah" is rare, because differentiating between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as ḥimār (donkey, masc.) and ḥimāra (she-donkey), is strange, and it is stranger in (ayy) because of its vagueness (end of his words). Among the rarity of feminising ayy is his saying:

"By which Book, or by which Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

As for his saying "it is stranger in ayy," if he means ayy in general, it is not correct, because what is widespread in vocative address is to feminise the vocative of a feminine noun, based on His saying: ﴿يا أيَّتُها النَّفْسُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]; and no one is known to masculinise it in saying "yā ayyuha al-mar'a," except the author of the book al-Badi' fi al-Nahw. If he means other than the vocative, then his words are correct, since feminising it is rare in interrogation and as a relative pronoun. And ma in His saying ﴿فَما أغْنى﴾ is negative, conditional, and interrogative in the sense of negation; and ma in ﴿ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is verbal-masdarial, or means "that which," and is in the place of the nominative. The pronoun in ﴿جاءَتْهُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾. His saying "(min al-'ilm)" comes as a mockery of them: in reality they have no knowledge, but rather they have fancies and dismissals of what the messengers brought; they repelled what the messengers brought with such words as: ﴿ولَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إلى رَبِّي لَأجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِنها مُنْقَلَبًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], or they believed that they had a knowledge by which they could dispense with the knowledge of the prophets, as the philosophers claim. The materialists, when they heard of the revelation of Allah, rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge.

When Socrates, may Allah curse him, heard of Musa, may the blessings of Allah be upon our Prophet and upon him, it was said to him: "If only you had migrated to him." He said: "We are a people who are refined, so we have no need for one who refines us."

On these two views the pronouns are consistent, referring to one single referent.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the messengers rejoiced in what they had been given of knowledge, and thanked Allah for it, when they saw the ignorance of those to whom they were sent and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the nations, and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the unbelievers rejoiced in what the messengers had of knowledge, with the joy of laughter and mockery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the aspects in the verse, in His saying ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾, is an exaggeration in negating their joy at revelation, which requires the utmost joy and happiness, in mockery of their extreme ignorance and emptiness of knowledge (end of his words).

A sentence whose affirmative form is apparent is expressed as a negated sentence, except in a little speech, such as their saying: "An evil that snarls at the one with a fang," with disagreement about it. When its matter came to the restricted giving (al-iyta' al-mahsur), it was permitted.

But in the verse it should not be taken as the rare case, because that mixes up the meanings of different sentences, and so none of them can be trusted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾ means their knowledge of worldly affairs and their awareness of managing them, as He says: ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ ظاهِرًا مِنَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وهم عَنِ الآخِرَةِ هم غافِلُونَ﴾ [al-Rum: 7]; that is the extent of their knowledge. When the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion, which are the furthest thing from their knowledge, since they called to abandoning the world and restraining from pleasures and desires, they did not pay attention to them, belittled them, mocked them, and believed that there is no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of gains than their own, so they rejoiced in it (end of his words).

This is a good interpretation, but it contains excess and verbosity.

﴿بَأْسَنا﴾, that is: Our severe punishment. It recounts the state of one who believes after the punishment has encompassed him, and that this does not benefit him. In this there is an urging to hasten to faith and a warning against delay. As for the people of Yunus, they saw the punishment had not yet befallen them, and their story has already passed.

﴿إيمانُهُمْ﴾ is in the nominative, either as the subject of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (its noun), or as the agent of ﴿يَنْفَعُهُمْ﴾.

The pronoun in (yakun) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), following the disagreement concerning *kāna yaqūmu Zaydun*. The negative particle entered upon the existence (al-kawn), not upon the negation, because it leads to the negation of validity, meaning it was not valid and was not right, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

As for the succession of these fā' particles: in ﴿So it did not avail﴾, it is because it was the consequence of His saying: "They were more numerous than them, and when their messengers came to them," and it functions as explanation and elaboration of His saying: ﴿so it did not avail them﴾. And ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ follows His saying: ﴿when there came to them﴾, as if He said: they disbelieved in it, then when they saw Our punishment they believed, but their faith did not benefit them when they saw the punishment of God. The word ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, meaning: what was done to them is ﴿the way of God﴾ which has passed and has been established among His servants, concerning the sending of messengers and their honouring (al-i'zāz), the punishment of those who denied them, their humiliation of them, their uprooting by destruction, and the non-benefit of faith at the time when the punishment has overtaken them.

There is also a place adverb (ẓarf makān) used for time, meaning: and the disbelievers lost at that time.

It has also been said: ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative by way of warning, meaning: beware of the way of God, O people of Makkah, regarding the sending of messengers.

[p-477] Allah commanded His Prophet to be patient, to comfort him, though he, peace be upon him, was already at the utmost of patience. He informed him that what He had promised him of victory, triumph, the elevation of His word, and the manifestation of His religion is true.

It has been said that the response (jawab) to ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: "then He will comfort your eye." It is not valid for ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ to be the response to both the conditional clause and its coordinated clause, because the structure ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ "some of what We promise them during your lifetime" followed by ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is not apparent. It can, however, be the response to ﴿أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, meaning ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾, so that We take vengeance on them and punish them because they did not follow you.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41] ﴿أوْ نُرِيَنَّكَ الَّذِي وعَدْناهم فَإنّا عَلَيْهِمْ مُقْتَدِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42], except that here the response to both conditions is stated explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, and the response to ﴿نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Then if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, which is their being killed on the day of Badr, then that is so; or if We take you (wafat) before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take vengeance on them with the utmost vengeance."

And ma in His saying ﴿فَما أغْنى﴾ is negative, conditional, and interrogative in the sense of negation; and ma in ﴿ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is verbal-masdarial, or means "that which," and is in the place of the nominative. The pronoun in ﴿جاءَتْهُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾. His saying "(min al-'ilm)" comes as a mockery of them: in reality they have no knowledge, but rather they have fancies and dismissals of what the messengers brought; they repelled what the messengers brought with such words as: ﴿ولَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إلى رَبِّي لَأجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِنها مُنْقَلَبًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], or they believed that they had a knowledge by which they could dispense with the knowledge of the prophets, as the philosophers claim. The materialists, when they heard of the revelation of Allah, rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge.

When Socrates, may Allah curse him, heard of Musa, may the blessings of Allah be upon our Prophet and upon him, it was said to him: "If only you had migrated to him." He said: "We are a people who are refined, so we have no need for one who refines us."

On these two views the pronouns are consistent, referring to one single referent.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the messengers rejoiced in what they had been given of knowledge, and thanked Allah for it, when they saw the ignorance of those to whom they were sent and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the nations, and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the unbelievers rejoiced in what the messengers had of knowledge, with the joy of laughter and mockery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the aspects in the verse, in His saying ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾, is an exaggeration in negating their joy at revelation, which requires the utmost joy and happiness, in mockery of their extreme ignorance and emptiness of knowledge (end of his words).

A sentence whose affirmative form is apparent is expressed as a negated sentence, except in a little speech, such as their saying: "An evil that snarls at the one with a fang," with disagreement about it. When its matter came to the restricted giving (al-iyta' al-mahsur), it was permitted.

But in the verse it should not be taken as the rare case, because that mixes up the meanings of different sentences, and so none of them can be trusted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾ means their knowledge of worldly affairs and their awareness of managing them, as He says: ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ ظاهِرًا مِنَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وهم عَنِ الآخِرَةِ هم غافِلُونَ﴾ [al-Rum: 7]; that is the extent of their knowledge. When the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion, which are the furthest thing from their knowledge, since they called to abandoning the world and restraining from pleasures and desires, they did not pay attention to them, belittled them, mocked them, and believed that there is no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of gains than their own, so they rejoiced in it (end of his words).

This is a good interpretation, but it contains excess and verbosity.

﴿بَأْسَنا﴾, that is: Our severe punishment. It recounts the state of one who believes after the punishment has encompassed him, and that this does not benefit him. In this there is an urging to hasten to faith and a warning against delay. As for the people of Yunus, they saw the punishment had not yet befallen them, and their story has already passed.

﴿إيمانُهُمْ﴾ is in the nominative, either as the subject of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (its noun), or as the agent of ﴿يَنْفَعُهُمْ﴾.

The pronoun in (yakun) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), following the disagreement concerning *kāna yaqūmu Zaydun*. The negative particle entered upon the existence (al-kawn), not upon the negation, because it leads to the negation of validity, meaning it was not valid and was not right, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

As for the succession of these fā' particles: in ﴿So it did not avail﴾, it is because it was the consequence of His saying: "They were more numerous than them, and when their messengers came to them," and it functions as explanation and elaboration of His saying: ﴿so it did not avail them﴾. And ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ follows His saying: ﴿when there came to them﴾, as if He said: they disbelieved in it, then when they saw Our punishment they believed, but their faith did not benefit them when they saw the punishment of God. The word ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, meaning: what was done to them is ﴿the way of God﴾ which has passed and has been established among His servants, concerning the sending of messengers and their honouring (al-i'zāz), the punishment of those who denied them, their humiliation of them, their uprooting by destruction, and the non-benefit of faith at the time when the punishment has overtaken them.

There is also a place adverb (ẓarf makān) used for time, meaning: and the disbelievers lost at that time.

It has also been said: ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative by way of warning, meaning: beware of the way of God, O people of Makkah, regarding the sending of messengers.

[p-477] Allah commanded His Prophet to be patient, to comfort him, though he, peace be upon him, was already at the utmost of patience. He informed him that what He had promised him of victory, triumph, the elevation of His word, and the manifestation of His religion is true.

It has been said that the response (jawab) to ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: "then He will comfort your eye." It is not valid for ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ to be the response to both the conditional clause and its coordinated clause, because the structure ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ "some of what We promise them during your lifetime" followed by ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is not apparent. It can, however, be the response to ﴿أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, meaning ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾, so that We take vengeance on them and punish them because they did not follow you.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41] ﴿أوْ نُرِيَنَّكَ الَّذِي وعَدْناهم فَإنّا عَلَيْهِمْ مُقْتَدِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42], except that here the response to both conditions is stated explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, and the response to ﴿نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Then if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, which is their being killed on the day of Badr, then that is so; or if We take you (wafat) before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take vengeance on them with the utmost vengeance."

A similar discussion by al-Zamakhshari has already appeared in Surat Yunus in his saying: ﴿وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ بَعْضَ الَّذِي نَعِدُهم أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ فَإلَيْنا مَرْجِعُهُمْ﴾ [Yunus: 46]; we responded to him there, so refer to it there.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ originally was ﴿فَإنْ نُرِكَ﴾, and ma is added (mazidah) to emphasise the meaning of the conditional, and for this reason the nun (of emphasis) is attached to the verb. Do you not see that you do not say: "If you honour me, I will honour you," but rather: "Amma tukrimni ukrimka?" (end of his words).

What he held regarding the obligatory combination of the extra ma and the nun of emphasis after the conditional particle in is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj.

Sibawayh held that if you wish you may use ma without the nun, and if you wish you may use the nun without ma. Sibawayh said in this matter: "And if you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as when you come with (in) you do not bring ma with it, and you do not bring ma with your use of the nun."

[The majority] read ﴿يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a yā' of absence and in the passive voice. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yā'. Talha ibn Musarrif, and Ya'qub in the narration of al-Walid ibn Hassan, read it with a fatha on the tā' of address.

Then Allah answered the Arabs in their denial of the sending of messengers. There is disagreement about the number of the messengers.

It is narrated that they were eight thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from others. It is also narrated: Allah sent four thousand prophets.

﴿مِنهم مَن قَصَصْنا عَلَيْكَ﴾, that is: those about whom We informed you. As for the Qur'an, (they are) eighteen.

﴿ومِنهم مَن لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that Allah sent a black prophet to the Abyssinians, and he is among those whom We did not relate to you.

﴿وما كانَ لِرَسُولٍ أنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ إلّا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: this is not up to them. When they proposed (signs) to the messengers, he said: "That is not up to me; no sign comes except by the permission of Allah."

﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾: a rejection and a warning following their demand for signs. "The command of Allah" is the Resurrection.

﴿المُبْطِلُونَ﴾ are the obstinate ones who propose signs, though the signs had come to them; they denied them and called them magic. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: when He wished to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decided that and executed it ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾, and every person of falsehood lost and incurred the corruption of his Hereafter. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the killing at Badr.

Then Allah mentioned signs for reflection and a enumeration of blessings, saying: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأنْعامَ﴾. These are the eight pairs. The view of those who include horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived is weak, as is the view of those who restrict it to camels, which is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنها﴾: these are the camels, since riding other than them is not customary.

﴿ومِنها تَأْكُلُونَ﴾: general for the eight pairs. The first (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the second (min) is for explaining the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because the camel is eaten from among them, (end of his words). It does not appear that it is for explaining the kind; it may be partitive and also for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Since riding from them is the greater benefit, as it contains the benefit of both eating and riding.

He also mentioned that in all of them there are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. He emphasised the benefit of riding by His saying: ﴿ولِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْها حاجَةً في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾, namely reaching by means of them long journeys, carrying loads to distant lands, performing the obligation of the Hajj, going on raids, and similar religious and worldly benefits.

Since riding and reaching the need that follows from it may be a means to moving for a obligatory or recommended matter, such as Hajj and seeking knowledge, the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) entered upon riding and upon what follows from it of attaining needs, making that the cause for Allah making the cattle ours.

Since eating and gaining benefits belong to the category of permissible things, He did not make that the cause in the making; rather, He mentioned that from them we eat, and for us in them are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. Just as He introduced the lam of causation in ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوها﴾ [al-Nahl: 8] and did not introduce it upon adornment in His saying: ﴿والخَيْلَ والبِغالَ والحَمِيرَ لِتَرْكَبُوها وزِينَةً﴾ [al-Nahl: 8].

When Allah mentioned what He had bestowed as favour of riding camels on land, He mentioned what He had bestowed as the blessing of riding at sea, saying: ﴿وعَلَيْها وعَلى الفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ﴾.

Since ﴿الفُلْكِ﴾ (ships) may correctly be said of it "he carried in the ship" (hamala fi al-fulk), as in His saying ﴿احْمِلْ فِيها﴾ [Hud: 40], and it may also correctly be said "he carried upon the ship" (hamala 'ala al-fulk), the particle ʿalā was taken into account to match His saying ﴿وعَلَيْها﴾, although fi is also correct.

﴿ويُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾, that is: His proofs and evidences of His oneness.

﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تُنْكِرُونَ﴾, that is: they are many, so which of them do you deny? That is: it is not possible to deny any of them by reason. ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿تُنْكِرُونَ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ﴾ came in the widespread dialect; your saying "fa-ayyatu ayat Allah" is rare, because differentiating between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as ḥimār (donkey, masc.) and ḥimāra (she-donkey), is strange, and it is stranger in (ayy) because of its vagueness (end of his words). Among the rarity of feminising ayy is his saying:

"By which Book, or by which Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

As for his saying "it is stranger in ayy," if he means ayy in general, it is not correct, because what is widespread in vocative address is to feminise the vocative of a feminine noun, based on His saying: ﴿يا أيَّتُها النَّفْسُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]; and no one is known to masculinise it in saying "yā ayyuha al-mar'a," except the author of the book al-Badi' fi al-Nahw. If he means other than the vocative, then his words are correct, since feminising it is rare in interrogation and as a relative pronoun. And ma in His saying ﴿فَما أغْنى﴾ is negative, conditional, and interrogative in the sense of negation; and ma in ﴿ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is verbal-masdarial, or means "that which," and is in the place of the nominative. The pronoun in ﴿جاءَتْهُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾. His saying "(min al-'ilm)" comes as a mockery of them: in reality they have no knowledge, but rather they have fancies and dismissals of what the messengers brought; they repelled what the messengers brought with such words as: ﴿ولَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إلى رَبِّي لَأجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِنها مُنْقَلَبًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], or they believed that they had a knowledge by which they could dispense with the knowledge of the prophets, as the philosophers claim. The materialists, when they heard of the revelation of Allah, rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge.

﴿مِنهم مَن قَصَصْنا عَلَيْكَ﴾, that is: those about whom We informed you. As for the Qur'an, (they are) eighteen.

﴿ومِنهم مَن لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that Allah sent a black prophet to the Abyssinians, and he is among those whom We did not relate to you.

﴿وما كانَ لِرَسُولٍ أنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ إلّا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: this is not up to them. When they proposed (signs) to the messengers, he said: "That is not up to me; no sign comes except by the permission of Allah."

﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾: a rejection and a warning following their demand for signs. "The command of Allah" is the Resurrection.

﴿المُبْطِلُونَ﴾ are the obstinate ones who propose signs, though the signs had come to them; they denied them and called them magic. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: when He wished to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decided that and executed it ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾, and every person of falsehood lost and incurred the corruption of his Hereafter. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the killing at Badr.

Then Allah mentioned signs for reflection and a enumeration of blessings, saying: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأنْعامَ﴾. These are the eight pairs. The view of those who include horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived is weak, as is the view of those who restrict it to camels, which is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنها﴾: these are the camels, since riding other than them is not customary.

﴿ومِنها تَأْكُلُونَ﴾: general for the eight pairs. The first (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the second (min) is for explaining the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because the camel is eaten from among them, (end of his words). It does not appear that it is for explaining the kind; it may be partitive and also for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Since riding from them is the greater benefit, as it contains the benefit of both eating and riding.

He also mentioned that in all of them there are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. He emphasised the benefit of riding by His saying: ﴿ولِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْها حاجَةً في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾, namely reaching by means of them long journeys, carrying loads to distant lands, performing the obligation of the Hajj, going on raids, and similar religious and worldly benefits.

Since riding and reaching the need that follows from it may be a means to moving for a obligatory or recommended matter, such as Hajj and seeking knowledge, the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) entered upon riding and upon what follows from it of attaining needs, making that the cause for Allah making the cattle ours.

Since eating and gaining benefits belong to the category of permissible things, He did not make that the cause in the making; rather, He mentioned that from them we eat, and for us in them are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. Just as He introduced the lam of causation in ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوها﴾ [al-Nahl: 8] and did not introduce it upon adornment in His saying: ﴿والخَيْلَ والبِغالَ والحَمِيرَ لِتَرْكَبُوها وزِينَةً﴾ [al-Nahl: 8].

When Allah mentioned what He had bestowed as favour of riding camels on land, He mentioned what He had bestowed as the blessing of riding at sea, saying: ﴿وعَلَيْها وعَلى الفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ﴾.

Since ﴿الفُلْكِ﴾ (ships) may correctly be said of it "he carried in the ship" (hamala fi al-fulk), as in His saying ﴿احْمِلْ فِيها﴾ [Hud: 40], and it may also correctly be said "he carried upon the ship" (hamala 'ala al-fulk), the particle ʿalā was taken into account to match His saying ﴿وعَلَيْها﴾, although fi is also correct.

﴿ويُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾, that is: His proofs and evidences of His oneness.

﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تُنْكِرُونَ﴾, that is: they are many, so which of them do you deny? That is: it is not possible to deny any of them by reason. ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿تُنْكِرُونَ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ﴾ came in the widespread dialect; your saying "fa-ayyatu ayat Allah" is rare, because differentiating between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as ḥimār (donkey, masc.) and ḥimāra (she-donkey), is strange, and it is stranger in (ayy) because of its vagueness (end of his words). Among the rarity of feminising ayy is his saying:

"By which Book, or by which Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

As for his saying "it is stranger in ayy," if he means ayy in general, it is not correct, because what is widespread in vocative address is to feminise the vocative of a feminine noun, based on His saying: ﴿يا أيَّتُها النَّفْسُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]; and no one is known to masculinise it in saying "yā ayyuha al-mar'a," except the author of the book al-Badi' fi al-Nahw. If he means other than the vocative, then his words are correct, since feminising it is rare in interrogation and as a relative pronoun. And ma in His saying ﴿فَما أغْنى﴾ is negative, conditional, and interrogative in the sense of negation; and ma in ﴿ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ is verbal-masdarial, or means "that which," and is in the place of the nominative. The pronoun in ﴿جاءَتْهُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾. His saying "(min al-'ilm)" comes as a mockery of them: in reality they have no knowledge, but rather they have fancies and dismissals of what the messengers brought; they repelled what the messengers brought with such words as: ﴿ولَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ إلى رَبِّي لَأجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِنها مُنْقَلَبًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], or they believed that they had a knowledge by which they could dispense with the knowledge of the prophets, as the philosophers claim. The materialists, when they heard of the revelation of Allah, rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge.

When Socrates, may Allah curse him, heard of Musa, may the blessings of Allah be upon our Prophet and upon him, it was said to him: "If only you had migrated to him." He said: "We are a people who are refined, so we have no need for one who refines us."

On these two views the pronouns are consistent, referring to one single referent.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the messengers rejoiced in what they had been given of knowledge, and thanked Allah for it, when they saw the ignorance of those to whom they were sent and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿فَرِحُوا﴾ refers to the nations, and in ﴿بِما عِنْدَهُمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, that is: the unbelievers rejoiced in what the messengers had of knowledge, with the joy of laughter and mockery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the aspects in the verse, in His saying ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾, is an exaggeration in negating their joy at revelation, which requires the utmost joy and happiness, in mockery of their extreme ignorance and emptiness of knowledge (end of his words).

A sentence whose affirmative form is apparent is expressed as a negated sentence, except in a little speech, such as their saying: "An evil that snarls at the one with a fang," with disagreement about it. When its matter came to the restricted giving (al-iyta' al-mahsur), it was permitted.

But in the verse it should not be taken as the rare case, because that mixes up the meanings of different sentences, and so none of them can be trusted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿فَرِحُوا بِما عِنْدَهم مِنَ العِلْمِ﴾ means their knowledge of worldly affairs and their awareness of managing them, as He says: ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ ظاهِرًا مِنَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وهم عَنِ الآخِرَةِ هم غافِلُونَ﴾ [al-Rum: 7]; that is the extent of their knowledge. When the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion, which are the furthest thing from their knowledge, since they called to abandoning the world and restraining from pleasures and desires, they did not pay attention to them, belittled them, mocked them, and believed that there is no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of gains than their own, so they rejoiced in it (end of his words).

This is a good interpretation, but it contains excess and verbosity.

﴿بَأْسَنا﴾, that is: Our severe punishment. It recounts the state of one who believes after the punishment has encompassed him, and that this does not benefit him. In this there is an urging to hasten to faith and a warning against delay. As for the people of Yunus, they saw the punishment had not yet befallen them, and their story has already passed.

﴿إيمانُهُمْ﴾ is in the nominative, either as the subject of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (its noun), or as the agent of ﴿يَنْفَعُهُمْ﴾.

The pronoun in (yakun) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), following the disagreement concerning *kāna yaqūmu Zaydun*. The negative particle entered upon the existence (al-kawn), not upon the negation, because it leads to the negation of validity, meaning it was not valid and was not right, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

As for the succession of these fā' particles: in ﴿So it did not avail﴾, it is because it was the consequence of His saying: "They were more numerous than them, and when their messengers came to them," and it functions as explanation and elaboration of His saying: ﴿so it did not avail them﴾. And ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ follows His saying: ﴿when there came to them﴾, as if He said: they disbelieved in it, then when they saw Our punishment they believed, but their faith did not benefit them when they saw the punishment of God. The word ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, meaning: what was done to them is ﴿the way of God﴾ which has passed and has been established among His servants, concerning the sending of messengers and their honouring (al-i'zāz), the punishment of those who denied them, their humiliation of them, their uprooting by destruction, and the non-benefit of faith at the time when the punishment has overtaken them.

There is also a place adverb (ẓarf makān) used for time, meaning: and the disbelievers lost at that time.

It has also been said: ﴿sunnata﴾ is in the accusative by way of warning, meaning: beware of the way of God, O people of Makkah, regarding the sending of messengers.

[p-477] Allah commanded His Prophet to be patient, to comfort him, though he, peace be upon him, was already at the utmost of patience. He informed him that what He had promised him of victory, triumph, the elevation of His word, and the manifestation of His religion is true.

It has been said that the response (jawab) to ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: "then He will comfort your eye." It is not valid for ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ to be the response to both the conditional clause and its coordinated clause, because the structure ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ "some of what We promise them during your lifetime" followed by ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is not apparent. It can, however, be the response to ﴿أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, meaning ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾, so that We take vengeance on them and punish them because they did not follow you.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41] ﴿أوْ نُرِيَنَّكَ الَّذِي وعَدْناهم فَإنّا عَلَيْهِمْ مُقْتَدِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42], except that here the response to both conditions is stated explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فَإلَيْنا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ﴾, and the response to ﴿نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "Then if We show you some of the punishment We promise them, which is their being killed on the day of Badr, then that is so; or if We take you (wafat) before the day of Badr, then to Us they will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, and We will take vengeance on them with the utmost vengeance."

A similar discussion by al-Zamakhshari has already appeared in Surat Yunus in his saying: ﴿وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ بَعْضَ الَّذِي نَعِدُهم أوْ نَتَوَفَّيَنَّكَ فَإلَيْنا مَرْجِعُهُمْ﴾ [Yunus: 46]; we responded to him there, so refer to it there.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: ﴿فَإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ originally was ﴿فَإنْ نُرِكَ﴾, and ma is added (mazidah) to emphasise the meaning of the conditional, and for this reason the nun (of emphasis) is attached to the verb. Do you not see that you do not say: "If you honour me, I will honour you," but rather: "Amma tukrimni ukrimka?" (end of his words).

What he held regarding the obligatory combination of the extra ma and the nun of emphasis after the conditional particle in is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj.

Sibawayh held that if you wish you may use ma without the nun, and if you wish you may use the nun without ma. Sibawayh said in this matter: "And if you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as when you come with (in) you do not bring ma with it, and you do not bring ma with your use of the nun."

[The majority] read ﴿يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a yā' of absence and in the passive voice. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the yā'. Talha ibn Musarrif, and Ya'qub in the narration of al-Walid ibn Hassan, read it with a fatha on the tā' of address.

Then Allah answered the Arabs in their denial of the sending of messengers. There is disagreement about the number of the messengers.

It is narrated that they were eight thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from others. It is also narrated: Allah sent four thousand prophets.

﴿مِنهم مَن قَصَصْنا عَلَيْكَ﴾, that is: those about whom We informed you. As for the Qur'an, (they are) eighteen.

﴿ومِنهم مَن لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾. It is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that Allah sent a black prophet to the Abyssinians, and he is among those whom We did not relate to you.

﴿وما كانَ لِرَسُولٍ أنْ يَأْتِيَ بِآيَةٍ إلّا بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: this is not up to them. When they proposed (signs) to the messengers, he said: "That is not up to me; no sign comes except by the permission of Allah."

﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾: a rejection and a warning following their demand for signs. "The command of Allah" is the Resurrection.

﴿المُبْطِلُونَ﴾ are the obstinate ones who propose signs, though the signs had come to them; they denied them and called them magic. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, that is: when He wished to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decided that and executed it ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾, and every person of falsehood lost and incurred the corruption of his Hereafter. Or: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the killing at Badr.

﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنها﴾: these are the camels, since riding other than them is not customary.

﴿ومِنها تَأْكُلُونَ﴾: general for the eight pairs. The first (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the second (min) is for explaining the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because the camel is eaten from among them, (end of his words). It does not appear that it is for explaining the kind; it may be partitive and also for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Since riding from them is the greater benefit, as it contains the benefit of both eating and riding.

He also mentioned that in all of them there are benefits, such as drinking milk, making garments and other things. Since ﴿الفُلْكِ﴾ (ships) may correctly be said of it "he carried in the ship" (hamala fi al-fulk), as in His saying ﴿احْمِلْ فِيها﴾ [Hud: 40], and it may also correctly be said "he carried upon the ship" (hamala 'ala al-fulk), the particle ʿalā was taken into account to match His saying ﴿وعَلَيْها﴾, although fi is also correct.

﴿ويُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾, that is: His proofs and evidences of His oneness.

﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تُنْكِرُونَ﴾, that is: they are many, so which of them do you deny? That is: it is not possible to deny any of them by reason. ﴿فَأيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿تُنْكِرُونَ﴾.
